title: BlackCat Ransomware & Triple Extortion (Analysis & Tactics)
preprocessed: Since its discovery in November 2021, the ALPHV group has operated the BlackCat ransomware-as-a-service platform—recruiting affiliates from BlackMatter, REvil and DarkSide with revenue shares up to 90%—and deployed sophisticated triple-extortion schemes that combine data theft, encryption of Linux and Windows systems, public data leaks on a Tor-hosted site active since December 2021, and DDoS attacks if ransoms ($400K-$3M, negotiable; +15% for Bitcoin) go unpaid; coded in Rust and compiled for multiple OS architectures, BlackCat uses the --access-token flag to thwart sandbox analysis, kills security and backup processes (e.g., sql*, oracle, msaccess, synctime), excludes critical folders and files (e.g., Windows, System Volume Information, AppData, ntuser.dat, thumbs.db), and supports customizable payloads that resist reverse engineering—enabling strikes on over twenty organizations across U.S. critical infrastructure, retail, transport, telecom and pharma, including Colonial Pipeline, German fuel terminals and Belgian energy firms—and signaling a shift toward more secure, high-performance ransomware that demands enhanced backup validation, network segmentation, process monitoring and proactive threat hunting to mitigate.

title: Flash Notice: Two Microsoft Zero-Day Vulnerabilities Exploited by Attackers
preprocessed: Microsoft’s August 2023 Patch Tuesday addressed two actively exploited zero-days—CVE-2023-36884, a remote code execution flaw in Microsoft Office that bypasses the Mark of the Web, and CVE-2023-38180, a .NET/Visual Studio vulnerability enabling DDoS attacks without requiring user privileges—after one was publicly disclosed pre-patch. The Russian actor Storm-0978 (aka RomCom/Underground), noted for Industrial Spy ransomware, leveraged crafted Office documents to execute payloads and extort victims, while CVE-2023-38180 attacks demand only network proximity. To mitigate these threats, Microsoft released an Office Defense-in-Depth update and a .NET/Visual Studio patch and recommends deploying both Office and Windows August updates, enabling cloud-delivered protection in Defender Antivirus, activating EDR block mode, enforcing attack surface reduction rules to block Office-spawned child processes, and applying the advisory’s update for CVE-2023-38180. Avertium validates these controls, provides IoCs for RomCom campaigns, and advocates continuous vulnerability management and its Fusion MXDR for Microsoft service to detect suspicious Office-to-script execution chains and remediate artifacts proactively.

title: Everything You Need to Know About Silent Skimming
preprocessed: BlackBerry researchers have identified “Silent Skimming,” a year-long, financially motivated campaign by a Chinese-language proficient threat actor that exploits a .NET deserialization flaw (CVE-2019-18935) in Progress Telerik UI for ASP.NET AJAX to remotely deploy malicious DLLs on internet-facing payment and POS servers across APAC, North America and Latin America. Following initial access, the actor leverages a suite of post-exploitation tools—BadPotato, Godzilla Webshell, Juicy Potato, SweetPotato, PowerShell RATs (server.ps1), HTML HTA downloaders and Cobalt Strike beacons—hosted on attacker-controlled HTTP file servers to escalate privileges, execute code, establish C2 via Cloudflare and exfiltrate billing and credit-card data. Attribution is supported by Simplified Chinese code, C2 infrastructure in Japan and region-specific VPS deployments, while intelligence links similar tactics to BlackSuit and Zeon groups. To mitigate risk, organizations should urgently patch Telerik components, monitor for anomalous DLL or webshell activity, enforce PCI DSS Requirement 6.5 for third-party applications, implement rigorous Governance, Risk and Compliance frameworks, and continuously assess payment-processing systems for insecure deserialization and unauthorized data flows.

title: An Update on Akira Ransomware
preprocessed: Since emerging in March 2023 and first profiled by Avertium in spring 2023, the Akira ransomware group has extorted an estimated $42 million from over 250 small and mid-sized organizations across North America, Europe and Australia, initially targeting firms like a UK architecture practice, a U.S. IT services provider and a European pharmaceutical company with ransom demands of $50,000–$500,000, before expanding beyond Windows to deploy a Linux/VMware ESXi variant; using phishing, exploitation of unpatched software and RDP brute-force for initial access, Akira actors exfiltrate data via FileZilla, WinRAR, WinSCP and RClone, establish persistence through domain controller abuse (notably creating an “itadm” account), harvest credentials via Kerberoasting, Mimikatz and LaZagne, conduct reconnaissance with SoftPerfect and Advanced IP Scanner, disable security software with PowerTool, then execute double-extortion by encrypting files with .akira (C++ Akira) or .powerranges/.akiranew (Rust-based Megazord/Akira_v2) using hybrid ChaCha20/RSA and deleting shadow copies; a March 2024 FBI/CISA/Europol/ NCSC-NL advisory underscores the need for organizations to enforce timely patching, multifactor authentication, network segmentation, RDP restrictions, robust backup strategies and vigilant monitoring for anomalous account activity and exfiltration channels to thwart Akira’s evolving tactics.

title: New Ransomware Strains - CACTUS and 3AM
preprocessed: In early 2023, ransomware postings dropped 41% month-on-month yet LockBit stayed dominant, and despite predictions of waning ROI, Q3 saw a surge—driven by CL0P’s mass exploits of file-transfer flaws—that surpassed the combined victim counts of 2021–22 and hit law firms, government, manufacturing, oil & gas, and logistics hardest. In Q4 two new strains surfaced: CACTUS, first observed by Kroll in March 2023, leverages critical Qlik Sense vulnerabilities (CVE-2023-41266, ‑41265, ‑48365) or VPN appliance flaws for initial access; embeds a decryption key in ntuser.dat via scheduled tasks; uses SoftPerfect Network Scanner, PowerShell, Cobalt Strike, Splashtop, AnyDesk and Chisel for reconnaissance, persistence and lateral movement; exfiltrates data over Tox and Rclone; and encrypts files with AES/OpenSSL (.cts1 extension) accompanied by cAcTuS.readme.txt demands. When a LockBit affiliate’s deployment failed, they defaulted to 3AM, a new Rust-based backup encryptor that halts services, deletes VSS snapshots, appends .threeamtime and a “0x666” marker, exfiltrates via Wput to FTP, and issues Tor-based ransom negotiations. To counter these evolving threats, organizations must patch VPN and Qlik Sense flaws, enforce least-privilege RDP with MFA, restrict unauthorized remote access tools, monitor for anomalous scheduled tasks, scanner and Tox/Rclone traffic, deploy EDR to flag Cobalt Strike and script-based execution, and maintain secure, offline backups.

title: An In-Depth Look at APT35 aka Charming Kitten
preprocessed: Since its emergence in 2013, Iran-linked APT35 (aka Charming Kitten/Phosphorus) has executed a series of high-value espionage campaigns—beginning with a 2014 social-media spying operation—and continued in 2019 with spear-phishing against U.S., French and Middle East academic institutions before Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit seized control of 99 APT35 domains; in late 2020 the group targeted oncology, genetics and neurology researchers in Israel and the U.S. via its “BadBlood” PDF-based spear-phishing campaign, while in 2021 it chained Exchange Server flaws (ProxyShell) for network intrusion and demonstrated TTP overlaps with Momento ransomware (CVE-2021-21972 exploiter); in January 2022 it performed mass Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) scans—over 80 percent of attempts originated in the U.S.—and later deployed a stealthy .NET-based PowerShell backdoor (“PowerLess”) that runs in-process to avoid detection, followed by Hyperscrape, a Windows .NET mailbox exfiltration tool for Outlook, Gmail and Yahoo! that quietly harvests emails once the actor possesses valid credentials or session cookies, and a companion Telegram dump utility; APT35 maintains persistence for intelligence collection or monetizes access when systems lack strategic value, underscoring the need for timely patching, multi-factor authentication and continuous monitoring.

title: An In-Depth Look at Cuba Ransomware
preprocessed: Cuba ransomware, first observed in late 2019 but only drawing widespread attention in November 2021 after infiltrating at least 49 organizations across government, healthcare, IT, manufacturing and finance, has since expanded its scope to compromise 101 victims globally (65 in the U.S., 36 abroad), demanded over $145 million in ransoms and collected more than $60 million. Operators gain initial access via Hancitor‐delivered loaders, phishing emails spoofing entities like Ukraine’s armed forces press service, unpatched Microsoft Exchange SSRF vulnerabilities (CVE-2022-41080/41040), compromised credentials and legitimate RDP, then deploy Cobalt Strike beacons via PowerShell and PsExec to execute memory‐injected payloads (“pones.exe,” “krots.exe”/KPOT), use Mimikatz for credential theft, and abuse Windows services to encrypt files with a “.cuba” extension. From 2022, affiliates such as “Tropical Scorpius” have employed the RomCom RAT (rmtpak.dll) for data exfiltration, industrial Spy ransomware tie-ins, and a kernel‐mode dropper (ApcHelper.sys, signed with a LAPSUS-stolen NVIDIA certificate) to terminate security tools, while adopting double-extortion by threatening public release of stolen data. High-impact incidents include attacks on Chilean government VMware and Microsoft ESXi servers, unpatched Microsoft Exchange environments, and The Philadelphia Inquirer in May 2023, which disrupted newspaper distribution and business operations. To counter this evolving threat, organizations should promptly apply Exchange and software patches, enforce multifactor authentication on RDP, restrict PowerShell/PsExec use, deploy EDR to detect Cobalt Strike and memory injection, monitor for malicious driver loads, and implement FBI/CISA mitigation guidelines.

title: Everything You Need to Know About the APT, Fancy Bear
preprocessed: Since its emergence in 2008, Russian GRU-linked APT Fancy Bear (aka APT28, Sofacy, Swallowtail) has advanced from low-key credential harvesting via spear-phishing emails and spoofed domains to high-impact operations, notably the 2016 DNC and WADA breaches—in which fake webmail domains tricked victims into password resets, enabling network infiltration, malware deployment and public data leaks. After a covert phase (2017–early 2022) targeting energy, government, media, aerospace and defense sectors, Fancy Bear reemerged in July 2022 exploiting Microsoft Office zero-day CVE-2022-30190 (“Follina”) via malicious RTF template injection, remote HTML retrieval and ms-msdt URI calls to execute PowerShell and load a .NET credential stealer that exfiltrates usernames, passwords and URLs from Edge and Chrome browsers in Ukrainian targets. The group maintains persistence with reconnaissance Trojans (Sofacy/Seduploader), X-Agent backdoors, .NET Shunnael encrypted tunnels and a Lojax UEFI rootkit for firmware-level access, typically delivered through visually deceptive domains. These activities underscore the urgent need for proactive Web Application Firewalls, real-time inbound/outbound traffic monitoring, rigorous patch management (including zero-day workarounds), and well-rehearsed incident response plans to detect and mitigate APT28’s evolving espionage and disruptive tactics.

title: Flash Notice: FARGO Ransomware Attacking Microsoft SQL Servers
preprocessed: FARGO ransomware (aka Mallox/TargetCompany) is actively targeting unpatched Microsoft SQL servers, with threat actors evolving from deploying Cobalt Strike beacons in February 2022 to hijacking vulnerable instances for proxy bandwidth by July 2022 and now encrypting databases and extorting owners. The infection chain begins with cmd.exe and PowerShell scripts to download a malicious .NET loader, followed by retrieval of additional malware, execution of a batch script to terminate critical services, disable recovery features, and kill related processes before encrypting files with a “.Fargo3” extension and dropping a “RECOVERY FILES.txt” ransom note demanding Bitcoin payment. These attacks leverage brute‐force login attempts against weak credentials or exploit known SQL vulnerabilities, threatening non‐payers with public data exposure via Telegram. To mitigate this risk, organizations should enforce robust password policies, apply the latest SQL patches, monitor login anomalies, and deploy threat detection for IOCs such as specific MD5, SHA‐1, SHA‐256, vhash, and imphash signatures to prevent severe disruption to business‐critical services.

title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview
preprocessed: A zero-day VPN vulnerability provided initial access for a sophisticated threat actor who employed publicly available penetration‐testing and exploitation tools—SoftPerfect Network Scanner for network discovery, PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the FiveHands ransomware variant using lattice-based NTRUEncrypt public key cryptography), and SombRAT for remote information theft—alongside RouterScan, grabff.exe, rclone.exe, and s3browser-9-5-3.exe to harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Once inside, the attacker leveraged Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) to enumerate and delete Volume Shadow Copies (Inhibit System Recovery, T1490), encrypted files (including those in recovery folders) for impact (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories, demanding payment to restore access. Post-encryption activities align with MITRE techniques such as Access Token Manipulation, Boot or Logon Autostart, PowerShell command and scripting interpreter, Domain Trust Discovery, Process Discovery, Screen Capture, and Kerberoasting. The combined use of FiveHands ransomware and SombRAT RAT resulted in both data theft and destruction of backup artifacts, underscoring the need for proactive patch management, network segmentation, strict credential hygiene, and rapid incident response to mitigate novel lattice-based encryption threats.

title: New Ransomware Strains - CryptNet, Mallox, and Xollam
preprocessed: After hitting a post-2019 low of 51.2 million incidents in Q1 2023, ransomware attacks surged 74% to 88.9 million in Q2 and generated $176 million more H1 revenue than in 2022, driven by new RaaS strains CryptNet, Mallox and Xollam: CryptNet, active since April 2023, leverages obfuscated .NET code derived from Chaos/Yashma with enhanced encryption speed, disables shadow copies and backup services, employs a 90%-affiliate revenue share, exfiltrates data, and uses a Tor-based chat negotiation portal and leak site; Mallox, first seen in June 2021, ramped up affiliate recruitment in early 2023, exploits MS-SQL vulnerabilities CVE-2020-0618 and CVE-2019-1068 plus brute-force and phishing, uses PowerShell to fetch payloads, deletes shadow copies and logs, and practices double-extortion; and Xollam, a February 2023 offshoot of the TargetCompany/Mallox family, shifts from MS-SQL exploitation to OneNote phishing and pseudo-fileless PowerShell reflective loading. These evolving tactics underscore the need for timely patching of SQL servers, shadow-copy monitoring, EDR capable of detecting obfuscated .NET and fileless techniques, strict network segmentation and ongoing user education to counter the rising multi-vector ransomware threat.

title: An In-Depth Look at Iranian APT "MuddyWater"
preprocessed: In February 2022, CISA, the FBI, US Cyber Command CNMF, NCSC-UK and NSA issued a joint advisory on Iranian Ministry of Intelligence–linked APT MuddyWater (aka MERCURY, Earth Vetala, Static Kitten, Seedworm, TEMP.Zagros), active since 2018 and focused on cyber espionage, intellectual property theft and ransomware against defense, oil & gas, government and telecom sectors across Asia, Africa, Europe and North America. Exploiting publicly disclosed vulnerabilities and open-source tools, MuddyWater delivers malicious PDFs with embedded links that display error messages prompting users to download Excel maldocs or Windows executables; these files host VBA macros that drop WSF scripts to execute PowerShell and VB payloads, leverage LoLBins, and stage RATs and malware families including PowGoop, Canopy, Small Sieve, POWERSTATS and Mori while communicating with C2 over HTTP and DNS and persisting via Registry Run keys. Cisco Talos observed regional campaigns in Turkey (Nov 2021), Pakistan (Aug 2021) and Armenia (Jun 2021) using decoy documents, signaling tokens and a consistent TTP set, suggesting a conglomerate of subgroups migrating techniques across regions. The resultant network access and data exfiltration underscore the imperative for proactive DFIR readiness, deployment of XDR/MDR platforms, rigorous vulnerability management, macro execution restrictions, PowerShell/LoLBin monitoring and ongoing user awareness training reinforced by incident response tabletop exercises.

title: Ragnar Locker Ransomware (Everything You Need To Know)
preprocessed: Ragnar Locker, active since December 2019 and first flagged by the FBI in April 2020, is a hybrid ransomware strain and operator gang responsible for breaching 52 organizations across 10 critical infrastructure sectors—including energy, manufacturing, financial services, government, IT and agriculture—employing double-extortion by exfiltrating sensitive data before encryption and threatening public leaks if ransoms go unpaid. Intrusions begin with RDP access via brute-force or stolen credentials, privilege escalation through CVE-2017-0213, and deployment of a VirtualBox VM running Windows XP to execute encryption, thereby evading host defenses; they delete shadow copies, disable antivirus (e.g., Sophos, Veeam) and remote management tools (Kaseya, ConnectWise), and spread laterally via PowerShell. Obfuscation is achieved through junk code, encrypted PE-embedded configs (".keys"), runtime string decryption, locale checks to avoid CIS targets and a custom Salsa20 cipher with a bespoke 64-byte key matrix appending “_RAGNAR_” to footers. Major attacks include Campari Group (2 TB, $15 M), Energias de Portugal (10 TB, 1 580 BTC), Capcom (1 TB) and Dassault Falcon Jet, with the FBI warning of heightened risks to food/agriculture during planting/harvest. Ragnar Locker pressures victims to avoid law enforcement, yet paying ransoms funds criminality and fails to guarantee data deletion; mitigation requires hardened RDP/MFA, patching CVE-2017-0213, network segmentation, behavioral EDR, offline backups and timely incident reporting to the FBI.

title: An In-Depth Look at Rhysida Ransomware
preprocessed: Since its emergence in May 2023, the Rhysida ransomware operation—self-styled as a “cybersecurity team” and symbolized by a centipede-inspired logo—has rapidly escalated from targeting education and government (notably the Chilean Army breach and document leak) to striking healthcare, most catastrophically Prospect Medical Holdings (disrupting 17 hospitals and 166 clinics, halting ERs and diverting ambulances), prompting an HHS HC3 sector alert; analysis by Check Point, SentinelOne and Trend Micro links Rhysida’s decline of Vice Society activity and shared TTPs—phishing-based initial access, Cobalt Strike for Lateral Movement, PsExec to deploy the g.ps1 PowerShell Trojan (killing AV, erasing shadow copies, altering RDP and AD credentials) and evolving into a full PowerShell-based payload—followed by file encryption using 4096-bit RSA, AES-CTR and ChaCha20, .rhysida file extension and a PDF ransom note (“CriticalBreachDetected.pdf”) demanding Bitcoin in a TOR-accessed portal; the group’s multi-extortion model, PDF-based notes, unreliable desktop-background changes and global detections (US, Germany, Indonesia) underscore the urgency for layered defenses—rigorous phishing prevention, EDR/memory-based detection, least-privilege access, regular patching of RDP and AD, shadow-copy protection and network segmentation—to detect early intrusion behaviors, block lateral spread and mitigate impact.

title: Everything You Need to Know About Royal Ransomware
preprocessed: Emerging January 2022 and initially attributed to Microsoft’s DEV-0569, the Royal ransomware gang—comprising vetted operators rather than affiliates—has rebranded itself in Tor-hosted README.TXT notes and leaked exfiltrated data via victim-specific negotiation pages, employing malvertising (including Google Ads through the Keitaro TDS), phishing (callback lures impersonating software or food delivery), malicious attachments, and forum/blog links to deliver signed BATLOADER payloads that leverage MSI Custom Actions, Nsudo and PowerShell/batch scripts to disable security controls and install remote-access tools (notably Zoho), then deploy either BlackCat’s encryptor or their own Zeon encryptor with a .Royal extension; since intensifying operations in September 2022, they’ve struck high-profile victims such as Silverstone Circuit and Travis Central Appraisal District, exfiltrating data and demanding $250K–$2M, prompting HC3, CISA and FBI alerts—particularly for healthcare—while continuously innovating defense-evasion and post-compromise techniques; organizations should proactively monitor IOCs, enforce MFA, patch systems, segment networks, restrict macros, audit remote-access deployments and maintain offline backups to mitigate this financially driven threat.

title: An In-Depth Look at Quantum Ransomware
preprocessed: In mid-2022 Sophos reported that 66% of healthcare organizations were hit by ransomware—a 94% year-over-year increase—underscoring the continued success of the RaaS model and the emergence of Quantum ransomware, a splinter group from Conti (originally Quantum Locker, AstroLocker, MountLocker and XingLocker) officially taken over by Conti Team Two in April 2022; since June 2022 Quantum has deployed its BazarCall variant “Jormungandr,” leveraging OSINT, spamming, design and call-center specialists to execute callback phishing that tricks victims into installing legitimate remote-access tools, while DFIR reports show initial access via IcedID payloads embedded in mountable ISO files and malicious LNK shortcuts, leading to hands-on-keyboard activity within two hours, rapid Cobalt Strike and RDP lateral movement, WMI and PsExec to push the ttsel.exe ransomware payload, encryption and exfiltration, and the dropping of README_TO_DECRYPT.html notes with demands ranging from $150K to $500K; Quantum’s brand-impersonation phishing campaigns (masquerading as Oracle, CrowdStrike and others) have compromised a New Jersey behavioral‐health system, Interim Healthcare, a biopharmaceutical research firm and an IVF clinic in Delhi, exposing high-value patient data and demonstrating the urgent need for proactive defenses—including call-back phishing awareness, tight remote-access policies, IcedID and Cobalt Strike detection, LSASS memory monitoring and rapid incident response—to thwart these fast, socially engineered RaaS attacks.

title: An In-Depth Look at Yanluowang Ransomware
preprocessed: Since at least August 2021, the Yanluowang ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation has targeted U.S. financial firms and other sectors—including manufacturing, IT services, consultancy, and engineering—using a toolkit and playbook that mirror veteran groups Thieflock and Fivehands and suggesting possible affiliate ties; Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team first observed an underdeveloped October 2021 deployment in which attackers used AdFind for Active Directory reconnaissance, then refined their approach with PowerShell-driven BazarLoader implants, registry-based RDP enablement, ConnectWise for persistent access, and SoftPerfect Network Scanner for lateral movement, followed by credential theft via KeeThief, custom secretdump.exe, and deployment of Cobalt Strike Beacon, culminating in file encryption and double-extortion ransom notes threatening DDoS, employee calls, repeated attacks, and data deletion if law enforcement or negotiation firms are engaged; this operation contributes to the $590 million in ransomware payments recorded in 2021 and 314 global double-extortion incidents in October alone, underscoring the need for hardened Active Directory security, RDP restrictions, EDR with credential-dump detection, network monitoring for AdFind and BazarLoader activity, and adherence to FBI/CISA incident response recommendations.

title: BadPilot network hacking campaign fuels Russian SandWorm attacks
preprocessed: Since 2021, BadPilot—a subgroup of Russia’s state-sponsored APT44 (also known as Seashell Blizzard/Sandworm)—has executed a multi-year campaign to compromise critical energy, oil & gas, telecom, shipping, arms manufacturing, government, military, transportation and logistics networks across Ukraine, Europe, Central/South Asia and the Middle East, intensifying after Russia’s 2022 invasion with intelligence gathering, operational disruption and at least three wiper-style destructive attacks in Ukraine; by 2023 its scope expanded to large-scale compromises across Europe, the United States and the Middle East, and in 2024 it added the UK, Canada and Australia. The actor exploits n-day vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-34473, CVE-2022-41352, CVE-2023-32315, CVE-2023-42793, CVE-2023-23397, CVE-2024-1709, CVE-2023-48788), conducts credential theft and supply-chain attacks via regionally managed IT service providers, deploys LocalOlive web shells and uses legitimate management tools (Atera Agent, Splashtop) for initial access and persistence; post-compromise, it harvests credentials with Procdump and registry modifications, exfiltrates data via Rclone, Chisel and Plink over covert Tor-routed tunnels, and performs lateral movement through DNS reconfiguration, new services, scheduled tasks and OpenSSH backdoors. Microsoft warns the subgroup’s near-global reach and horizontal scaling capabilities, and has published hunting queries, IoCs and YARA rules to enable defenders to detect and disrupt its operations.

title: New wave of ‘fake interviews’ use 35 npm packages to spread malware
preprocessed: Socket Threat Research has identified a new DPRK “Contagious Interview” campaign deploying 35 malicious npm packages—typosquatting trusted libraries such as react-plaid-sdk, vite-plugin-next-refresh and framer-motion-ext—submitted across 24 accounts and downloaded over 4,000 times (six still active). North Korean operatives pose as recruiters on LinkedIn, lure developers into running test assignments hosted on Google Docs or Bitbucket outside container environments during screen-sharing, and hide a HexEval loader that fingerprints hosts and uses eval() to fetch BeaverTail, which exfiltrates browser cookies and crypto-wallets before dropping InvisibleFerret, a persistent cross-platform backdoor enabling remote control, file theft and screenshots; a selective low-level keylogger is deployed on high-value targets. Mirroring a March Lazarus npm incident, this campaign underscores the need for rigorous code vetting, containerized execution and enhanced monitoring of npm dependencies.

title: Qantas discloses cyberattack amid Scattered Spider aviation breaches
preprocessed: On Monday Qantas detected unusual activity on a third-party call-centre customer-service platform used by six million customers and immediately contained the system, confirming that a “significant” volume of data—names, email addresses, phone numbers, birth dates and frequent flyer numbers—was likely stolen while credit card and personal financial data, as well as passwords, PINs and login details, remained secure; the airline, which operates globally across six continents, has notified the Australian Cyber Security Centre, the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner and the Australian Federal Police and reports all Qantas systems are currently secure. Although attribution remains unconfirmed, the breach shares hallmarks of the Scattered Spider threat group (aka 0ktapus, UNC3944, Scatter Swine, Starfraud, Muddled Libra), known for social-engineering and identity-based attacks—including phishing, SIM swapping, MFA bombing and help-desk phone calls—and recent pivots to aviation targets such as Hawaiian Airlines and WestJet (which was breached via a self-service password reset exploit). To defend against these tactics, organizations should gain complete visibility across infrastructure and identity systems and harden self-service password reset portals, help desks and third-party identity vendors, leveraging hardening guides published by Google Threat Intelligence Group and Palo Alto Networks.

title: Government webmail hacked via XSS bugs in global spy campaign
preprocessed: Operation RoundPress, attributed with medium confidence to Russian state-sponsored APT28 (Fancy Bear), has since 2023 exploited stored and reflected XSS flaws in widely used webmail platforms—initially leveraging Roundcube CVE-2020-35730 to inject malicious JavaScript into email bodies, then CVE-2023-43770 and additional n-day vulnerabilities in Roundcube, Horde, MDaemon and Zimbra in early 2024—to execute upon email open without clicks or redirects. Through spear-phishing emails crafted with timely political or news excerpts, the hidden script auto-fills victim credentials via invisible input fields, scrapes DOM content—including emails, contacts, webmail settings, login history, 2FA tokens and passwords—and exfiltrates data via HTTP POST to hardcoded C2 servers. Targets span high-value government entities in Greece, Ukraine, Serbia and Cameroon, military units in Ukraine and Ecuador, defense contractors in Ukraine, Bulgaria and Romania, and critical infrastructure in Ukraine and Bulgaria. The lack of persistence mechanisms confines execution to session scope but underscores the necessity for timely patching of XSS vulnerabilities, disabling HTML rendering in webmail clients, enforcing strict input sanitization and multifactor authentication, and monitoring anomalous outbound traffic to mitigate credential theft and data exfiltration.

title: FBI: Androxgh0st malware botnet steals AWS, Microsoft credentials
preprocessed: CISA and the FBI have warned that since its discovery by Lacework Labs in 2022—when FortiGuard Labs observed it controlling over 40,000 devices—threat actors deploying the Python-scripted Androxgh0st malware have been building a botnet to steal AWS, Microsoft Office 365, SendGrid and Twilio credentials by scanning for RCE vulnerabilities CVE-2017-9841 (PHPUnit), CVE-2021-41773 (Apache HTTP Server) and CVE-2018-15133 (Laravel) and harvesting .env files; once inside, operators abuse SMTP, API and web shell functions to test email-sending limits for spam campaigns, create fake pages as backdoors, deploy further tools, and spin up new AWS instances and user policies to expand scans for vulnerable targets. FBI/CISA mitigation guidance urges patching all systems (notably Apache 2.4.49/2.4.50), denying unnecessary URI access, disabling Laravel debug mode, removing and revoking .env credentials, auditing for unauthorized access, scanning for unrecognized PHP (especially under /vendor/phpunit), monitoring outgoing cURL GETs to file hosts, and reporting sightings; CISA has added CVE-2018-15133 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog (joining the earlier additions of CVE-2021-41773 and CVE-2017-9841) and ordered federal agencies to harden systems by February 6.

title: Apple fixes first zero-day bug exploited in attacks this year
preprocessed: In early June 2024, Apple patched its first zero-day exploited this year—CVE-2024-23222—a WebKit confusion flaw allowing arbitrary code execution by processing maliciously crafted web content on vulnerable iOS 16.7.5+, iPadOS 16.7.5+, macOS Monterey 12.7.3+, and tvOS 17.3+ devices, including iPhone 8/X and later, iPad 5th gen and newer, all Macs on Monterey or later, and Apple TV HD/4K; while Apple confirmed in-the-wild use without attributing a researcher or specific threat actor, the targeted exploitation through web-based tactics underlines ongoing attacker focus on browser engines, prompting backports of November’s CVE-2023-42916/42917 WebKit patches to older models and reflecting a 2023 pattern of 20 zero-days leveraged for remote code execution, thereby emphasizing the urgent need for organizations and users to apply updates immediately to prevent device takeover.

title: Hackers start exploiting critical Atlassian Confluence RCE flaw
preprocessed: Since Atlassian’s disclosure last week of CVE-2023-22527—a critical unauthenticated template-injection RCE affecting Confluence Server and Data Center versions 8.0.x–8.5.3—Shadowserver has logged over 39,000 exploitation attempts from more than 600 unique IPs (predominantly Russian) executing callbacks such as “whoami” to assess privilege levels, while its scanners identify roughly 11,100 internet-accessible Confluence instances (not all vulnerable). No specific IoCs have been released by Atlassian, leaving organizations to assume potential compromise if running pre-December 5, 2023 releases. Patches are available in Confluence 8.5.4 (LTS), 8.6.0 (Data Center), and 8.7.1 (Data Center), and administrators are urged to upgrade immediately, treat outdated instances as compromised, perform comprehensive forensics and cleanup, and bolster defenses against both state-sponsored threat actors and opportunistic ransomware groups.

title: Google fixes first actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2024
preprocessed: Google released emergency patches for Chrome’s Stable Desktop channel less than a week after researchers reported CVE-2024-0519, a high-severity out-of-bounds memory access flaw in the V8 JavaScript engine that remote attackers can trigger via a crafted HTML page to corrupt the heap, read sensitive data beyond buffer limits, crash the browser or bypass ASLR en route to code execution; updated versions 120.0.6099.224/225 (Windows), 120.0.6099.234 (macOS) and 120.0.6099.224 (Linux) are rolling out globally, with auto-updates or manual checks ensuring broad coverage, while Google retains exploit details until most users are protected. In parallel, two additional V8 vulnerabilities—CVE-2024-0517 (out-of-bounds write) and CVE-2024-0518 (type confusion)—were fixed to close arbitrary code execution paths. Though specific threat actors remain unnamed, active in-the-wild exploitation has been confirmed, echoing last year’s eight Chrome zero-days used to deploy spyware against high-risk targets like journalists and dissidents. Organizations should immediately verify Chrome version levels, enforce prompt patching and strengthen endpoint defenses to mitigate ongoing browser-based intrusions.

title: Citrix warns of new Netscaler zero-days exploited in attacks
preprocessed: Citrix on Tuesday issued an urgent advisory to patch customer-managed NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances against two actively exploited zero-days (CVE-2023-6548 enabling remote code execution with a logged-in low-privilege account via NSIP/CLIP/SNIP management interfaces and CVE-2023-6549 causing denial-of-service on VPN virtual servers or AAA virtual servers), affecting NetScaler ADC/Gateway 14.1 before 14.1-12.35, 13.1 before 13.1-51.15, 13.0 before 13.0-92.21, 13.1-FIPS before 13.1-37.176, and 12.1-FIPS/NDcPP before 12.1-55.302, with Shadowserver reporting over 1,500 exposed management interfaces worldwide; exploits have already been observed, prompting Citrix and the HHS HC3 to urge immediate installation of patched versions or, for those unable to update, logical or physical segregation of management interfaces, network traffic blocking, removal of internet exposure, and upgrade off end-of-life 12.1 releases to thwart potential ransomware and intrusion campaigns—an alert amplified by the October patch of a prior critical Netscaler flaw (CVE-2023-4966 “Citrix Bleed”) that threat actors have leveraged since August against government agencies and high-profile tech firms such as Boeing.

title: Fortra warns of new critical GoAnywhere MFT auth bypass, patch now
preprocessed: Fortra has disclosed CVE-2024-0204, a critical (CVSS 9.8) authentication-bypass flaw in GoAnywhere MFT versions 6.0.1–7.4.0 that enables remote attackers to create arbitrary admin users via the web administration portal, potentially leading to full device takeover, data theft, malware deployment, and lateral movement; discovered December 1, 2023 by Mohammed Eldeeb and Islam Elrfai of Spark Engineering Consultants, it was patched in GoAnywhere MFT 7.4.1 on December 7 2023, and users unable to upgrade immediately can mitigate by deleting or emptying the InitialAccountSetup.xhtml file and restarting services. Although no in-the-wild exploitation has been observed, the publication of mitigations may spur PoC releases. This advisory follows January–February 2023 Clop ransomware attacks leveraging the unpatched CVE-2023-0669 remote-code-execution flaw to breach 130 organizations—including Crown Resorts, CHS, Hatch Bank, Rubrik, City of Toronto, Hitachi Energy, Procter & Gamble, and Saks Fifth Avenue—underscoring the critical need for timely patching and monitoring of MFT environments.

title: GitHub rotates keys to mitigate impact of credential-exposing flaw
preprocessed: On December 26, 2023, GitHub’s Bug Bounty Program flagged an unsafe reflection flaw (CVE-2024-0200) in GitHub.com that—if chained with an organization owner’s authentication—could expose environment-variable credentials in production containers and enable remote code execution; GitHub patched the same day, rotated all potentially exposed keys out of caution (assessed at high confidence as never exploited), and in March updated its public SSH and secrets-scanning processes. On the following Tuesday, GitHub released Enterprise Server fixes (GHES 3.8.13, 3.9.8, 3.10.5, 3.11.3) that also remediate a second high-severity command-injection bug (CVE-2024-0507) exploitable by Management Console users with editor rights to escalate privileges. While most customers need no action, those using the commit-signing, Actions, Codespaces or Dependabot encryption keys must import new public keys, and GitHub strongly recommends routinely pulling keys via the API. Previous key and certificate rotations—in March for an accidentally exposed private SSH key and late 2022 for stolen Desktop/Atom code-signing certificates—underscore the company’s proactive secrets-management and incident-response posture.

title: Over 5,300 GitLab servers exposed to zero-click account takeover attacks
preprocessed: On January 11, 2024, GitLab released patches for CVE-2023-7028—a critical (CVSS 10.0) zero-click account-takeover flaw in Community and Enterprise Edition versions 16.1–16.7—that lets attackers send password reset emails to an adversary-controlled address and hijack any account lacking two-factor authentication; 13 days post-disclosure, ShadowServer reported 5,379 internet-exposed instances (964 in the US, 730 in Germany, 721 in Russia, 503 in China, 298 in France, 122 in the UK, 117 in India and 99 in Canada) still vulnerable, placing them at risk of supply-chain compromise, proprietary code and API-key exfiltration, and other malicious activities. Defenders should inspect gitlab-rails/production_json.log for `/users/password` requests with JSON arrays of multiple emails and gitlab-rails/audit_json.log for `PasswordsController#create` entries, apply the fixes in 16.7.2, 16.6.4 and 16.5.6 (or backports 16.1.6, 16.2.9, 16.3.7), enforce 2FA, rotate all credentials, API tokens, certificates and other secrets, and review source code and environment configurations per GitLab’s incident-response guide, since unpatched servers may already be compromised despite no confirmed active exploitation to date.

title: Exploit released for Fortra GoAnywhere MFT auth bypass bug
preprocessed: On December 4 Fortra issued a private advisory on CVE-2024-0204, a critical authentication bypass in its GoAnywhere MFT 7.x, and silently patched it on December 7 in version 7.4.1 but only publicly disclosed the flaw today; now Horizon3’s Attack Team has released a proof-of-concept exploit that leverages a path traversal vulnerability to access the /InitialAccountSetup.xhtml endpoint and create unauthorized administrator accounts on unpatched instances, prompting defenders to immediately upgrade or delete/replace the InitialAccountSetup.xhtml file, restart services, and monitor the GoAnywhere “Admin Users” list for new entries. While Fortra reports no confirmed exploits in the wild, the public PoC is expected to trigger widespread scanning and compromises, echoing Clop’s January 2023 campaign that abused a GoAnywhere RCE (CVE-2023-0669) to breach over 100 organizations—including Community Health Systems, Procter & Gamble, Rubrik and the City of Toronto—and underscoring a broader pattern of MFT platform assaults seen in the 2020 Accellion FTA, 2021 SolarWinds Serv-U and 2023 MOVEit Transfer incidents.

title: Kasseika ransomware uses antivirus driver to kill other antiviruses
preprocessed: Trend Micro analysts uncovered in December 2023 a new ransomware strain dubbed Kasseika—likely developed by former BlackMatter affiliates or buyers of its source code—that employs a Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) attack by abusing TG Soft’s Martini driver (Martini.sys/viragt64.sys) to disable antivirus and security tools before encryption. Kasseika’s chain begins with credential-harvesting phishing emails for initial access, followed by PsExec-driven execution of malicious .bat scripts that terminate any running Martini.exe, deploy the vulnerable Martini.sys driver (without which the attack halts), and leverage its flaws to kill 991 hard-coded processes. The threat then runs Martini.exe to neutralize defenses, launches its main ransomware binary (smartscreen_protected.exe), encrypts files with ChaCha20 and RSA—appending pseudo-random strings to filenames—drops ransom notes and wallpaper warnings, and erases event logs via wevutil.exe. Victims face a 72-hour deadline to pay 50 BTC (~$2 million) with $500,000 added every 24 hours of delay and must post proof to a private Telegram group within five days; Trend Micro has separately published related IoCs.

title: Mastodon vulnerability allows attackers to take over accounts
preprocessed: Mastodon has addressed a critical origin-validation bypass in CVE-2024-23832 (CVSS 9.4) present in all versions before 3.5.17, 4.0.13, 4.1.13 and 4.2.5 that allowed remote attackers to forge authenticated requests, impersonate any user and fully hijack accounts across its 11,000 federated instances serving nearly 12 million users; the patch, delivered in 4.2.5 released yesterday and highlighted via a prominent admin banner, must be applied by mid-February—users should confirm their instance’s upgrade—while Mastodon withholds full exploit details until February 15 to curb active attacks; this incident echoes the July 2023 TootRoot flaw (CVE-2023-36460), which enabled malicious “toots” to deploy web shells and compromise server integrity, underscoring the urgent need for admins to enforce timely updates, validate federation traffic and monitor for anomalous account activity to prevent reputation damage and data exposure.

title: Russian hackers stole Microsoft corporate emails in month-long breach
preprocessed: In November 2023, Russian state-sponsored group Nobelium (aka Midnight Blizzard/APT29) executed a month-long breach of Microsoft’s corporate email environment by conducting a password-spray brute-force attack against a legacy non-production test tenant lacking multi-factor authentication, enabling pivoting to a small subset of high-value accounts—including leadership, cybersecurity and legal team mailboxes—from which they exfiltrated emails and attachments; discovered on January 12, 2024, the campaign underscores the risk of poorly secured account configurations rather than software vulnerabilities, prompting Microsoft to notify impacted employees, reaffirm its MFA mandate, and reinforce zero-trust controls. This incident, following Nobelium’s SolarWinds and 2021 support-tool intrusions, highlights the necessity of enforcing MFA, minimizing default permissions, and hardening non-prod assets to mitigate advanced persistent threats.

title: PurpleFox malware infects thousands of computers in Ukraine
preprocessed: Ukraine’s CERT-UA has uncovered a January 2024 PurpleFox (aka DirtyMoe) campaign that has infected over 2,000 Windows devices via malicious MSI installers, exploiting known vulnerabilities and brute-forcing credentials to self-propagate; PurpleFox, first spotted in 2018, is a modular botnet with a rootkit for persistence, capable of downloading second-stage payloads, providing backdoor access and acting as a DDoS bot, and since October 2021 has shifted to WebSocket C2 communications and in January 2022 was distributed under the guise of a Telegram desktop app. Using IoCs from Avast and TrendMicro and tracking activity as UAC-0027, CERT-UA identified 486 intermediate control server IPs—mostly in China—by monitoring high (>10000) port connections, registry entries (e.g., HKLM\ControlSet001\Services\AC0[0-9] on XP; HKLM\Software\Microsoft\DirectPlay8\Direct3D on Windows 7), MSIInstaller event IDs 1040/1042, random-named Program Files folders and AppPatch/.sdb files (MsXXXXXXXXApp.dll). To contain the threat, CERT-UA recommends isolating outdated systems via VLAN or physical segmentation, filtering incoming/outgoing traffic, detecting infections with network and registry checks, and removing the malware by running an Avast Free AV “SMART” scan or manually deleting services and rootkit components from a LiveUSB-mounted drive (using lsblk, fdisk, mount with sector offset, rm on AppPatch and System32 modules), then re‐enabling Windows firewall to block SMB and RPC ports (135, 137, 139, 445) to prevent reinfection.

title: AMD, Apple, Qualcomm GPUs leak AI data in LeftoverLocals attacks
preprocessed: Trail of Bits researchers Tyler Sorensen and Heidy Khlaaf disclosed CVE-2023-4969 (“LeftoverLocals”), a GPU memory-isolation flaw in AMD, Apple (M2), Qualcomm and Imagination Technologies devices that lets any adversary running a GPU compute workload (OpenCL, Vulkan, Metal) deploy a “listener” kernel to dump residual local memory left by a legitimate “writer” process, exposing sensitive LLM/ML data—inputs, outputs, weights and intermediates—at rates up to 5.5 MB per invocation (181 MB per query on an AMD Radeon RX 7900 XT with llama.cpp). In multi-tenant cloud or shared GPU environments, attackers can eavesdrop on others’ sessions with high-accuracy model reconstruction. Coordinated disclosure via CERT/CC began September 2023; Imagination issued a fix in DDK v23.3 (Dec 2023), Qualcomm delivered firmware v2.0.7 (partial), Apple patched A17/M3 (M2 remains vulnerable), and AMD/Google are still finalizing mitigations. To eliminate risk, vendors should enforce automatic local memory clearing between kernel calls despite performance trade-offs, and operators should avoid untrusted multi-tenant GPU use or deploy user-level cleansers.

title: Chinese hackers exploit VMware bug as zero-day for two years
preprocessed: In a multi-year espionage campaign uncovered by Mandiant, the Chinese UNC3886 group exploited a critical VMware vCenter Server zero-day (CVE-2023-34048) from late 2021 until its October 2023 patch, triggering vmdird service crashes and removing core dumps to stealthily gain privileged access, then delivering VirtualPita and VirtualPie backdoors via malicious vSphere Installation Bundles on ESXi hosts; they subsequently chained the VMware Tools authentication bypass flaw (CVE-2023-20867) to escalate privileges, harvest and exfiltrate files from guest VMs. UNC3886—targeting defense, government, telecom and technology sectors in the US and APJ—also abused a Fortinet firewall zero-day (CVE-2022-41328) to deploy Castletap and Thincrust implants, demonstrating advanced reverse-engineering of FortiOS. This campaign highlights the urgent need for rapid patching of virtualization and firewall platforms, deployment of EDR solutions and preservation of forensic artifacts to detect and thwart such sophisticated attacks.

title: Ukraine remains Russia’s biggest cyber focus in 2023
preprocessed: In Q1 2023, Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) found that over 60 percent of Russian state-backed phishing campaigns were aimed at Ukraine, led by FROZENBARENTS (aka Sandworm, GRU Unit 74455), which abused globally compromised EXIM mail servers, SMS-delivered phishing links and fake Windows update payloads deploying the Rhadamanthys stealer, then maintained persistence via webshells and Adminer to exfiltrate data to the CyberArmyofRussia_Reborn Telegram channel across government, defense, energy (notably the Caspian Pipeline Consortium), transport, education and humanitarian sectors while conducting information operations. Simultaneously, FROZENLAKE (APT28) leveraged reflected XSS on Ukrainian government sites to redirect users to phishing domains hosted on free services, with harvested credentials sent to compromised Ubiquiti devices; Belarusian PUSHCHA continued targeted low-volume campaigns against regional webmail providers; and IRA-linked actors deployed coordinated YouTube Shorts and Blogger posts to amplify pro-Wagner, anti-Ukrainian narratives. Financially motivated Cuba ransomware affiliates pivoted to intelligence collection using RomCom malware via ChatGPT/OpenAI-spoofed domains against conference attendees. TAG’s takedowns and Safe Browsing protections, coupled with targeted Gmail alerts, underscore the need for organizations to enable Enhanced Safe Browsing, patch mail servers, monitor for unauthorized EXIM access, and guard against reflected XSS and SMS phishing.

title: Initial access broker repurposing techniques in targeted attacks against Ukraine
preprocessed: In April–August 2022, TAG tracked UAC-0098—composed in part of former Conti affiliates—shifting from IcedID banking trojan distribution to an initial access broker role for Conti, Quantum and FIN12/WIZARD SPIDER, targeting Ukrainian government, European humanitarian NGOs and the hospitality sector. The campaign chronology began in late April with phishing lures (“Project Active citizen,” “Mobilization register.xls”) deploying AnchorMail via the newly identified LackeyBuilder SMTP backdoor installer, then progressed through mid-May attacks impersonating Ukraine’s Cyber Police, Starlink and Microsoft using MSI installers hosting IcedID on attacker-controlled domains (gov.uz.ua, starlinkua.info, microsoftua.com), followed by ZIP/XLL payload drops via Stolen Images Evidence and dropfiles.me, and EtterSilent-built Excel documents fetching Cobalt Strike. On June 10 and 19, UAC-0098 weaponized CVE-2022-30190 (“Follina”) in over 10,000 spam emails mimicking the State Tax Service, retrieving Cobalt Strike beacons (ked.dll) from 64.190.113.51:8000. Key indicators include domains blinkin.top, kompromatua.info, IPs 84.32.190.34 and 5.199.173.152, and shared Conti cryptor signatures. These activities highlight the convergence of financial and geopolitical motivations in Eastern Europe, underscoring the need to block listed hashes, domains and exploit vectors while reinforcing email security and vulnerability patching.

title: Internet Explorer 0-day exploited by North Korean actor APT37
preprocessed: In late October 2022, Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) discovered that North Korean government-backed actor APT37 was exploiting a never-before-seen Internet Explorer JScript engine vulnerability (CVE-2022-41128) via malicious Microsoft Office documents themed on the Itaewon Halloween tragedy to achieve arbitrary code execution on Windows hosts; the attack chain began when a user disabled Protected View on a Word document that fetched a remote RTF template hosting HTML rendered through IE, triggering a JIT optimization–induced type-confusion bug in jscript9.dll, which checked for a unique cookie to evade sandboxing, reported to its C2 infrastructure both pre- and post-exploit, and deployed a custom-hashed shellcode that cleared IE cache/history before downloading follow-on payloads; TAG reported the flaw to Microsoft on October 31 and a patch shipped on November 8, and defenders should ensure CVE-2022-41128 is remediated, monitor related IOCs (e.g., word-template[.]net, openxmlformat[.]org) and document hashes, and harden Office macro and remote-template protections against similar APT37 tactics.

title: Russian threat group COLDRIVER expands its targeting of Western officials to include the use of malware
preprocessed: Russian threat group COLDRIVER (UNC4057/Star Blizzard/Callisto), long relied upon for credential phishing against high-value targets in Ukraine, NATO governments, NGOs and academic institutions, has expanded its espionage toolkit since November 2022 by deploying a custom Rust-based backdoor named SPICA via “encrypted” PDF lures from impersonation accounts; once a target complains of gibberish text, they’re sent a cloud-hosted “decryption” utility (e.g., Proton-decrypter.exe with SHA256 37c52481711631a5c73a6341bd8bea302ad57f02199db7624b580058547fb5a9 and C2 at 45.133.216[.]15:3000/ws) that installs SPICA, presents a decoy PDF, establishes persistence through an obfuscated PowerShell scheduled task, and awaits JSON-over-WebSocket commands for shell execution, browser cookie theft, file upload/download, filesystem enumeration and document exfiltration; TAG has identified four lure PDF variants (e.g., SHA256 0f6b9d2ada67…), added all known domains and hashes to Safe Browsing blocklists, issued government-backed attacker alerts to targeted Gmail/Workspace users, provided a YARA rule for SPICA detection, and recommends blocking IOCs, enabling Enhanced Safe Browsing and updating all systems to mitigate this evolving threat.

title: Exposing initial access broker with ties to Conti
preprocessed: In early September 2021, Google’s Threat Analysis Group exposed EXOTIC LILY, a financially motivated initial access broker linked to Russian gangs FIN12/WIZARD SPIDER that exploited Microsoft MSHTML CVE-2021-40444 before transitioning to delivering custom BazarLoader and a new “BUMBLEBEE” loader via ISO files with hidden DLLs and LNK shortcuts—identifiable by shared machine identifiers, unique command-line arguments and a “bumblebee” user-agent—to deploy Conti and Diavol ransomware. At its peak, EXOTIC LILY sent over 5,000 spear-phishing emails daily to 650 organizations across IT, cybersecurity, healthcare and other sectors, using human-operated TTPs such as TLD-switched domain and employee identity spoofing (leveraging AI-generated or harvested RocketReach/CrunchBase profiles), live chat to build trust, and legitimate file-sharing services (WeTransfer, TransferNow, OneDrive) to evade detection. Operators worked a standard 9-to-5 schedule in a Central/Eastern Europe timezone, customized business proposals, scheduled calls, and used WMI-based data collection in BUMBLEBEE to exfiltrate system details in JSON and fetch Cobalt Strike payloads. Overlaps with Microsoft’s DEV-0413 and Abnormal reporting confirm shared infrastructure, underscoring the need for enhanced domain/identity spoofing defenses, monitoring of file-sharing notifications, and threat hunting for ISO/LNK artifacts with unique metadata or “bumblebee” indicators.

title: Phishing campaign targets YouTube creators with cookie theft malware
preprocessed: Since late 2019, a hack-for-hire group recruited via Russian-language forums has conducted coordinated phishing campaigns against YouTube creators by posing as legitimate companies (e.g., VPNs, antivirus, photo editors, “Covid19 news” software) to deliver non-persistent cookie-theft malware (RedLine, Vidar, Predator The Thief, Nexus Stealer, Azorult, Raccoon, Grand Stealer, Vikro Stealer, Masad, Kantal, Sorano, AdamantiumThief) via fake landing pages on over 1,011 domains and forged social-media pages; upon infection they exfiltrate session cookies for channel hijack and resale ($3–$4,000 USD) or crypto-scam livestreams. In partnership with YouTube, Gmail, Trust & Safety, Cybercrime Investigation and Safe Browsing teams, Google’s Threat Analysis Group reduced related Gmail phishing by 99.6% since May 2021—blocking 1.6 M messages, warning 62 K users, blocking 2.4 K files and restoring ~4 K accounts—while observing a shift to email.cz, seznam.cz, post.cz and aol.com and messaging apps. Protections include heuristic email filters, Safe Browsing blocks, hardened authentication and channel recovery workflows; users are urged to heed Safe Browsing warnings, scan files via antivirus or VirusTotal, enable Enhanced Safe Browsing and enforce 2-Step Verification.

title: 0-days exploited by commercial surveillance vendor in Egypt
preprocessed: Last week Google’s Threat Analysis Group, in partnership with The Citizen Lab, exposed an in-the-wild exploit chain developed by the commercial surveillance vendor Intellexa in Egypt that leverages a man-in-the-middle injection on HTTP traffic to silently redirect targets first to c.betly[.]me and then to sec-flare[.]com, delivering Predator spyware without any user interaction; on iOS this chain combined Safari RCE (CVE-2023-41993), certificate validation bypass (CVE-2023-41991) and XNU kernel local privilege escalation (CVE-2023-41992) and was patched in iOS 16.7/17.0.1, while on Android initial Chrome renderer RCE (CVE-2023-4762), delivered via MITM or one-time links, was patched on September 5; this campaign highlights the serious risk posed by proliferating commercial spyware, underscores the urgency of enforcing universal HTTPS and enabling Chrome’s HTTPS-First Mode, and demonstrates the critical need for organizations and users to apply the latest OS and browser updates, deploy encrypted-traffic protections, and monitor for anomalous network redirects to mitigate future attacks.

title: Countering threats from Iran
preprocessed: Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) has observed a 33% year-over-year increase in government-backed phishing warnings—over 50,000 sent to users so far in 2021—driven in part by a large APT28 (Fancy Bear) campaign and sustained by ongoing operations from Iran-aligned APT35. Since early 2021, APT35 has compromised a UK university website to host a phishing kit targeting Gmail, Yahoo and Hotmail credentials—including second-factor codes—and continues its credential harvesting campaigns against government, academia, journalism and NGOs using hijacked sites and link-shortening redirects. In May 2020 it attempted to distribute spyware disguised as a VPN on Google Play Store (blocked before installation) and has pursued similar Android C2 apps on other platforms. The group also impersonates conference officials (e.g., Munich Security, T20 Italy) to initiate phishing, embedding JavaScript to relay visitor IP, user-agent and locale via Telegram bots—a tactic TAG disrupted by reporting the bots. TAG’s layered defenses include batch-sent warnings, Workspace admin alerts, Safe Browsing domain blocks and urging high-risk users to enable two-factor authentication or enroll in Advanced Protection.

title: New Iranian APT data extraction tool
preprocessed: Google’s TAG disclosed that Charming Kitten (Iranian APT35) has been using a custom .NET Windows tool called HYPERSCRAPE—active since 2020—to siphon inbox data from fewer than two dozen Gmail, Yahoo! and Outlook accounts in Iran by leveraging hijacked or pre-obtained credentials; the tool validates connectivity via hardcoded/Base64-obfuscated C2s (e.g. 136.243.108.14, 173.209.51.54), spoofs an outdated browser UA to force basic HTML view, switches the account language to English, iteratively downloads emails as .eml files while preserving unread status, reverts language settings, deletes Google security alerts, and reports system metadata via HTTP POST without exfiltrating content, with early builds also offering an automated Google Takeout option using pipe communication; TAG re-secured compromised accounts, issued Government-Backed Attacker Warnings and published detection data—including numerous SHA-256 hashes for HYPERSCRAPE binaries and a related Live DLL—to aid defenders, and urges high-risk users to enroll in Google’s Advanced Protection Program and enable Enhanced Safe Browsing.

title: Magniber ransomware actors used a variant of Microsoft SmartScreen bypass
preprocessed: Google’s Threat Analysis Group uncovered that Magniber ransomware operators exploited a previously unpatched SmartScreen bypass (CVE-2023-24880) to deliver MSI installers signed with malformed Authenticode certificates that trigger a parsing error in smartscreen.exe, causing shdocvw.dll’s DoSafeOpenPromptForShellExec to proceed without displaying warnings—resulting in over 100,000 downloads since January 2023 (80 percent in Europe) before Microsoft issued a Patch Tuesday fix; this mirrors a prior bypass (CVE-2022-44698) used in late 2022 to spread Magniber via JScript and later adopted by Qakbot, with virtually identical signatures suggesting shared tooling, and highlights a systemic root-cause in SmartScreen’s error-handling logic—specifically NULL cert_context or NULL psIndirectData paths—that attackers now exploit by corrupting the SPC_INDIRECT_DATA_OBJID ASN.1 identifier, demonstrating the urgent need for holistic SmartScreen hardening and end-to-end certificate validation.

title: Active North Korean campaign targeting security researchers
preprocessed: Since January 2021, Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) has tracked a government-backed North Korean campaign that leverages social engineering via X (formerly Twitter) and encrypted messaging apps to befriend security researchers and deliver malicious files containing at least one unpatched 0-day in a popular software package; upon exploitation the custom shellcode performs anti-virtual-machine checks, captures system data and screenshots, and exfiltrates them to C2 infrastructure (e.g., 23.106.215[.]105, www.blgbeach[.]com), with the latest vulnerability reported and patched on September 12, 2023 (see TAG’s published RCA). In parallel, the actors published a seemingly benign Windows tool called GetSymbol on GitHub (https://github.com/dbgsymbol/) that quietly downloads debugging symbols—and arbitrary code—from attacker domains, requiring full OS reinstalls for compromised hosts. TAG has added malicious sites to Safe Browsing, issued government-backed attacker alerts to targeted Gmail and Workspace users, and urges researchers to enable Enhanced Safe Browsing, keep software up to date, and verify system integrity after using third-party tools.

title: Spyware vendors use 0-days and n-days against popular platforms
preprocessed: Google’s Threat Analysis Group (TAG) has documented how over 30 commercial spyware vendors are selling 0-day and n-day exploits to government-backed actors, enabling targeted campaigns against dissidents, journalists and human rights workers on Android, iOS and Samsung Internet Browser; in November 2022, TAG observed a smishing campaign using bit.ly links to deliver two parallel exploit chains—on iOS (CVE-2022-42856 WebKit RCE with a PAC bypass technique also seen in Cytrox’s Predator, and CVE-2021-30900 AGXAccelerator sandbox escape) that installed a GPS-pinging IPA stager, and on Android (CVE-2022-3723 Chrome type confusion, CVE-2022-4135 GPU sandbox bypass analyzed by Sergei Glazunov, and CVE-2022-38181 ARM privilege escalation) with Intent redirection to Chrome—both remaining effective until patched in Chrome 107/108 and Pixel January 2023 updates; in December 2022, TAG uncovered a one-time SMS link campaign targeting UAE users via a Heliconia-style landing page delivering a C++-based Android spyware suite after chaining four faults—CVE-2022-4262 Chrome type confusion, CVE-2022-3038 Chrome sandbox escape, CVE-2022-22706 Mali GPU kernel exploit and CVE-2023-0266 Linux kernel race (with auxiliary info-leak 0-days)—against unpatched Samsung Internet Browser (Chromium 102), underscoring that smaller surveillance vendors now stockpile and share advanced exploits historically limited to nation-state developers, highlighting the critical need for immediate patch deployment, comprehensive mitigations (PAC, V8 sandbox, MiraclePTR) and continuous IOC monitoring to disrupt these highly targeted intrusion operations.

title: Analyzing a watering hole campaign using macOS exploits
preprocessed: In late August 2021, TAG uncovered a sophisticated, state-backed watering-hole campaign targeting Hong Kong media and pro-democracy sites that leveraged dual iframes to deliver encrypted iOS exploits (partial chain using CVE-2019-8506 in Safari) and a full macOS exploit chain against Catalina (10.15), combining an n-day WebKit RCE (CVE-2021-1789) with a 0-day XNU local privilege escalation (CVE-2021-30869) to load a patched, embedded Mach-O via Capstone.js, escape the Safari sandbox, elevate to root through a port-type confusion variant of CVE-2020-27932, and deploy a highly modular “MACMA” backdoor over DDS for fingerprinting, file transfer, keylogging, screen/audio capture and remote command execution; with rid counters in the 200s confirming scale, researchers disclosed IOCs (e.g. 103[.]255[.]44[.]56, appleid-server[.]com) to enable blocking and urged immediate application of Apple’s Jan 5 and Sept 23 patches.

title: Government-backed actors exploiting WinRAR vulnerability
preprocessed: Government-backed actors have rapidly weaponized CVE-2023-38831, a logic flaw in WinRAR versions prior to 6.23 that abuses Windows ShellExecute’s handling of filenames with embedded spaces to trigger default extension resolution and execute unintended “.cmd” or “.bat” payloads; although RARLabs patched the bug in August 2023, public proof-of-concepts surfaced within hours, enabling multiple APTs and financially motivated groups to launch spear-phishing and drive-by campaigns. TAG observed Russian GRU-linked FROZENBARENTS (aka SANDWORM) in September luring energy sector and financial targets with a faux Ukrainian drone-training PDF that dropped a packed Rhadamanthys infostealer, FROZENLAKE (aka APT28) using a free hosting redirect chain and a decoy Razumkov Centre invite to deploy a BAT-delivered reverse SSH shell and IRONJAW PowerShell stealer, and Chinese-linked ISLANDDREAMS (aka APT40) targeting Papua New Guinea via Dropbox-hosted archives that sideload an XOR-encoded DLL to load a Donut-generated BOXRAT backdoor in-memory. These operations underscore the urgency of immediate patch deployment, throttled n-day mitigation, Google Safe Browsing/Gmail defenses, and ongoing monitoring for exploit indicators to prevent credential theft, unauthorized code execution, and persistent C2 channels.

title: Zimbra 0-day used to target international government organizations
preprocessed: In June 2023, Google TAG discovered CVE-2023-37580, a reflected XSS in Zimbra Collaboration that injected malicious scripts via the “st” URL parameter, and Zimbra issued a hotfix on GitHub on July 5, an advisory on July 13, and an official patch on July 25; despite this, TAG observed four distinct campaigns: an initial state-sponsored operation targeting a Greek government using a Volexity-documented email-stealing framework to exfiltrate mail data and set auto-forward rules; Winter Vivern (UNC4907) launching attacks against Moldovan and Tunisian government domains from July 11–25 via custom scripts at applicationdevsoc[.]com; an unidentified actor days before July 25 deploying a phishing page for Vietnamese webmail credentials on a compromised government domain; and, in August, a post-patch n-day campaign in Pakistan exfiltrating Zimbra authentication tokens to ntcpk[.]org—underscoring that threat actors rapidly mine public fixes to harvest credentials, tokens, and sensitive emails and reinforcing the imperative for organizations to apply updates immediately and audit mail-server code for XSS.

title: The BadPilot campaign: Seashell Blizzard subgroup conducts multiyear global access operation | Microsoft Security Blog
preprocessed: Microsoft’s research exposes the BadPilot campaign—a multiyear initial-access subgroup of Russian GRU-aligned Seashell Blizzard active since at least 2021—that has opportunistically scanned for and exploited Internet-facing vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-34473 Exchange, CVE-2022-41352 Zimbra, CVE-2023-32315 OpenFire, CVE-2023-42793 TeamCity, CVE-2023-23397 Outlook, CVE-2024-1709 ConnectWise ScreenConnect, CVE-2023-48788 FortiClient EMS and various JBOSS flaws) to compromise a globally diverse set of high-value sectors (energy, oil and gas, telecommunications, shipping, arms manufacturing and government). Following initial access, BadPilot employs stealthy persistence, credential harvesting, lateral movement and common tools such as Cobalt Strike and DarkCrystalRAT to sustain footholds and support tailored network operations, including at least three destructive cyberattacks in Ukraine since 2023. After focusing on Ukraine, Europe, Central/South Asia and the Middle East during 2021–2023, the subgroup scaled horizontally into the United States, United Kingdom, Canada and Australia in early 2024, reflecting Russia’s evolving strategic objectives and underscoring the urgency of patching Internet-facing services, implementing comprehensive logging and anomaly detection, and applying threat-informed incident-response practices to disrupt its operational lifecycle.

title: StilachiRAT analysis: From system reconnaissance to cryptocurrency theft | Microsoft Security Blog
preprocessed: In November 2024, Microsoft Incident Response researchers uncovered StilachiRAT, a novel remote‐access Trojan delivered via unknown vectors that uses its WWStartupCtrl64.dll module to perform comprehensive system reconnaissance through WMI/COL/Web‐based Enterprise Management queries (gathering OS details, hardware IDs, camera presence, RDP sessions and GUI apps) and generates a unique device ID in the registry; targets 20 Chrome cryptocurrency wallet extensions (including MetaMask, Trust Wallet and TronLink) by inspecting PreferenceMACs registry keys; extracts and decrypts Chrome’s master encryption key via Windows DPAPI to steal stored credentials; continuously monitors clipboard content (using TRX‐specific regex) and active windows; establishes C2 communications over TCP ports 53, 443 or 16000 with app[.]95560[.]cc and 194.195.89.47 (delaying two hours and checking for tcpview.exe to evade analysis); employs anti‐forensic measures (event-log clearing, sandbox evasion, multi-layer API obfuscation); achieves persistence via Windows SCM services and watchdog threads; and supports versatile C2‐issued commands (system reboot, log clearing, registry updates, application execution, network socket management, RDP session impersonation and system suspension), enabling credential theft, cryptocurrency exfiltration and potential lateral movement, prompting urgent deployment of Microsoft detection tools, hunting queries and security hardening guidance to mitigate impact.

title: New Russia-affiliated actor Void Blizzard targets critical sectors for espionage | Microsoft Security Blog
preprocessed: Since at least April 2024 Microsoft Threat Intelligence has tracked a Russia-affiliated cyberespionage actor dubbed Void Blizzard (aka LAUNDRY BEAR) conducting high-volume, targeted operations against government, defense, transportation, media, NGO and healthcare organizations—particularly in NATO member states and Ukraine—by leveraging stolen credentials procured via commodity infostealer ecosystems for password spray attacks and Exchange/SharePoint Online access, then automating bulk email and file collection (and in some cases Teams messages) via cloud APIs and tools like AzureHound; in April 2025 the actor evolved to adversary-in-the-middle spear phishing using a typosquatted domain and the open-source Evilginx framework with a malicious QR-coded PDF to harvest Entra authentication data; this widespread success underscores that even unsophisticated TTPs pose major intelligence risks to critical sectors, so organizations should enforce sign-in risk policies and phishing-resistant MFA (e.g., FIDO/passkeys), centralize identity management with Conditional Access, monitor risky sign-ins and mailbox auditing, apply least-privilege credential hygiene, and promptly rotate credentials after infostealer detections to disrupt Void Blizzard’s operations.

title: Financially motivated threat actors misusing App Installer | Microsoft Security Blog
preprocessed: Since mid-November 2023 Microsoft Threat Intelligence has tracked financially motivated actors—Storm-0569, Storm-1113, Sangria Tempest and Storm-1674—abusing the ms-appinstaller URI scheme and MSIX file format to distribute signed malicious application packages that bypass SmartScreen and browser warnings and deliver loaders, backdoors and ransomware. In early December Storm-0569 leveraged SEO poisoning and malvertising on spoofed Zoom, Tableau, TeamViewer and AnyDesk download sites to install BATLOADER via App Installer, which in turn dropped Cobalt Strike Beacons, exfiltrated data with Rclone and handed off to Black Basta ransomware; Storm-0569 also sells custom MSI/MSIX landing-page frameworks to other criminals. Storm-1113 has deployed EugenLoader via search ads mimicking Zoom to drop Gozi, RedLine, IcedID, Smoke Loader, NetSupport RAT, SectopRAT or Lumma stealer, acting as both access broker and “malware-as-a-service” provider. Sangria Tempest delivered Storm-1113’s EugenLoader to deploy Carbanak and Gracewire or POWERTRASH scripts loading NetSupport and Gracewire for data theft and extortion. From December Storm-1674 combined Teams-based phishing with malicious installers to deploy SectopRAT or DarkGate, often using Storm-1113’s frameworks. In response Microsoft disabled the ms-appinstaller handler by default, updated App Installer, and recommends phishing-resistant authentication, conditional access, user education on URL and publisher validation, Defender SmartScreen, Safe Links and attack surface reduction rules to thwart this human-operated ransomware and data-exfiltration chain.

title: Cadet Blizzard emerges as a novel and distinct Russian threat actor | Microsoft Security Blog
preprocessed: Since at least 2020, Microsoft Threat Intelligence has tracked a novel GRU-affiliated Russian group—now named Cadet Blizzard (formerly DEV-0586)—that has executed destructive cyber campaigns against government, law enforcement, NGO and IT service providers primarily in Ukraine, Europe and Latin America, peaking January–June 2022 with the WhisperGate MBR-wiper and website defacements, then re-emerging in January 2023 to renew hack-and-leak operations under the “Free Civilian” forum; Cadet Blizzard leverages exploitation of perimeter web servers (notably CVE-2021-26084 Confluence, Exchange CVE-2022-41040/ProxyShell), living-off-the-land tactics for lateral movement (Impacket modules, PowerShell get-volume, reg save), credential harvesting via renamed procdump64 dumps of LSASS, persistence with commodity and custom web shells (P0wnyshell, reGeorg, PAS variants), and socket-based tunneling tools (NetCat, GOST) often via scheduled tasks; operational mistakes have limited scale compared to Forest or Seashell Blizzard yet still risk significant network disruption, data exfiltration and strategic intelligence leakage; defenders should prioritize patching exposed web services, monitor for known IoCs and anomalous web-shell activity, LSASS and registry dumps, unusual scheduled tasks or renamed tunneling binaries, and collaborate with CERT-UA and global partners for timely threat intelligence sharing and incident response.

title: Defending new vectors: Threat actors attempt SQL Server to cloud lateral movement | Microsoft Security Blog
preprocessed: Attackers exploited an unpatched SQL injection vulnerability in an application to gain elevated permissions on a Microsoft SQL Server instance running in an Azure VM, then enumerated databases, schemas, network settings and enabled xp_cmdshell via “sp_configure” commands to execute OS-level commands, deploy encoded PowerShell scripts, establish persistence via scheduled tasks, dump SAM and SECURITY hives, and exfiltrate data discreetly using webhook[.]site. In a novel twist on known techniques, they attempted lateral movement to additional cloud resources by querying the Azure Instance Metadata Service (169.254.169.254) to obtain the managed identity’s OAuth2 token and abuse its privileges, but the move failed due to an error. Microsoft Defender for SQL triggered alerts for potential SQL injection, abnormal shell spawning, and IMDS calls from SQL Server, while Defender for Cloud and Defender for Endpoint provide further visibility into anomalous cloud-identity and xp_cmdshell activity. Although no breach of downstream cloud services was confirmed, this case underscores the critical need to enforce least privilege on managed identities, disable or tightly control xp_cmdshell, patch applications, monitor metadata endpoint access, and leverage Defender XDR’s detection capabilities to thwart SQL Server–to-cloud lateral movement.

title: Diamond Sleet supply chain compromise distributes a modified CyberLink installer | Microsoft Security Blog
preprocessed: Microsoft Threat Intelligence has uncovered a supply chain attack by the North Korean group Diamond Sleet in which a legitimate CyberLink Corp. multimedia installer was trojanized—tracked as LambLoad (SHA-256 166d1a6ddcde4e859a89c2c825cd3c8c953a86bfa92b343de7e5bfbfb5afb8be) and signed with a valid CyberLink code-signing certificate—and hosted on CyberLink’s own update infrastructure; the loader enforces a narrow execution window, checks for EDR processes (CrowdStrike’s csfalconservice.exe, FireEye’s xagt.exe, Tanium’s taniumclient.exe) to evade detection, then downloads, decrypts, and in-memory loads a second-stage payload masquerading as a PNG file (SHA-256 089573b3a1167f387dcdad5e014a5132e998b2c89bff29bcf8b06dd497d4e63d; decrypted PE 915c2495e03ff7408f11a2a197f23344004c533ff87db4b807cc937f80c217a1) from compromised domains before calling back for commands; observed since October 2023 on over 100 devices across Japan, Taiwan, Canada, and the US and targeting IT, defense, and media organizations for espionage and data theft, Microsoft has alerted CyberLink, notified Defender for Endpoint customers, reported the payload to GitHub for takedown, blacklisted the abused certificate, published detections (Trojan:Win32/LambLoad; Diamond Sleet activity group alerts), provided hunting queries and IOCs, and recommended cloud-delivered protection, network protection, automated remediation, attack surface reduction rules, and immediate isolation and credential resets upon compromise.

title: Flax Typhoon using legitimate software to quietly access Taiwanese organizations | Microsoft Security Blog
preprocessed: Microsoft has identified a China-based nation-state threat actor tracked as Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda) conducting espionage against dozens of Taiwanese organizations since mid-2021 by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java and SQL servers to deploy the China Chopper web shell, escalate privileges with Juicy Potato and BadPotato, and establish persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN bridge over HTTPS on port 443 for stealthy command-and-control.
