Once inside, the actor leverages WinRM and WMIC for lateral movement and deploys Mimikatz to dump LSASS and SAM for pass-the-hash attacks, yet conducts minimal post-persistence activity, suggesting long-term credential harvesting rather than immediate data exfiltration. To mitigate, organizations must enforce rigorous patch management, monitor registry changes and RDP configurations, deploy file integrity and behavioral monitoring on public-facing servers, isolate and forensically examine compromised systems, and rotate or disable exposed credentials.

title: Social engineering attacks lure Indian users to install Android banking trojans | Microsoft Security Blog
preprocessed: Microsoft telemetry has uncovered ongoing cybercriminal campaigns targeting Indian Android users via WhatsApp and Telegram social engineering, distributing malicious APKs that impersonate banks, government services, and utilities to harvest sensitive data and facilitate financial fraud. In two observed cases—one posing as a KYC app and another as a payment-card form—the trojans request dangerous Receive_SMS and Send_SMS permissions, intercept OTPs, and display counterfeit UIs asking for mobile numbers, ATM PINs, PAN details, credit-card data, and incoming SMS; all collected information is exfiltrated to a hard-coded C2 server (e.g., biogenetic-flake[.]000webhostapp.com/add.php and save_sms.php) and via SMS to attacker phone numbers. The analyzed sample (SHA-256: 6812a82edcb49131a990acd88ed5f6d73da9f536b60ee751184f27265ea769ee, package djhgsfjhfdgf.gjhdgsfsjde.myappl876786ication) also hides its icon for persistence and consumes device resources. Evolving from prior link-based Rewards plus campaigns, these tactics bypass official app-store controls, resulting in unauthorized transactions, privacy breaches, and degraded device performance. Organizations should enforce app-store-only policies, monitor for anomalous app behavior and battery/data spikes, conduct user-awareness training, and deploy robust mobile threat defenses.

title: Malware distributor Storm-0324 facilitates ransomware access | Microsoft Security Blog
preprocessed: Since at least 2016, financially motivated distributor Storm-0324 (aka DEV-0324, TA543, Sagrid) has operated a highly evasive malware distribution chain—initially using exploit kits and email-based lures referencing invoices or DocuSign/QuickBooks and traffic distribution systems like BlackTDS and Keitaro to evade sandboxes—to deliver first-stage payloads such as Nymaim, Gozi v3, TrickBot, Gootkit, Dridex, IcedID and Sage/GandCrab ransomware; by 2019 it shifted to primarily deploying JSSLoader, which drops variants via JavaScript-embedded DLLs (hosted on SharePoint ZIP archives, Office docs, WSF or VBScript files) exploiting CVE-2023-21715 bypasses and protected-document social engineering, then hands off network access to the ransomware-as-a-service actor Sangria Tempest (ELBRUS/Carbon Spider/FIN7) for ransomware deployment, and in July 2023 began using open-source TeamsPhisher to send phishing lures over Microsoft Teams; defenders can disrupt this chain by leveraging Microsoft 365 Defender/XDR detections (TrojanSpy:MSIL/JSSLoader, Trojan:Win32/{Gootkit, IcedID, Trickbot}), enforcing phishing-resistant auth via Conditional Access, least-privilege and credential hygiene, tightening Teams external collaboration settings and ‘EXTERNAL’ tagging, enabling Safe Links and Zero-hour Auto Purge, applying attack surface reduction rules to block script/executable launches, turning on cloud-delivered protection and auditing, and educating users on social engineering and MFA code safety to significantly limit initial access and downstream ransomware impact.

title: Midnight Blizzard conducts targeted social engineering over Microsoft Teams | Microsoft Security Blog
preprocessed: Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed the Russia-based SVR actor Midnight Blizzard (aka NOBELIUM, APT29/UNC2452/Cozy Bear) launch a highly targeted social-engineering campaign since at least late May 2023 by leveraging previously compromised small-business Microsoft 365 tenants to create security-themed onmicrosoft.com domains and Teams accounts that masquerade as technical-support entities; attackers then initiate Microsoft Teams chat requests to elicit approval of MFA prompts or codes via Microsoft Authenticator, enabling credential theft, access to fewer than 40 global organizations across government, NGOs, IT services, technology, manufacturing and media sectors, and subsequent post-compromise activities including data exfiltration and attempts to add managed devices via Microsoft Entra ID to bypass conditional access. Microsoft has mitigated the malicious domains, directly notified affected customers, and recommends phishing-resistant authentication, Conditional Access policies, Microsoft Teams best practices, auditing, and user education to detect and prevent unsolicited MFA requests.

title: New macOS vulnerability, Migraine, could bypass System Integrity Protection | Microsoft Security Blog
preprocessed: Microsoft’s MSVR team discovered “Migraine” (CVE-2023-32369), a macOS System Integrity Protection (SIP) bypass that leverages the com.apple.rootless.install.heritable entitlement of the systemmigrationd daemon to tamper with Apple-signed binaries—drop_sip, bash and perl—clearing the CS_EXEC_INHERIT_SIP flag via csops (CS_OPS_CLEARINSTALLER) and enabling arbitrary code execution without SIP checks. Found during routine malware hunting and analogous to Shrootless (CVE-2021-30892), the exploit injects environment variables with launchctl, mounts a crafted Time Machine backup via hdiutil, and automates Migration Assistant with –MBDebug/–ResumeBuddyYes flags and AppleScript to trigger setup without logout. Unpatched until Apple’s May 18, 2023 update, Migraine facilitates stealthy rootkits, undeletable malware protected by SIP attributes, and expands both userland and kernel attack surfaces—threatening endpoint security tools like Microsoft Defender for Endpoint and underscoring the criticality of coordinated vulnerability disclosure and entitlement-based defenses.

title: Multiple North Korean threat actors exploiting the TeamCity CVE-2023-42793 vulnerability | Microsoft Security Blog
preprocessed: Since early October 2023, Microsoft has tracked North Korean nation-state groups Diamond Sleet (ZINC) and Onyx Sleet (PLUTONIUM) opportunistically exploiting the TeamCity CVE-2023-42793 RCE flaw to infiltrate DevOps build servers, deploy backdoors and establish persistent access. Post-exploit, Diamond Sleet leverages PowerShell to install its ForestTiger backdoor (Forest64.exe/4800-84DC-063A6A41C5C, decrypted with static key “uTYNkfKxHiZrx3KJ”), schedules it for startup, dumps LSASS credentials and conducts DLL search-order hijacking via DSROLE.dll (RollSling) and Version.dll (FeedLoad) chains to launch memory-resident malware and relay C2 traffic, while Onyx Sleet creates a fake “krtbgt” admin account, executes system discovery cmdlets, drops a HazyLoad proxy tool via encrypted PE resources, abuses RDP and LSASS dumping for lateral movement, and remains undetected. Microsoft assesses these campaigns pose high risk for espionage, data theft and supply-chain compromise; organizations should immediately apply JetBrains patches or mitigations, deploy IOCs and Defender protections, block malicious IPs, isolate compromised hosts and reset credentials to disrupt these advanced persistent threats.

title: Peach Sandstorm password spray campaigns enable intelligence collection at high-value targets | Microsoft Security Blog
preprocessed: Since February 2023, Microsoft has tracked an Iranian nation-state threat actor known as Peach Sandstorm (a.k.a. APT33/Elfin/Refined Kitten) conducting high-volume password spray attacks—often via Tor IPs and a “go-http-client” user agent—against thousands of satellite, defense, and pharmaceutical organizations worldwide to gain initial access for state-sponsored intelligence collection; upon successful logins the group employed Go-based AzureHound or Roadtools for Microsoft Entra ID reconnaissance, established persistence through malicious Azure subscriptions and Azure Arc, and in parallel attempted remote exploitation of internet-facing Zoho ManageEngine (CVE-2022-47966) and Confluence (CVE-2022-26134) vulnerabilities. In later stages Peach Sandstorm deployed AnyDesk RMM, executed Golden SAML attacks to mint Microsoft 365 tokens, used DLL search-order hijacking via legitimate VMware binaries, tunneled traffic with custom EagleRelay VMs, leveraged RDP for lateral movement, and in a subset of intrusions exfiltrated sensitive data. Microsoft’s assessment underscores the risk to confidentiality and urges defenders to reset compromised passwords and session cookies, revoke unauthorized MFA changes, implement conditional-access policies, block legacy authentication, patch known CVEs, and apply the Azure Security Benchmark to harden identity infrastructures against evolving Peach Sandstorm tradecraft.

title: Star Blizzard increases sophistication and evasion in ongoing attacks | Microsoft Security Blog
preprocessed: Since mid-November 2024, Russian nation-state actor Star Blizzard has significantly escalated its evasion tradecraft following public exposure by Microsoft Threat Intelligence: shifting from a single registrar (NameCheap) to multiple registrars (Hostinger, RealTime Register, GMO Internet) and implementing multi-stage redirection chains—embedding Microsoft 365 Safe Links in PDF lures that pass through Bitly and Cuttly shortened URLs and legitimate open-redirect sites (e.g., mechengsys[.]net) before landing on an Evilginx-equipped VPS (vidmemax[.]com)—to mount AiTM spear-phishing campaigns that harvest email credentials, including MFA tokens. Between July and August 2024 they also experimented with altered OneDrive file-share notifications—using ProtonMail accounts to spoof trusted senders and rewire the “Open” button URL to their Evilginx infrastructure—targeting individuals in politics, diplomacy, NGOs and think tanks. In October 2024, Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit disrupted core infrastructure, and ongoing collaboration with UK NCSC, NSA and FBI ensures rapid customer notification and defenses. Historically, since 2022 Star Blizzard has iteratively refined detection evasion—employing server-side fingerprinting scripts, HubSpot and MailerLite email platforms to mask domains, DNS obfuscation, password-protected PDFs and randomized DGAs—with each ephemeral TTP swiftly modified, underscoring the need for continuous updates to email security controls, link inspection and behavioral detection.

title: Flax Typhoon using legitimate software to quietly access Taiwanese organizations | Microsoft Security Blog
preprocessed: Microsoft has traced a stealthy espionage campaign by Flax Typhoon (aka Ethereal Panda), a China-based nation-state actor active since mid-2021, targeting dozens of Taiwanese organizations (with spill-over in Southeast Asia, North America, and Africa) by exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing VPN, web, Java, and SQL services to deploy the China Chopper web shell for initial access; the group escalates privileges via open-source exploits like Juicy Potato and BadPotato, then establishes persistence by disabling RDP network-level authentication, hijacking the Sticky Keys (sethc.exe) binary to launch Task Manager as SYSTEM, and installing a renamed SoftEther VPN-over-HTTPS bridge (conhost.exe/dllhost.exe) as a service to maintain covert C2 over port 443; leveraging LOLBins such as PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest, certutil, bitsadmin, WinRM, and WMIC for lateral movement, vulnerability scanning, and remote execution, it harvests credentials from LSASS memory and the SAM registry hive using Mimikatz for pass-the-hash attacks; although no exfiltration or final objectives have been observed, organizations are urged to enforce rigorous patch and vulnerability management on internet-exposed systems, monitor registry and file-integrity changes, deploy web application firewalls, reset compromised credentials, isolate and forensically examine affected hosts, and leverage detections in Microsoft 365 Defender to disrupt living-off-the-land tactics.

title: Multiple North Korean threat actors exploiting the TeamCity CVE-2023-42793 vulnerability | Microsoft Security Blog
preprocessed: Since early October 2023 Microsoft has tracked two North Korean nation-state actors, Diamond Sleet (ZINC) and Onyx Sleet (PLUTONIUM), exploiting CVE-2023-42793, a remote-code execution flaw in JetBrains TeamCity CI/CD servers, to opportunistically breach build environments and deploy tailored post-exploitation tooling for persistent access and credential theft. Diamond Sleet leveraged two distinct attack paths: first, PowerShell scripts to download Forest64.exe and an encrypted payload (using static key “uTYNkfKxHiZrx3KJ”) which, when decrypted, installs the ForestTiger backdoor via a scheduled task and dumps LSASS memory; second, DLL search-order hijacking with malicious DSROLE.dll loaded by wsmprovhost.exe (RollSling) to deobfuscate and launch PE payloads in memory (e.g., wksprt.exe for C2) and Version.dll loaded by clip.exe (FeedLoad) which uses a readme.md XOR key to deploy a remote access trojan and spawns iexpress.exe, followed by additional LSASS dumps. Onyx Sleet, after exploiting the same flaw, creates a fake “krtbgt” admin account, executes system discovery commands, stops the TeamCity service, and deploys a PowerShell-downloaded proxy tool (HazyLoad) via temp.exe and ADFSbginetmgr.exe to maintain C2, uses RDP for lateral movement, and harvests credentials from LSASS and browsers. JetBrains has released patches and mitigations, and Microsoft urges organizations to apply updates, use provided IOCs and Defender Antivirus (detecting ForestTiger, RollSling, FeedLoad, HazyLoad), enable cloud-delivered protection, Safe DLL Search Mode and attack surface reduction rules, block identified IPs, isolate and credential-reset compromised hosts, and hunt for related activity with Microsoft 365 Defender, Defender Vulnerability Management, Defender for Endpoint alerts, and Sentinel TI mapping.

title: Volt Typhoon targets US critical infrastructure with living-off-the-land techniques | Microsoft Security Blog
preprocessed: Since mid-2021, Microsoft has tracked Volt Typhoon, a China-linked state-sponsored actor, conducting stealthy living-off-the-land campaigns against U.S. critical infrastructure—spanning communications, utilities, transportation, manufacturing, government and education—aimed at post-compromise credential access, network discovery and long-term espionage with an eye toward potential disruption of Asia-U.S. communications in future crises. Initial access is achieved via internet-exposed Fortinet FortiGuard devices, whose AD credentials are harvested to move laterally; all traffic is proxied through compromised SOHO routers, firewalls and VPN hardware (ASUS, Cisco, D-Link, NETGEAR, Zyxel) to blend with legitimate activity. Post-compromise hands-on-keyboard operations rely almost exclusively on LOLBins and valid credentials to dump LSASS memory and use Ntdsutil.exe to create domain controller installation media for offline hash cracking, enumerate systems via PowerShell, WMIC and ping, collect browser and system data into staged archives, then exfiltrate via password-protected files. In rare cases, Volt Typhoon deploys custom Impacket or FRP-based C2 over portproxy, observable as unusual successful sign-ins and command-line activity from anomalous IPs. Detection is challenging due to use of built-in binaries and normal sign-in channels; Microsoft 365 Defender and cloud-delivered Microsoft Defender Antivirus yield behavioral alerts (e.g., SuspPowershellExec, SuspNtdsUtilUsage), while Defender for Endpoint flags suspicious LSASS dumps, wmic.exe executions and domain-controller media creation. Mitigation hinges on closing or rotating compromised accounts, enforcing strong MFA or passwordless authentication, disabling internet-facing device management interfaces, enabling LSASS Protective Process Light and Credential Guard on Windows 11, applying attack surface reduction rules to block LSASS and PSExec/WMI abuse, and running EDR in block mode to thwart post-compromise artifacts.

title: Agonizing Serpens (Aka Agrius) Targeting the Israeli Higher Education and Tech Sectors
preprocessed: Unit 42’s investigation into Agonizing Serpens (aka Agrius), an Iranian-linked APT active since 2020, reveals that between January and October 2023 the group executed multi‐stage destructive attacks against Israeli higher education and tech organizations, beginning with exploitation of internet-facing web servers and deployment of ASPXSpy and Uploader.aspx web shells for initial access, followed by reconnaissance with Nbtscan (systems.txt), WinEggDrop and NimScan port scanners; credential theft attempts using Mimikatz, SMB spraying/brute-force and SAM dumping (all blocked by Cortex XDR); lateral movement via Plink tunnels; database exfiltration using the custom Sqlextractor tool to harvest PII (IDs, passport scans, emails, addresses) into .csv files later archived with 7za/7zG and exfiltrated via WinSCP and pscp; and final endpoint destruction with multiple wipers—novel MultiLayer (multi-stage .NET wiper with timestomping, shadow copy deletion, boot-sector overwrite and self-deletion), PartialWasher and BFG Agonizer—designed to thwart recovery and sow disruption without requesting ransom, while demonstrating shared code overlap with prior tools (Apostle, IPsec Helper, Fantasy) and rotating between known PoCs and custom utilities to evade detection; XDR and XSIAM successfully detected and prevented key execution flows, reinforcing the need for robust EDR/EDR-bypass hunting, web‐shell monitoring, credential-theft anomaly detection and behavior-based machine learning profiles to safeguard sensitive data and ensure business continuity.

title: Hacking Employers and Seeking Employment: Two Job-Related Campaigns Bear Hallmarks of North Korean Threat Actors
preprocessed: Unit 42 researchers identified two North Korea–linked campaigns, Contagious Interview (CL-STA-0240) and Wagemole (CL-STA-0241), active since December 2022 and March 2023 respectively, that exploit job-seeking and recruitment processes to compromise targets: Contagious Interview poses as anonymous employers, lures software developers into installing malicious NPM packages hosted on free GitHub repos, and deploys the BeaverTail JavaScript stealer/loader to harvest browser-stored cryptocurrency wallet and credential data before retrieving the cross-platform InvisibleFerret Python backdoor for follow-on intrusion, while Wagemole involves DPRK operators submitting fraudulent resumes and conducting unauthorized remote employment with U.S. and global organizations to facilitate espionage or funnel wages to weapons programs; both campaigns leverage open-source supply-chain tactics, Node.js execution, code obfuscation and minimal detection footprints to enable cryptocurrency theft, staging for additional attacks and sensitive data exfiltration, underscoring the need for rigorous vetting of employers, candidates and development-environment artifacts.

title: BlackCat Climbs the Summit With a New Tactic
preprocessed: BlackCat ransomware operators have introduced “Munchkin,” a new VM-based utility—delivered as an Alpine ISO loaded in VirtualBox—that automates propagation of the Rust-based BlackCat payload to remote machines and SMB/CIFS shares to evade host-level defenses. At boot, Munchkin’s ISO resets the VM root password, spawns a tmux “controller” session to run the /app/controller binary, decrypts strings via single-byte XOR, validates and deserializes a serialized /app/config file containing access tokens, victim credentials, target hosts/shares and block-lists, then mounts a /payloads directory to generate customized BlackCat samples from a template before iterating through configured tasks to encrypt network shares. The VM also houses numerous Python scripts for lateral movement and credential harvesting. This evolution in BlackCat’s RaaS toolkit reflects a broader trend of leveraging embedded VMs to thwart security solutions, expands the group’s global targeting footprint and underscores the need for defenses tuned to detect ISO-based VM deployments and tmux-launched malware.

title: Blitz Malware: A Tale of Game Cheats and Code Repositories
preprocessed: Blitz is a modular two-stage Windows malware discovered in 2024 and actively developed into early 2025 by a Russian-speaking actor using the moniker sw1zzx who distributed backdoored Standoff 2 game cheat packages (Nerest_CrackBy@sw1zzx_dev.zip and Elysium_CrackBy@sw1zzx_dev.zip) via a Telegram channel. The first stage is a stealthy downloader (ieapfltr.dll) retrieved through a PowerShell one-liner from pastebin/paste.rs URLs after passing anti-sandbox and VM detection checks (timing loops, floating-point instruction counters, processor count and screen resolution heuristics), which then establishes persistence via HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript and HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. Upon reboot, the downloader connects to a FastAPI-based C2 infrastructure hosted on a Hugging Face Space to fetch the second-stage Blitz bot that performs keylogging, screenshot capture, denial-of-service attacks on web servers and can deploy an XMRig Monero miner as follow-up. This campaign leverages Hugging Face Spaces for file hosting and C2 communications, and the malware developer promoted cheats on social media before announcing departure in May 2025; Hugging Face subsequently locked the account and blocked blob IDs. The impact includes credential theft, resource exploitation, unauthorized cryptocurrency mining and potential service disruption, and Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire, URL Filtering, DNS Security, Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR and XSIAM effectively detect and block Blitz activities, with Unit 42 standing by for incident response.

title: CL0P Seeds ^_- Gotta Catch Em All!
preprocessed: CL0P, a prolific ransomware affiliate of TA505 that exploited the MOVEit Transfer zero-day in May 2023 to compromise over 3,000 U.S. and 8,000 global organizations, has shifted its data-leak operations from slow Tor-hosted zip downloads to decentralized BitTorrent distribution using magnet links and DHT trackers to handle terabytes of stolen data and re-pressure non-paying victims, enabling researchers to rapidly join swarms and identify 100 percent seeders by monitoring leak-site announcements, capturing peer IPs, torrent client fingerprints and connection metadata; this technique not only exposes CL0P’s initial seeding infrastructure and tradecraft opsec gaps but also underscores the need for organizations to deploy behavioral threat protection (e.g., Cortex XDR/XSIAM), continuously scan for MOVEit Transfer exposures (Cortex Xpanse), and engage Unit 42 incident response for tailored threat hunting and mitigation.

title: Threat Brief: Citrix Bleed CVE-2023-4966
preprocessed: On Oct. 10, 2023, Citrix released patches for Netscaler ADC and Gateway to address Citrix Bleed (CVE-2023-4966, CVSS 9.4), a memory-leak vulnerability allowing unauthenticated attackers to exfiltrate session tokens via crafted requests and hijack sessions; public proof-of-concept code from Assetnote and Python exploit scripts rapidly empowered ransomware affiliates and other threat actors to gain footholds, with Unit 42 Incident Response and Managed Threat Hunting teams observing exploitation-linked remote PowerShell sessions spawning cmd.exe, reconnaissance commands (whoami, WMIC, tasklist, net user), deployment of XScan (s.exe), Python HTTP servers, and mRemoteNG on VDI hosts—though no lateral movement beyond VDI was detected. Cortex Xpanse identified nearly 8,000 exposed Netscaler Gateway and 6,000 ADC IPs worldwide (3,100 US, 800 Germany, 450 China, 400 UK), prompting addition to the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog. Palo Alto Networks advises immediate patching (including CVE-2023-4967), engagement of Unit 42 for incident response and continuous hunting, deployment of Next-Generation Firewalls with Advanced Threat Prevention signature 94483, updated Advanced WildFire ML models, Cortex Xpanse Threat Response Event, and Cortex XDR/XSIAM behavioral, anti-webshell, and credential-gathering protections to detect and block post-exploitation activity.

title: Conti Ransomware Gang: An Overview
preprocessed: Conti ransomware, a profit-driven RaaS syndicate linked by the FBI to over 400 global attacks (75% in the U.S.) with demands up to $25 million, has spent more than a year targeting high-stakes environments—hospitals, 911 dispatch centers, EMS and law enforcement—where IT outages can be life-threatening, exemplified by Ireland’s mid-May healthcare system shutdown that halted X-ray services and COVID testing; it gains initial access through Spearphishing Attachment (T1566.001), Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190) and lacking MFA, then uses Cobalt Strike and PowerShell for discovery (T1083, T1135), lateral movement (SMB Shares T1021.002), privilege escalation (DLL Injection T1055.001) and defense evasion (Obfuscated Files T1027, Deobfuscate/Decode T1140), before executing “double extortion” (Data Encrypted for Impact T1486, Inhibit System Recovery T1490) and often reneging on decryption promises; actionable defenses include enforcing MFA, applying NGFW Threat Prevention with secure Vulnerability Protection Profiles, WildFire file analysis, Cortex XDR’s anti-malware/exploit modules, regular WildFire updates, Cortex XSOAR playbooks, and tracking IoCs via Unit 42’s GitHub and TAXII feeds.

title: CryptoClippy Speaks Portuguese
preprocessed: Unit 42 uncovered CryptoClippy, a Portuguese-targeted cryptocurrency clipper campaign that leverages SEO poisoning via Google Ads and a traffic distribution system (TDS) to redirect “WhatsApp Web” searchers to malicious Portuguese-language domains, trick victims into downloading a .zip containing a .lnk file that launches an obfuscated PowerShell chain (Ricoly.bat → Ricoly.ps1 → reflectively loaded loader ps/sc), injects the clipper into svchost.exe via SysWhispers2 syscalls, and sets clipboard hooks to replace copied Bitcoin and Ethereum addresses with actor-controlled wallets (0.039954 BTC ≈ $983, 0.1109 ETH ≈ $186); the variant also deploys an RC4-encrypted PowerShell backdoor using WMI, registry, net/icacls commands and log clearing for persistence, communicates with C2 servers, and evades signature- and heuristic-based detection (low VirusTotal coverage), opportunistically impacting manufacturing, IT services and real estate endpoints, with protections available through Cortex XDR, Advanced URL Filtering and DNS Security for Next-Generation Firewall.

title: Diplomats Beware: Cloaked Ursa Phishing With a Twist
preprocessed: Between April and May 2023, Russia’s SVR-linked Cloaked Ursa (aka APT29, Cozy Bear, Midnight Blizzard/Nobelium) repurposed a legitimate “BMW 5 for sale in Kyiv” flyer—initially circulated by a Polish diplomat and likely harvested via a compromised mail server—into malicious Word documents that leverage URL‐shortening services (t[.]ly/tinyurl[.]com) to redirect victims to a co-opted landing page (hxxps://resetlocations[.]com/bmw.htm) where Windows shortcut files masquerading as PNG images deploy a silent payload; this campaign targeted at least 22 of 80+ foreign missions in Kyiv (80 percent via publicly listed embassy addresses, 20 percent via unpublished contacts) and follows a February–March lure impersonating Turkish MFA earthquake relief guidance, both demonstrating Cloaked Ursa’s hallmark TTPs—phishing lures themed to individual diplomat needs, code overlap with known malware, exploitation of benign attachments requiring a web browser to trigger—and highlights that one payload SHA256 (311e9c8cf6d0b295074ffefaa9f277cb1f806343be262c59f88fbdf6fe242517) is vendor-detected while the other (8902bd7d085397745e05883f05c08de87623cc15fe630b36ad3d208f01ef0596) remains undetected, underscoring the need for region-specific APT training, vigilant URL redirection checks, cautious handling of web‐based attachments (.hta, .svg, .html), scrutiny of archive contents (.zip, .rar, .iso), JavaScript disablement where feasible, and deployment of protections such as Cortex XDR, WildFire and DNS Security to mitigate espionage risk.

title: CloudKeys in the Air: Tracking Malicious Operations of Exposed IAM Keys
preprocessed: Unit42’s “EleKtra-Leak” campaign, active since December 2020, uses automated scripts to clone public GitHub repos every few minutes, extract exposed AWS IAM keys within five minutes, then—if not blocked by GitHub-AWS quarantine policies—execute rapid AWS reconnaissance (DescribeRegions), create security groups, and launch hundreds of EC2 instances across regions via VPN for Monero cryptojacking, generating over 400 API calls in seven minutes. Between Aug. 30 and Oct. 6, 2023, researchers tracked 474 actor-controlled miners. The actor employs custom mining software and blocklists high-profile AWS account IDs to avoid honey traps. Leveraging the Prisma Cloud HoneyCloud project’s ephemeral key leaks and policy overrides, Unit42 obtained full visibility, informing Prisma Cloud Secrets Security, CI/CD IaC scanning, Cortex XDR, and recommendations for independent repo scanning, strict IAM policies, and continuous monitoring.

title: Exploring a Critical Risk in Google Workspace's Domain-Wide Delegation Feature
preprocessed: Unit 42 researchers identified a critical risk in Google Workspace’s domain-wide delegation feature whereby any Google Cloud Platform (GCP) identity with token-generation privileges can request access tokens for a delegated service account and thus impersonate Workspace users; in a typical attack, a malicious insider (for example, a developer with editor rights or an external attacker wielding a stolen Compute Engine default service account token) abuses domain-wide delegation scopes to access Gmail, Drive, Calendar and Docs data or perform actions on behalf of any user, enabling full domain compromise and lateral movement from GCP into Workspace. The vulnerability stems from a mismatch between GCP’s permission model and the high sensitivity of domain-wide delegation, and detection requires correlating GCP audit logs for service account key creation with Google Workspace authorization logs. Recommended mitigations include placing delegated service accounts at higher levels in the GCP resource hierarchy to restrict which identities can generate tokens, enforcing least-privilege roles and specific OAuth scopes, and leveraging Google’s Recommender API and audit-log monitoring; Palo Alto Networks customers are protected via Cortex XDR and Prisma Cloud.

title: Over the Kazuar’s Nest: Cracking Down on a Freshly Hatched Backdoor Used by Pensive Ursa (Aka Turla)
preprocessed: Since its debut in 2017 as an advanced .NET second-stage backdoor, Kazuar—attributed to Russian FSB–linked Pensive Ursa (Turla)—reemerged in July 2023 targeting Ukraine’s defense sector alongside a new Capibar first-stage loader, marking its first wild appearance since late 2020. This upgraded variant features extensive stealth and anti-analysis countermeasures—fake 2008 compilation timestamps, custom multi-layer string encryption, assembly-location checks and GUID-based pseudorandom directory and mutex generation—and boasts 45 C2-driven commands for comprehensive system profiling, data collection and credential theft from cloud platforms, source control and Signal. It supports six injection modes (inject, zombify, combined, remote, single and non-interactive), a multithreaded architecture for asynchronous task execution, and a hybrid AES–RSA encryption scheme for task/result files, complicating forensic recovery. Organizations can detect and block Kazuar with Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR/XSIAM and WildFire, and engage Unit 42 Incident Response teams for targeted hunting and mitigation guidance.

title: Lampion Is Back With ClickFix Lures
preprocessed: Unit 42 researchers uncovered a targeted Lampion infostealer campaign in late 2024–early 2025 against Portuguese government, finance and transportation organizations that reuses infrastructure and TTPs dating back to 2019 while introducing ClickFix social-engineering lures—victims receive a phishing email with a malicious ZIP attachment containing an HTML redirect to autoridade-tributaria[.]com, where they are duped into copying a “#Habilitar Visualização de ficheiro” PowerShell command into the Run dialog; this command downloads an obfuscated Visual Basic script (stage 1) that writes a second-stage downloader in %TEMP% and schedules its execution, which in turn fetches a third-stage 30–50 MB VBS stager responsible for reconnaissance (WMI AV checks, VM/sandbox detection, MD5-based victim ID Base64 exfiltration) and constructs a hostname-named .cmd file in the Startup folder to trigger system shutdown and launch a fourth-stage >700 MB DLL loader via rundll32.exe using Portuguese-named exports, although the final Lampion payload download was commented out—this dispersed, highly obfuscated multi-stage chain highlights the need for enhanced PowerShell/VBScript monitoring, advanced detection (Cortex XDR VBS Local Analysis, WildFire, URL Filtering, DNS Security) and ClickFix awareness training to thwart sophisticated banking-credential theft.

title: Threat Group Assessment: Muddled Libra (Updated May 16, 2025)
preprocessed: Since mid-2022, Unit 42 has attributed over 100 high-value cryptocurrency and BPO incidents to Muddled Libra—a fluid subset of the Scattered Spider collective—initially executing structured smishing and 0ktapus phishing campaigns (leveraging over 200 realistic mobile-auth portals) against large business process outsourcers, then evolving in 2023 into an ALPHV/BlackCat affiliate with multi-million-dollar extortion demands, later resuming high-profile attacks in late 2024 and expanding through May 2025 into software automation, telecom, hospitality, finance and retail verticals; their adaptable tradecraft blends social engineering of IT helpdesks to reset passwords and MFA, inside BPO access, legitimate remote management tools for CRM exfiltration, NSOCKS/TrueSocks anonymizing proxies, custom virtual machines, the open-source “bedevil” rootkit on VMware vCenter, email-forwarding rules to hijack incident response communications, and AI-driven voice spoofing for vishing, with members cycling via Discord and Telegram to refresh niche skills and spawn offshoots such as Scatter Swine and Octo Tempest, while leveraging deep incident response framework knowledge to persist in environments and repeatedly reclaim stolen data before affiliating with DragonForce for ransomware; defenders should deploy interwoven modern security architectures (Cortex XSIAM/XDR, Advanced URL Filtering, DNS Security, App-ID), enforce strict access controls, conduct rigorous awareness training, and maintain vigilant MITRE-mapped monitoring (T1566, T1556, T1215, T1562) to thwart these multifaceted, evolving extortion campaigns.

title: P2PInfect: The Rusty Peer-to-Peer Self-Replicating Worm
preprocessed: On July 11, 2023, Unit 42 discovered P2PInfect, a cross-platform, self-replicating worm written in Rust that exploits the critical Lua sandbox escape vulnerability CVE-2022-0543 (CVSS 10.0) to compromise both Linux and Windows Redis instances, identifying over 307,000 publicly accessible systems—934 of which are currently vulnerable. Following initial exploitation, P2PInfect’s dropper establishes a TLS 1.3-secured peer-to-peer C2 network over variable ports to distribute OS-specific binaries (scanners, potential miner components, PowerShell scripts) and auto-update its configuration; infected hosts then scan exposed Redis and SSH services, join the botnet to serve payloads, and form a resilient propagation mechanism in cloud container environments. No definitive cryptomining activity was observed, nor any links to established Redis-focused groups (e.g., PurpleUrchin, TeamTNT, Kinsing). Recommended actions include immediate patching of CVE-2022-0543, restriction of Redis exposure, monitoring for anomalous P2P traffic, and deployment of advanced cloud and firewall threat protections.

title: Over the Kazuar’s Nest: Cracking Down on a Freshly Hatched Backdoor Used by Pensive Ursa (Aka Turla)
preprocessed: Unit 42 researchers have uncovered a new, substantially upgraded variant of the Kazuar .NET backdoor—previously observed in 2017 as a second-stage payload by Russian Federal Security Service–linked Pensive Ursa (Turla/Uroburos)—that re-emerged in July 2023 targeting Ukrainian defense organizations via a multi-stage Capibar loader to steal Signal messages, cloud and source-control credentials and other high-value data. This variant adds robust anti-analysis checks (Assembly.Location byte-array loader validation, faked 2008 compilation timestamps), extensive string encryption (multiple custom and ConfuserEx ciphers), hybrid AES payload encryption with RSA-encrypted IV/key plus HMAC-MD5 integrity, and obfuscation of IOCs. It supports 45 discrete commands for system profiling, credential theft and automated task workflows in a multithreaded solver component that writes AES- and RSA-protected result files. Kazuar also implements multiple injection modes (inject, browser- and svchost.exe-centric zombify, combined fallback, remote proxy, single and headless) and uses GUID-derived pseudorandom directories and mutexes to evade detection, while hard-coded agent and build identifiers enable variant tracking. Code overlap with Sunburst underscores its sophistication. Unit 42 has released detailed IOCs, artifacts and a GitHub appendix, and recommends Palo Alto Networks NGFW Advanced Threat Prevention, Cortex XDR, XSIAM, Advanced WildFire and Unit 42 incident response engagement to detect, hunt and mitigate this persistent threat.

title: Chinese PlugX Malware Hidden in Your USB Devices?
preprocessed: In a Unit 42 incident response to a suspected Black Basta breach, analysts discovered a novel USB-spreading variant of the decade-old Chinese-linked PlugX implant alongside GootLoader and Brute Ratel C4, revealing that attackers hijack the digitally-signed x32dbg.exe debugger via DLL side-loading (MITRE T1574.002) by deploying a malicious, unsigned x32bridge.dll to load an encrypted payload (x32bridge.dat) into memory, then infect both host and attached removable media by creating hidden no-break space (U+00A0) directory trees (e.g., \\u00A0\\u00A0\\RECYCLER.BIN\\files) with custom desktop.ini icons and obfuscated .lnk shortcuts that execute via %comspec%/q/c to evade Windows Explorer and cmd.exe (visible only through Unix-like mounts or forensic tools); a related PlugX variant further exfiltrates Adobe PDF and Word files into a concealed “da520e5” subfolder, underscoring evolving persistence, lateral-spread and data-theft capabilities used in high-profile incidents (e.g., the 2015 OPM breach), and highlighting the need for robust detection and prevention via solutions like Cortex XDR and WildFire.

title: Inside SnipBot: The Latest RomCom Malware Variant
preprocessed: In early April, Palo Alto Networks’ Advanced WildFire and Cortex XDR uncovered SnipBot—a new v5.0 iteration of the RomCom RAT family—employing advanced window message–based control-flow obfuscation and anti-sandbox checks (filename hash and HKCU\…\RecentDocs entries) in a multi-stage chain beginning with a PDF-labeled EXE downloader signed using a likely stolen certificate; the downloader contacts xeontime[.]com for config-pdf.dll, which uses registry-based COM hijacking to load keyprov.dll from drvmcprotect[.]com into explorer.exe, decrypts payloads stored in HKCU\Software\AppDataSoft\Software, and opens a TCP listener on port 1342 for commands to update, delete, or execute modules. The main backdoor single.dll (mutex “SnipMutex”) supports 27 encrypted commands for drive and process enumeration, file upload/download, and remote module execution, facilitating network pivoting and targeted file exfiltration. Active since December 2023 (RomCom activity since 2022), SnipBot’s tactics, stolen certificates, unique obfuscation, and sophisticated loader underscore a high-risk threat actor likely focused on intelligence gathering; Palo Alto products classify its samples, URLs, and domains as malicious to prevent compromise.

title: Fake CVE-2023-40477 Proof of Concept Leads to VenomRAT
preprocessed: On Aug. 17, 2023, the Zero Day Initiative publicly reported an RCE vulnerability in WinRAR (CVE-2023-40477) originally disclosed to the vendor on June 8; just four days later, an actor using the alias whalersplonk published a fake PoC on GitHub that repurposed a GeoServer CVE-2023-25157 exploit script to launch an infection chain rather than trigger the WinRAR flaw. Analysis of poc.py shows it writes a batch file to %TEMP%, executes an encoded PowerShell script that downloads c.ps1 and, subsequently, a VenomRAT v6.0.3 payload named Windows.Gaming.Preview.exe from checkblacklistwords[.]eu, installs it under %APPDATA%\Drivers, creates a scheduled task for persistence, enables keylogging to %APPDATA%\MyData\DataLogs_keylog_offline.txt, and contacts C2 at 94.156.253.109:4449. This RAT supports HVNC, stealer, grabber and commands such as plu_gin, HVNCStop, loadofflinelog, keylogsetting, filterinfo, and Po_ng. The malicious domain was registered at least 10 days before the CVE’s disclosure, indicating pre-positioned infrastructure aimed at opportunistically compromising researchers or other miscreants, not end users directly. Although the fake PoC repo was removed by the time of analysis, Palo Alto Networks WildFire and Advanced URL Filtering had already auto-categorized the domain as malicious and blocked the chain. Unit 42 researchers, alongside CTA partner Broadcom/Symantec, have published full IoCs and SHA lists on GitHub to support proactive defenses across WinRAR’s 500 million-strong user base.

title: Apache ERP Zero-Day Underscores Dangers of Incomplete Patches
preprocessed: On December 26, 2023, Apache disclosed a critical zero-day in its OfBiz ERP framework (CVE-2023-51467) that permits unauthenticated attackers to bypass authentication and trigger server-side request forgery leading to remote code execution—despite an earlier December 5 patch for a related XML-RPC RCE flaw (CVE-2023-49070), SonicWall researcher Hasib Vhora (with Gao Tian and L0ne1y) reverse-engineered the fix, reported additional auth-bypass vectors on December 14, and by December 21 unknown groups were already probing the vulnerability, highlighting adversaries’ tactic of diff-analyzing incomplete patches to circumvent defenses; because OfBiz underpins software supply chains such as Atlassian Jira, this oversight risked widespread compromise, prompting the Apache Security Response Team to deploy a second patch within hours and urge users to update to the latest release, enforce least-privilege access, and strengthen patch validation and monitoring.

title: Microsoft: Russia's Sandworm APT Exploits Edge Bugs Globally
preprocessed: Since late 2021, Russia’s GRU-aligned Sandworm APT (Seashell Blizzard) has deployed an initial-access subgroup dubbed BadPilot to stealthily breach high-value telecom, oil and gas, shipping, arms-manufacturing and government networks worldwide by exploiting critical CVSS 9.8 vulnerabilities—Zimbra CVE-2022-41352, Exchange CVE-2021-34473 and Outlook CVE-2023-23397—and, from early 2024, remote-monitoring-and-management flaws such as Fortinet FortiClient EMS CVE-2023-48788 and ScreenConnect CVE-2024-1709 (CVSS 10.0). Following initial access, BadPilot establishes persistence via its custom LocalOlive web shell or legitimate RMM tools (“ShadowLink”) configured as Tor hidden services, harvests credentials, performs lateral movement, exfiltrates data and stages follow-on operations. These agile, low-noise TTPs have underpinned Sandworm’s high-impact campaigns—from NotPetya and 2018 Olympic disruptions to multiple destructive power-grid outages in Ukraine and an attack on Denmark’s energy sector—advancing Russia’s strategic objectives. Critical organizations must therefore enforce timely patching of Internet-facing services, continuous asset monitoring and robust defense-in-depth controls.

title: Iranian APT 'BladedFeline' Hides in Network for 8 Years
preprocessed: ESET’s analysis of the Iranian APT “BladedFeline,” assessed with medium confidence as a subgroup of APT34/OilRig, reveals the actor infiltrated Kurdish and Iraqi government networks as early as September 2017 and remained undetected until 2023–2024, maintaining strategic espionage access to high-ranking officials tied to Western diplomatic relations and regional oil reserves. The group deployed a suite of proprietary and modified implants—most notably the simple, uncompressed 64-bit Shahmaran backdoor, the Whisper backdoor, the PrimeCache IIS module, the VideoSRV reverse shell, PowerShell executors and multiple reverse tunnels—via unknown initial vectors and a likely internet-facing web server exploit, using unencrypted C2 channels over normal traffic to execute commands, manipulate files and exfiltrate data. ESET identified code overlaps between PrimeCache and OilRig’s RDAT and common usage of VideoSRV, expects continued implant development, and advises defenders to maintain detailed inventories of VIP-used applications, establish network baselines to detect stealthy exfiltration paths and anomalies, and audit internet-facing servers to thwart initial compromise.

title: Critical Bluetooth Flaw Exposes Android, Apple & Linux Devices to Takeover
preprocessed: Security researcher Marc Newlin of SkySafe disclosed CVE-2023-45866, a critical, decade-old keystroke-injection flaw in the Bluetooth host state-machine that exploits an unauthenticated pairing mechanism in the Bluetooth specification to trick macOS (13.3.3), iOS (16.6, even in Lockdown Mode), Android (from 4.2.2 through 14 on devices including Pixel 7/6/4a, Pixel 2, Nexus 5, BLU DASH), and Linux BlueZ stacks (Ubuntu 18.04–23.10) into pairing with a malicious emulated keyboard, enabling remote attackers within Bluetooth range to run a Python-based script, inject arbitrary keystrokes, install apps, forward emails or texts, and execute commands without user confirmation or biometric/password authentication. After informing Apple, Google, Canonical, and the Bluetooth SIG between August and September, patches have been released for Android 11–14 and BlueZ (via GitHub) but Apple has yet to announce a timeline for CVE-2023-42929, proof-of-concept exploit scripts will be published in January, and no active in-the-wild exploitation has been observed to date.

title: Comcast Xfinity Breached via CitrixBleed; 35M Customers Affected
preprocessed: Since at least August 2023, threat actors have exploited CVE-2023-4966 (CitrixBleed), a 7.5-rated flaw in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway, culminating in an October 16–19 breach at Comcast Xfinity that exposed 35,879,455 customers’ usernames, hashed passwords, names, contact details, last four SSN digits, dates of birth and security Q&A; despite Citrix’s October 10 patch and Comcast’s claim of prompt mitigation, attackers used publicly available proofs-of-concept and rumored Python automation scripts to extract session tokens from device memory, hijack active sessions and bypass authentication, a tactic linked by ReliaQuest to at least five threat groups including LockBit; this incident highlights the necessity not only of timely patching and reboots but also of invalidating all active and persistent session tokens, enforcing multi-factor authentication, resetting credentials and maintaining continuous 24x7 monitoring to prevent further data exfiltration and ransomware deployment.

title: Ferret Malware Added to 'Contagious Interview' Campaign
preprocessed: Researchers have observed a North Korean “Contagious Interview” campaign leveraging a macOS malware family dubbed Ferret—first documented in December 2023 and again in December 2024/January 2025—to lure targets via fake virtual job‐interview links that prompt installation of shell scripts, persistence agents and a Google Chrome update imposter; these installers drop the BeaverTail JavaScript loader, which in turn deploys the Python backdoor InvisibleFerret to harvest web‐browser credentials and crypto‐wallet data. Variants in the campaign include FROSTYFERRET_UI, FRIENDLYFERRET_SECD, MULTI_FROSTYFERRET_CMDCODES and, as of February 3, the newly revealed under‐the‐radar FlexibleFerret, suggesting DPRK actors are honing evasion and expanding beyond job‐seeker targeting to developers more broadly. Apple’s recent XProtect signature update aims to block known variants, but organizations should urgently apply patches, monitor for anomalous shell script execution, persistence agent installs and spoofed update processes, and inspect network traffic for BeaverTail/InvisibleFerret command-and-control indicators to disrupt this evolving threat.

title: A New, Spookier Gh0st RAT Malware Haunts Global Cyber Targets
preprocessed: Originally released by the Chinese C.Rufus Security Team in March 2008, the open-source Gh0st RAT has reemerged in late August 2023 as SugarGh0st RAT, deployed by a China-linked actor against South Korean targets and Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs via phishing-delivered archives containing Windows .LNK shortcuts that execute embedded JavaScript, display customized decoy documents, and install the 32-bit C++ DLL. The backdoor collects system data, grants full remote control—including process and file manipulation, log removal, keylogging, screenshot and camera access, and arbitrary command execution—and now evades legacy detection by altering its C2 protocol packet header from 5 to 8 magic bytes. Cisco Talos highlights these cosmetic yet effective modifications as a blind spot in signature-based defenses, underscoring the urgent need for updated heuristics and layered monitoring.

title: Google Patches Another Chrome Zero-Day as Browser Attacks Mount
preprocessed: On November 29, 2023, Google’s Threat Analysis Group disclosed and patched CVE-2023-6345, an actively exploited integer-overflow vulnerability in the Skia 2D graphics library that permits sandbox escape via a malicious file on Chrome versions prior to 119.0.6045.199—its seventh zero-day this year and fourth since August—underscoring a broader surge of critical browser flaws such as WebP heap overflow CVE-2023-4863 impacting Chrome, Safari and Firefox; Chromium-fork bug CVE-2023-5217 in Edge, Opera, Brave and Vivaldi; and four Apple WebKit zero-days (CVE-2023-28205, ‑32409, ‑28204, ‑32373) that commercial spyware vendors like Predator and likely state-sponsored actors have exploited to drop malware, steal credentials and exfiltrate data. Experts attribute this trend to browsers’ ubiquitous role in delivering web applications, expanded device-access features (USB, Bluetooth, WebGPU) and Chromium’s cross-platform reach, which amplifies an exploit’s impact across multiple browsers; they recommend organizations prioritize rigorous patch management, real-time version tracking and strict network segmentation to contain infection pathways and mitigate future attacks.

title: Evasive Jupyter Infostealer Campaign Showcases Dangerous Variant
preprocessed: Security researchers have identified a sophisticated new variant of the Jupyter infostealer (aka Yellow Cockatoo/Solarmarker/Polazert) that since late October 2023 has leveraged digitally signed payloads, PowerShell modifications and InnoSetup installers to backdoor Windows machines, harvest credentials—including admin privileges, browser cookies, password manager data, crypto-wallet logins and remote-access app credentials—and enable encrypted C2 communications for additional payload deployment. Distributed via SEO poisoning, search-engine redirects, drive-by downloads and phishing-themed executables (e.g., “An-employers-guide-to-group-health-continuation.exe”), Jupyter uses shellcode hollowing and staged in-memory execution to evade detection. Morphisec, BlackBerry and VMware findings rank Jupyter among the top ten infostealers amid a broader rise in remote-work attacks, underscoring the need for enhanced endpoint monitoring, strict certificate validation and user education to disrupt this persistent data-stealing threat.

title: Attackers Exploit 6-Year-Old Microsoft Office Bug to Spread Spyware
preprocessed: Attackers are leveraging the six-year-old CVE-2017-11882 Microsoft Office RCE vulnerability via malicious Excel attachments in socially engineered “orders” and “invoices” emails to initiate a multi-stage infection chain that delivers the Agent Tesla RAT and advanced keylogger. Once a user opens the Excel file on an unpatched Office build, it connects to a malicious server to retrieve a heavily obfuscated VBS script, which in turn downloads a JPEG containing a Base64-encoded DLL. The VBS launches PowerShell to extract and load the DLL, then abuses RegAsm.exe—disguised as a legitimate registry utility—to inject a thread that fetches and executes the Agent Tesla payload. Deployed Agent Tesla uses clipboard and window hooking for keystroke logging, screen capture and browser, mail and FTP credential theft, exfiltrating data via attacker-controlled Telegram bots. Zscaler’s detailed IoCs—including malicious URLs, file hashes and Telegram endpoints—underscore the critical need for organizations to patch legacy Office versions, deploy email defenses, and monitor for the described artifacts to prevent credential compromise and system takeover.

title: Microsoft Outlook Zero-Click Security Flaws Triggered by Sound File
preprocessed: In December 2023, Akamai researchers disclosed a chained zero-click remote code execution (RCE) exploit against Microsoft Outlook by combining a patched-but-bypassed privilege-escalation flaw (CVE-2023-35384, the second bypass of the March-patched CVE-2023-23397) with a newly found Windows Media Foundation sound-file parsing error (CVE-2023-36710); by sending an email reminder with a UNC path, Outlook’s improper URL zone validation retrieves and auto-plays a malicious audio file, enabling arbitrary code execution without user interaction, password-hash theft and unauthorized Exchange access—techniques already observed in the wild by Russia’s Fancy Bear—despite Microsoft’s March, May and August patches (including MapUrlToZone mitigations) being repeatedly bypassed, underscoring the risks of complex patch-over fixes; organizations should immediately apply the latest security updates, disable or remove custom notification sounds and consider deprecating the vulnerable reminder feature to prevent future exploit chains.

title: Qantas Airlines Breached, Impacting 6M Customers
preprocessed: On June 30, 2025, Qantas Airlines discovered that hackers had exploited a vulnerability in a third-party call-center platform to access personally identifiable information (PII) for approximately six million customers—names, email addresses, phone numbers, birth dates and frequent-flyer numbers—but not passports or payment data—before the breach was contained shortly thereafter; in response, Qantas has launched a dedicated support line and webpage, tightened IT monitoring and access controls, and is investigating alongside federal authorities.  Cybersecurity experts from CyberCX attribute “all the hallmarks” of the attack to the advanced persistent threat group Scattered Spider (aka UNC3944, 0ktapus/Roasted Oktapus, Scatter Swine, Octo Tempest, Muddled Libra), which the FBI recently warned is increasingly targeting aviation, while government minister Tony Burke cautioned Australians to resist cold calls or unsolicited emails and to verify Qantas communications via published contact channels to thwart follow-on phishing campaigns.  Apollo Information Systems CISO Andy Bennett highlights attackers’ use of AI to amalgamate PII from multiple breaches for highly personalized social‐engineering, underscoring the need for rigorous vendor security assessments, proactive threat hunting and cross-sector collaboration under Australia’s $1.67 billion cybersecurity strategy and new critical-infrastructure legislation.

title: Threat Group Using Rare Data Transfer Tactic in New RemcosRAT Campaign
preprocessed: UNC-0050, a suspected politically motivated threat group, has launched a new RemcosRAT campaign against Ukrainian government agencies using job-themed phishing emails purporting Israeli Defense Forces consultancy opportunities to distribute .lnk stagers that harvest system details and fetch a 6.hta HTML app via native Windows binaries; the HTML app executes a PowerShell script to download additional payloads (word_update.exe and ofer.docx), culminating in the installation of RemcosRAT—an RAT used since 2016 for remote surveillance, system and user data exfiltration, and backdoor command execution—while evading antivirus and EDR tools. Uniquely, UNC-0050 leverages Windows anonymous pipes for one-way interprocess communication to covertly channel data off compromised hosts, a relatively rare but stealthy technique marking a leap in the group’s sophistication. Uptycs researchers Karthickkumar Kathiresan and Shilpesh Trivedi note this tactic’s ability to bypass endpoint defenses, reinforcing the campaign’s threat to Windows-reliant government sectors. This activity follows multiple 2023 CERT-UA alerts documenting mass-phishing campaigns distributing RemcosRAT via telecom-, judicial- and debt-themed attachments in November and December, underscoring UNC-0050’s persistence in Ukraine-focused intelligence collection and the urgent need for enhanced email filtering, IPC monitoring, and behavior-based detection.

title: Payment Card-Skimming Campaign Now Targeting Websites in North America
preprocessed: Since at least May 2023, BlackBerry researchers have identified a technically sophisticated Chinese-speaking threat actor—dubbed Silent Skimmer—that after over a year skimming card data from Asia/Pacific e-commerce and point-of-sale sites has expanded its campaign to North and Latin America, compromising organizations across multiple sectors by exploiting known web application vulnerabilities—most notably CVE-2019-18935 in Progress Software’s Telerik UI previously used by China’s Hafnium and Vietnam’s XE Group—on IIS servers to upload a malicious DLL and achieve remote code execution; using a multi-stage toolkit comprising privilege escalation exploits, a remote access tool, stagers/downloaders, and post-exploit utilities along with open-source binaries and scripts to inject card-skimming code into payment pages; and dynamically rotating short-lived, regionally co-located Microsoft Azure VPS-based C2 servers (each active less than a week) to blend exfiltration traffic with normal operations, mirroring Magecart tactics that have impacted hundreds of thousands of sites (e.g., British Airways, Ticketmaster, Newegg), and highlighting the imperative for prompt patching of third-party components, comprehensive web-app security audits, and vigilant monitoring of anomalous C2 infrastructure to thwart credential and payment data theft.

title: Syrian Threat Group Peddles Destructive SilverRAT
preprocessed: Cyfirma’s January 3, 2024 threat analysis exposed Anonymous Arabic—a Turkish/Syrian-linked cybercriminal group run by developers “Dangerous silver” and “Monstermc”—as the creators of SilverRAT v1, a Windows-only remote access Trojan builder leaked in October 2023 that enables keylogging, ransomware deployment, antivirus evasion, system restore point deletion, configurable IP- or web-based C2 infrastructure, and delayed payload execution, with the developers still refining an Android version; the group markets malware-as-a-service, cracked RATs, and DDoS-on-demand via Telegram, Turkhackteam, 1877 and Russian forums, leveraging a BossNet botnet to target large entities, and exhibits a recruitment pipeline from teenage game hackers—underscoring escalating technical sophistication in Middle East underground markets and indicating a pressing need for targeted juvenile diversion programs.

title: Global TeamCity Exploitation Opens Door to SolarWinds-Style Nightmare
preprocessed: Russia’s APT29 (aka Cozy Bear/Nobelium) has been exploiting a critical unauthenticated remote-code-execution flaw in JetBrains TeamCity (CVE-2023-42793, CVSS 9.8) since September—shortly after JetBrains issued a patch and Rapid7 published a proof-of-concept—to gain initial access to SDLC management servers, escalate privileges, move laterally, deploy stealthy backdoors that persist through updates, and potentially manipulate build pipelines or insert malicious updates in SolarWinds-style supply-chain attacks; CISA, FBI, NSA and international partners warn that around 800 internet-exposed instances remain vulnerable (with uncounted internally reachable servers also at risk), and that North Korea’s Lazarus and Andariel groups have similarly weaponized the same flaw, prompting Fortinet to report multi-actor post-exploit techniques in live incidents; mitigation guidance urges immediate upgrading to TeamCity 2023.05.4, removal of public exposure, comprehensive IoC-based threat hunting across servers and build agents, and full compromise assessments to eradicate entrenched backdoors.

title: North Korea Debuts 'SpectralBlur' Malware Amid macOS Onslaught
preprocessed: In August, the DPRK–linked APT TA444 (aka APT38, BlueNoroff, BlackAlicanto, Coperenicum, Sapphire Sleet and Stardust Chollima) deployed SpectralBlur, a custom post-exploitation macOS backdoor that leverages command-and-control instructions to upload/download files, spawn a shell, update its configuration, delete files or enter hibernation/sleep mode; Proofpoint researcher Greg Lesnewich identified code overlaps with the KandyKorn macOS data stealer—earlier tied to Lazarus Group phishing campaigns against blockchain engineers—linking both tools through shared strings and infrastructure. This rapid iteration of proprietary macOS malware underscores TA444’s dedicated development capability and signals an intensified DPRK espionage focus on Apple users, particularly within the cryptocurrency sector, demonstrating persistent operational tempo and advanced post-exploitation tactics.

title: Russia's 'Star Blizzard' APT Upgrades Its Stealth, Only to Be Unmasked Again
preprocessed: Since at least 2017, the Kremlin-sponsored APT group Star Blizzard (aka Seaborgium, BlueCharlie, Callisto Group, Coldriver) has conducted credential-theft and influence campaigns against NATO-aligned NGOs, think tanks, journalists, academic institutions and Ukraine supporters, and despite a Microsoft disruption in August 2022 and ongoing Recorded Future monitoring, its December 2023 upgrade unveiled five new evasion tricks: weaponizing MailerLite and HubSpot email-marketing platforms to provision dedicated subdomains and sender addresses that redirect via URLs into actor-controlled Evilginx infrastructure; embedding links in password-protected PDFs or cloud-hosted files whose passwords are sent alongside to bypass filters; using a DNS provider as a reverse proxy to obscure VPS IPs; deploying server-side JavaScript to thwart automated scans; and employing a more randomized domain generation algorithm—though Namecheap registrations and Let’s Encrypt TLS certificates remain persistent hallmarks. Recent operations have targeted U.S. grants-management portals, UK officials including former MI6 chief Richard Dearlove and MP Stewart McDonald, and employees at U.S. nuclear labs, demonstrating successful credential harvesting and hack-and-leak influence tactics; defenders should monitor for sudden spikes in password-protected document deliveries, anomalies in marketing-platform subdomains and redirect chains, DGA-style naming patterns, and reverse-proxy DNS usage to detect and disrupt future intrusions.

title: APTs Swarm Zimbra Zero-Day to Steal Government Info Worldwide
preprocessed: At least four distinct campaigns exploited CVE-2023-37580, a reflected XSS zero-day in Zimbra Collaboration Suite, to siphon emails, attachments, user credentials and authentication tokens from government organizations worldwide before the July 5 hotfix and July 25 official patch; in chronological order, unidentified actors targeted Greece on June 29 via malicious URLs that, when clicked during active Zimbra sessions, deployed a data-theft framework and auto-forward rules, Winter Vivern’s APT leveraged unique exploit links to hit Moldova and Tunisia between July 11 and 25, another group used a phishing-style XSS link in Vietnam to harvest webmail credentials and exfiltrate them to a compromised government domain, and on August 25 unknown attackers employed an N-day variant to steal tokens from Pakistan’s mail servers; Google’s Threat Analysis Group warns these campaigns underscore the urgency of promptly applying open-source fixes, hardening mail-server code to prevent XSS, and maintaining vigilant patch management as attackers continuously monitor public repositories for unpatched vulnerabilities.

title: Attackers Target Max-Severity Apache ActiveMQ Bug to Drop Ransomware
preprocessed: On Oct. 27 the Apache Software Foundation disclosed CVE-2023-46604, a critical (CVSS 10.0) insecure-deserialization flaw in Apache ActiveMQ (all versions prior to 5.18.3 and Legacy OpenWire Module before 5.17.6) that enables unauthenticated remote code execution, and by Nov. 2 threat actors had begun exploiting publicly available proof-of-concept code to drop HelloKitty ransomware on at least two Rapid7 customer networks; ShadowServer data show some 3,329 internet-exposed brokers remain unpatched, making small and midsize organizations running outdated ActiveMQ instances prime targets, and the attackers—characterized by Rapid7 as “clumsy” due to repeated failed encryption attempts—have employed rudimentary double-extortion tactics, prompting ASF to release patched versions and urgent recommendations to upgrade immediately to mitigate widespread ransomware impact.

title: IAM Credentials in Public GitHub Repositories Harvested in Minutes - SecurityWeek
preprocessed: Over the past two years, the EleKtra-Leak threat actor has leveraged automated tools to clone public GitHub repositories in real time—typically harvesting plaintext AWS IAM credentials within five minutes of exposure while blocklisting decoy or high-risk repositories to evade honey traps—and used those credentials, when not flagged by GitHub or quarantined by AWS, to spin up multiple EC2 instances across accessible regions via VPN for cryptojacking; Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 identified 474 unique malicious miners between August 30 and October 6, mining privacy-focused Monero and obscuring gains, which underscores persistent cloud resource abuse and gaps in coordinated protection, prompting a strong recommendation for independent CI/CD security practices such as pre-commit and periodic secret scanning to safeguard repository hygiene and prevent credential leakage.

title: Fog Ransomware Attack Employs Unusual Tools - SecurityWeek
preprocessed: In May 2025, Fog ransomware operators stealthily compromised a financial institution in Asia two weeks before detonating their payload, first infecting two Exchange servers and initiating their chain with GC2—a Google Sheets/SharePoint command-and-control and exfiltration tool linked to APT41 in 2023—then using Stowaway as a proxy to deploy Syteca (formerly Ekran) employee-monitoring software loaded with libraries for screen capture and keystroke logging. For lateral movement they invoked PsExec, SMBExec, Syteca and GC2, while Freefilesync and MegaSync exfiltrated data; the Adaptix C2 Agent Beacon, an open-source post-exploitation framework akin to Cobalt Strike, established command-and-control, a custom Windows service ensured persistence, and Impacket likely executed the Fog payload. Symantec notes this unusual fusion of legitimate monitoring tools, open-source pentesting utilities and ransomware indicates a primary espionage objective—with ransomware serving as a decoy or revenue stream—mirroring evolving TTPs that leverage compromised VPN credentials, vulnerable Veeam Backup & Replication servers (CVE-2024-40711) and phishing for initial access, and marking Fog’s shift since its 2024 emergence targeting the U.S. education sector.

title: Qantas Confirms 5.7 Million Impacted by Data Breach - SecurityWeek
preprocessed: On June 30, threat actors exploited a vulnerability in a third-party call-center platform used by Qantas to exfiltrate 5.7 million unique customer records—none of which involved direct compromise of Qantas’s own systems—and on July 7 the airline confirmed a likely extortion attempt when the hacker made contact; after deduplication Qantas found 4 million records contained names, email addresses and Frequent Flyer details, 1.2 million contained only names and emails, and 1.7 million included additional data such as addresses (1.3 million), dates of birth (1.1 million), phone numbers (900 000), gender (400 000) and meal preferences (10 000), while no credit card, financial or passport information was stored on the breached platform. The company has begun notifying affected customers, deployed enhanced security controls, and is collaborating closely with the Australian Cyber Security Centre, the National Cyber Security Coordinator and the Australian Federal Police to investigate the supply-chain weakness, reinforce third-party risk management, and bolster monitoring and incident response capabilities to mitigate future breaches.

title: Russian APT Exploiting Mail Servers Against Government, Defense Organizations - SecurityWeek
preprocessed: Active since at least 2004 and linked to the Russian GRU, APT28 (Fancy Bear, Forest Blizzard, Sednit, Sofacy) has been exploiting XSS vulnerabilities in Roundcube, Horde, MDaemon and Zimbra mail servers across Europe, Africa and South America since September 2023 under “Operation RoundPress,” targeting governments tied to the Ukraine conflict—such as Ukraine’s government and defense firms in Bulgaria and Romania—and more broadly French organizations after France’s recent attribution of a dozen government and other entities, including a decade-old TV5Monde attack. Employing CVE-2020-35730 (Roundcube; CISA KEV June 2023), CVE-2023-43770 (Roundcube; KEV February 2024) and zero-day CVE-2024-11182 (MDaemon), APT28 injects malicious JavaScript implants (“SpyPress”) via phishing emails that bypass spam filters and execute in the victim’s browser context to steal webmail credentials through hidden forms or counterfeit login pages, harvest messages and contacts, create forwarding rules, and defeat two-factor authentication. ESET’s findings highlight the convenience of remote-triggered webmail XSS, the prevalence of unpatched servers, and the urgent need for organizations to apply KEV-listed patches, enforce robust email filtering, and monitor for anomalous mailbox behaviors to mitigate email exfiltration and credential compromise.

title: Russian Government Hackers Caught Buying Passwords from Cybercriminals - SecurityWeek
preprocessed: Microsoft’s latest joint report with Dutch intelligence exposes a year-long espionage campaign by the Russia-linked APT “Void Blizzard,” which has systematically purchased stolen credentials from infostealer markets to fuel password-spraying attacks against European and North American government and defense contractors—particularly NATO states and Ukraine—before pivoting in recent weeks to adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) spear-phishing via a typo-squatted Microsoft Entra login page and malicious QR code for a sham European defense summit. Leveraging the open-source Evilginx framework, the group captures usernames, passwords and session cookies, then abuses legitimate cloud APIs such as Exchange Online and Microsoft Graph to enumerate mailboxes (including shared folders), automate bulk exfiltration of emails, files and, in some cases, Microsoft Teams chats, and uses AzureHound to harvest Entra ID tenant configurations. Since mid-2024, Void Blizzard’s straightforward playbook—steal credentials, infiltrate Exchange or SharePoint Online, and automate data downloads—has compromised telcos, defense suppliers, digital services providers, healthcare and IT firms, posing an elevated risk of wartime intelligence siphoning for Kremlin military and diplomatic operations.

title: Threat Actors Target Accounting Software Used by Construction Contractors - SecurityWeek
preprocessed: Since mid-September, unknown cybercriminals have been conducting large-scale brute-force attacks against internet-exposed instances of Foundation Accounting Software—widely used by construction sub-industries such as plumbing, HVAC and concrete—by targeting the default “sa” administrator and a second high-privilege account within the MSSQL database accessible via TCP port 4243 (opened for Foundation’s mobile app). After an observed peak of roughly 35,000 rapid login attempts to obtain valid credentials, the attackers enable an extended stored procedure (e.g., xp_cmdshell) to execute OS-level commands and scripts, automating lateral movement and data theft across multiple unrelated victims. Huntress has identified just 33 hosts left with unchanged default passwords, alerted all impacted and at-risk customers, and urges organizations to rotate all Foundation credentials, remove direct internet exposure, and disable the exploited stored procedure to mitigate further compromise.

title: AI-Generated Malware Found in the Wild - SecurityWeek
preprocessed: In June 2024, HP’s Threat Research team led by Patrick Schlapfer intercepted a low-grade phishing campaign leveraging HTML smuggling via an AES-encrypted HTML attachment containing JavaScript-embedded decryption logic—a novel twist on typical encrypted archives—which, when decrypted, mimicked a legitimate website but dropped a fully commented, French-language VBScript that registered variables in the Windows Registry, staged a JavaScript payload as a scheduled task, and invoked a PowerShell script to deploy the freely available AsyncRAT infostealer. Schlapfer and co-lead Alex Holland’s analysis, including comparison with generative-AI–produced code, concluded the well-structured, human-readable script was likely authored by gen-AI by a low-skill newcomer benefitting from reduced entry barriers, with no obfuscation or complex infrastructure beyond a single C2 server. This first definitive proof of AI-generated malware in the wild underscores the need for defenders to adapt detection strategies to AI-crafted droppers, monitor anomalous AES-in-JavaScript decryption patterns, and anticipate more sophisticated AI-generated payloads poised to emerge within the next two years, thereby heightening the risk to network and endpoint security.

title: Magnet Goblin Delivers Linux Malware Using One-Day Vulnerabilities - SecurityWeek
preprocessed: Since 2022, Check Point has observed the financially motivated threat actor Magnet Goblin exploiting one-day vulnerabilities in public-facing services—beginning with Magento (CVE-2022-24086) and later targeting Ivanti VPNs (CVE-2023-46805, CVE-2024-21887, CVE-2024-21888, CVE-2024-21893), Qlik Sense (CVE-2023-41265, CVE-2023-41266, CVE-2023-48365) and potentially Apache ActiveMQ—to deliver its custom Linux backdoors NerbianRAT and a streamlined MiniNerbian variant. In recent Ivanti attacks, Magnet Goblin chained the Warpwire JavaScript credential stealer with NerbianRAT, the open-source tunneling tool Ligolo, and RMM platforms (ScreenConnect, AnyDesk) to establish stealthy AES-encrypted raw socket C2 channels (and HTTP C2 for MiniNerbian), enabling system reconnaissance and arbitrary command execution. This campaign underscores the urgent need for aggressive patch management, edge-device hardening, and monitoring for anomalous RMM and tunneling activities.

title: New 'Hadooken' Linux Malware Targets WebLogic Servers - SecurityWeek
preprocessed: Aqua Security’s Nautilus team has uncovered Hadooken, a new Linux malware targeting Oracle WebLogic servers via weak passwords. Post-compromise, attackers deploy redundant shell and Python scripts to ensure download and execution of Hadooken, which enumerates SSH directories to harvest credentials, moves laterally, and clears logs. Hadooken then drops a three-path cryptominer and a Tsunami backdoor with a randomized name, the latter reserved for potential later-stage attacks. Persistence is achieved through multiple cronjobs under varied names and frequencies stored across cron directories. The malware is hosted on two IPs—one German address linked to TeamTNT and Gang 8220, the other inactive in Russia—where researchers also identified a Mallox ransomware PowerShell loader targeting Windows. Static analysis links Hadooken to Rhombus and NoEscape families. With over 230,000 internet-connected WebLogic instances—hundreds of which expose vulnerable admin consoles—this campaign underscores the dual risk of cryptojacking and ransomware across Linux and Windows environments.

title: Magento Vulnerability Exploited to Deploy Persistent Backdoor - SecurityWeek
preprocessed: Threat actors are actively exploiting CVE-2024-20720, a critical Magento OS command injection flaw (CVSS 9.1) patched by Adobe in February 2024, to deploy a persistent backdoor on unpatched ecommerce sites by injecting a crafted XML payload into the database layout template; this payload leverages the Magento layout parser and the default beberlei/assert package to execute system commands tied to the checkout cart, causing the backdoor to be automatically added to the CMS controller and reinjected on each request, enabling remote code execution via POST and facilitating the deployment of a fake Stripe payment skimmer to harvest customer payment data. Users should immediately update to Magento 2.4.6-p4, 2.4.5-p6 or 2.4.4-p7 and perform thorough malware scans to detect and remove any infection.

title: Necro Trojan Infects Google Play Apps With Millions of Downloads - SecurityWeek
preprocessed: Kaspersky researchers have uncovered a new variant of the multi-stage Necro Trojan—first observed in 2019’s CamScanner compromise—that over recent weeks infected two Google Play apps (Wuta Camera, 10 M+ downloads; Max Browser, 1 M+ downloads) and unofficial mods for Spotify, WhatsApp and popular games by exploiting an untrusted advertising-integration SDK; in the Spotify mod the SDK exfiltrated device/app data to a known Necro C&C server and fetched a payload hidden in an image, while in the WhatsApp mod a loader abused Firebase Remote Config for C&C before deploying identical Necro payloads sharing code, structure and C&C infrastructure. Once installed, Necro’s latest variant downloads modules to display and click invisible ads, execute JavaScript in hidden WebViews, download executables and third-party apps, redirect traffic through compromised devices as proxies and subscribe victims to premium services. Between August 26 and September 15, tens of thousands of devices in Russia, Brazil, Vietnam, Ecuador and Mexico were targeted before Google removed the infected apps. Organizations should rigorously vet third-party SDKs, monitor remote-config channels and anomalous network traffic for image-based payload retrieval and invisible ad click-fraud behaviors to mitigate this evolving mobile threat.
