title: Suspicious NuGet Package Harvesting Information From Industrial Systems - SecurityWeek
preprocessed: ReversingLabs discovered that SqzrFramework480, a .NET library published to NuGet in January 2024 under the guise of a Bozhon Precision Industry Technology Co. robot-calibration and GUI framework, contains undocumented routines to harvest industrial system data—capturing primary-screen screenshots every minute in a continuous loop, sending heartbeat ping packets to verify a remote exfiltration server’s availability, opening sockets for data transfer, and extracting credentials, configuration settings and proprietary information from cameras and robotic arms—and, although each function alone is innocuous, their orchestration strongly suggests a supply-chain espionage campaign targeting developers using Bozhon tools; with over 2,400 downloads to date, no clear activation vector beyond explicit invocation by consuming code, and Bozhon unresponsive to inquiries, organizations relying on this package are urged to enforce strict dependency vetting, implement real-time monitoring for anomalous socket and screenshot activity, and report similar findings to NuGet administrators.

title: Chrome Update Patches Zero-Day Vulnerabilities Exploited at Pwn2Own - SecurityWeek
preprocessed: Google released Chrome 123.0.6312.86/.87 on Tuesday to address seven security flaws—four reported by external researchers and three zero-days demonstrated at Pwn2Own Vancouver 2024—including the most severe CVE-2024-2883, a use-after-free bug in ANGLE that earned its finder a $10,000 bounty, and CVE-2024-2885, another high-severity use-after-free in the Dawn renderer. Two additional zero-days, CVE-2024-2886 (use-after-free in WebCodecs) and CVE-2024-2887 (WebAssembly type confusion), were exploited by Seunghyun Lee of KAIST Hacking Lab ($145,000 total reward) and Manfred Paul ($42,500), respectively, with Paul’s broader contributions to Safari and Firefox exploits netting over $200,000 and the contest win. Mozilla proactively patched the flaws first, and although Google reports no known in-the-wild abuse, organizations should urgently deploy the update to mitigate these high-impact memory corruption vulnerabilities.

title: Malware Upload Attack Hits PyPI Repository - SecurityWeek
preprocessed: Maintainers of the Python Package Index (PyPI) were forced this week to suspend new project creation and user registrations after Checkmarx researchers discovered a multi-stage malware upload campaign leveraging typo-squatting to push multiple malicious Python packages created via automation tools. Each package’s setup.py script automatically executed on installation and dynamically constructed a command-and-control URL—by appending the package name as a query parameter—to fetch an additional payload. That payload operated as an advanced info-stealer, harvesting crypto wallets, browser cookies, extensions data and credentials, and deployed a persistence mechanism to survive reboots. Although PyPI has since resolved the incident, the attack underscores the ongoing risk of supply-chain compromises in software ecosystems and highlights the need for stringent package provenance verification, automated code review, two-factor authentication for maintainers and continuous monitoring of repository uploads to prevent similar threats and minimize impact.

title: Windows Zero-Day Exploited by North Korean Hackers in Rootkit Attack - SecurityWeek
preprocessed: Avast researchers uncovered that North Korea’s Lazarus group leveraged a Windows zero-day privilege escalation flaw in Microsoft’s AppLocker “appid.sys” driver (CVE-2024-21338) to execute a truly fileless kernel attack during 2023 intrusions, sending a proof-of-concept exploit to Microsoft in August and prompting a February 2024 patch and subsequent advisory update once active exploitation was confirmed; by abusing a ubiquitous signed driver rather than importing custom code (BYOVD), Lazarus gained kernel read/write primitives, manipulated kernel objects to deploy an enhanced FudModule rootkit—now capable of evading AhnLab V3, Defender, CrowdStrike Falcon and HitmanPro—and bypassed driver allowlisting, then deployed a new remote access trojan for persistent access, underscoring the need for immediate patching, vigilant driver integrity monitoring and behavior-based detection to thwart stealthy, living-off-the-land attacks.

title: Black Basta, Bl00dy Ransomware Exploiting Recent ScreenConnect Flaws - SecurityWeek
preprocessed: Following ConnectWise’s February 19 disclosure of two critical ScreenConnect flaws—CVE-2024-1709 (CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass) and CVE-2024-1708 (CVSS 8.4 path traversal)—an updated advisory two days later warned of active exploitation, and by week’s end a public SlashAndGrab PoC enabled threat actors to mimic admin roles, delete users and seize control. Trend Micro reports Black Basta leveraging these bugs for reconnaissance, AD discovery, privilege escalation, creation of new admin accounts, deployment of Cobalt Strike beacons and scripts to trace recent AD connections before dropping ransomware. Bl00dy similarly abused leaked Conti and LockBit builders to plant ransom notes, while other groups installed XWorm RAT, disabled Windows Defender real-time protection and deployed alternate RMM tools (Atera, Syncro). Immediate patching to ScreenConnect 23.9.8 is critical to halt ongoing remote-access intrusions, ransomware deployment and potential data theft.

title: Over 100 Organizations Targeted in Recent 'StrelaStealer' Attacks - SecurityWeek
preprocessed: Between November 2023 and February 2024, operators of the StrelaStealer infostealer—first documented in November 2022—conducted three large-scale phishing campaigns that leveraged localized spam to target over 100 US and EU organizations across high-tech, finance, legal, manufacturing, government, utilities, energy, insurance and construction sectors. In place of earlier ISO-based LNK/HTML chains, these campaigns delivered ZIP attachments containing JScript droppers that deploy a malicious DLL configured to harvest credentials from popular email clients and exfiltrate them to attacker-controlled C&C servers. The actors enhanced obfuscation, removed debugging symbols and changed attachment types to evade signature-based detection and frustrate forensic analysis. To defend against StrelaStealer’s evolving tactics, security teams should monitor for ZIP-delivered script droppers, anomalous DLL loads and suspicious external connections, and bolster email gateway filtering, endpoint behavior analytics and credential-monitoring controls.

title: Recent TeamCity Vulnerability Exploited in Ransomware Attacks - SecurityWeek
preprocessed: On March 4 JetBrains released patches for two critical TeamCity authentication-bypass flaws (CVE-2024-27198 and CVE-2024-27199) that allow unauthenticated remote attackers to create admin accounts or tokens, but misaligned disclosure with Rapid7—whose researchers publicly detailed the bugs hours after the fixes—triggered mass exploitation: by March 6 LeakIX recorded rogue user creation on approximately 1,400 servers and GuidePoint Security linked the BianLian ransomware group to CVE-2024-27198–driven initial access. Despite JetBrains’ efforts to obfuscate patches and limit reverse engineering time, unpatched customers reported at least two file-encryption incidents and one DDoS-prep compromise. This chain of events underscores the necessity of coordinated vendor–researcher disclosure, accelerated patch deployment, and enhanced patch hardening to mitigate rapid exploit development and reduce organizational exposure.

title: 'Vultur' Android Malware Gets Extensive Device Interaction Capabilities - SecurityWeek
preprocessed: The NCC Group’s latest analysis reveals that the Android banking malware Vultur—originally documented in March 2021 for leveraging AlphaVNC and ngrok to automate screen recording and key-logging—has been upgraded into a full remote-interaction platform: delivered via an SMS phishing campaign that tricks users into installing a modified McAfee Security APK hosting the Brunhilda dropper, Vultur now unfolds across three payloads (first registering with its C&C to gain Accessibility Service privileges, second deploying AlphaVNC/ngrok tunnels, and third loading a Dalvik backdoor) and introduces native-code decryption, multi-payload obfuscation, and AES-encrypted C&C to evade analysis. The new build adds seven C&C methods for clicks, scrolls, swipes and more, plus 41 Firebase Cloud Messaging commands to issue instructions without persistent connections, allows attackers to display custom notifications, bypass lock screens, lock users out of targeted apps, and download, upload, install, search for or delete files—capabilities that dramatically expand credential theft, data exfiltration and device takeover potential—though Google Play Protect remains capable of detecting known variants by default.

title: 'WallEscape' Linux Vulnerability Leaks User Passwords - SecurityWeek
preprocessed: Security researchers have disclosed CVE-2024-28085, dubbed “WallEscape,” a vulnerability in the util-linux package’s setgid “wall” command—present by default on Ubuntu 22.04 (mesg=y) and Debian Bookworm but not on CentOS/Red Hat—that fails to sanitize escape sequences in user-supplied messages, enabling unprivileged local attackers to inject crafted payloads that leak user passwords (e.g., during sudo, OpenSSH login or command-not-found prompts), alter command outputs, and even modify clipboards on certain terminals; introduced in 2013 and fixed in util-linux v2.40, WallEscape is exploitable via proof-of-concept code to harvest credentials and potentially achieve account takeover (per NIST), so organizations should promptly upgrade to util-linux ≥2.40, remove setgid from wall or disable mesg, and monitor for anomalous terminal activity.

title: 3AM: New Ransomware Family Used As Fallback in Failed LockBit Attack | Symantec Enterprise Blogs
preprocessed: During a recent incident, a LockBit affiliate conducted initial intrusions using gpresult for policy dumping, Cobalt Strike loaders and PsExec for privilege escalation, followed by reconnaissance (whoami, netstat, quser, net view), lateral movement, persistence via a new user account, and data exfiltration over FTP with Wput; when deployment of LockBit (SHA256 079b99f6…) was blocked on the target network, the attacker pivoted to a newly observed Rust-written ransomware family dubbed 3AM (SHA256 307a1217…), which appends “.threeamtime” to encrypted files, stops over 100 security and backup services via net stop and wbadmin/bcdedit/wmic commands, deletes Volume Shadow copies with vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet, and drops a Tor‐accessible ransom note requiring a 32-character “-k” access key and offering decryption/mystical-themed extortion; although 3AM encryption succeeded on only one of three attempted hosts, its Conti-style “-m” (local/net) and “-h” parameters, heavy service-termination payload, and aggressive VSS wipe underscore its potential as a fallback vector—defenders should update Symantec/Broadcom signatures, monitor for the .threeamtime extension, suspicious Rust binaries, command-line flags “-k” and “-m”, and mass service stoppage activity, and block associated IOCs (185.202.0[.]111, 212.18.104[.]6, 85.159.229[.]62) to mitigate future 3AM use.

title: New Backdoor Targeting Taiwan Employs Stealthy Communications | Symantec Enterprise Blogs
preprocessed: An attack leveraging the recently patched PHP CGI argument injection vulnerability CVE-2024-4577 on a Taiwanese university deployed a novel DLL-based backdoor named Msupedge (installed as csidl_drive_fixed\xampp\wuplog.dll under Apache and csidl_system\wbem\wmiclnt.dll under an unknown parent), which stealthily tunnels C2 traffic over DNS using a dnscat2-derived framework: it resolves structured hostnames to receive commands, encodes execution results as fifth-level domains, and interprets the third octet of the resolved IP (ctl.msedeapi[.]net) minus seven as a switch to perform actions—0x8a (process creation via DNS TXT), 0x75 (file download), 0x24/0x66 (sleep intervals), and 0x38/0x3c (create/remove a temp file)—while error notifications report memory allocation, decompression, and command execution status; although multiple actors have been observed scanning for CVE-2024-4577, attribution remains unknown, underscoring the urgent need to apply patches, monitor DNS tunneling patterns, and deploy Symantec Endpoint protections against indicators e08dc1c3987d17451a3e86c04ed322a9424582e2cb6352c892b7e0645eda43, f5937d38353ed431dc8a5eb32c119ab575114a10c24567f0c864cb2ef47f9f36 and a89ebe7d1af3513d146a831b6fa4a465c8edeafea5d7980eb5448a94a4e34480.

title: Buckeye: Espionage Outfit Used Equation Group Tools Prior to Shadow Brokers Leak | Symantec Enterprise Blogs
preprocessed: Beginning in March 2016, the Chinese-linked espionage group Buckeye (aka APT3/Gothic Panda) conducted a series of global attacks—against targets in Hong Kong, Belgium, Luxembourg, the Philippines and Vietnam—by deploying a custom exploit tool (Trojan.Bemstour) that chained two Windows flaws (the later-patched CVE-2017-0143 and an unreported SMB zero-day, CVE-2019-0703) to install bespoke variants of the Equation Group’s DoublePulsar backdoor (Backdoor.DoublePulsar) and custom in-memory payloads, achieving remote kernel code execution and persistent access for intelligence collection; technical analysis shows these variants, which boasted enhanced obfuscation and 64-bit support, predated and differed from those released by the Shadow Brokers in August 2016, suggesting Buckeye independently acquired or reverse-engineered them, and although Buckeye purportedly ceased operations in mid-2017 after U.S. indictments, Bemstour and DoublePulsar continued to appear in attacks through September 2018—implying hand-off to another actor or extended Buckeye activity—prompting Symantec to report the zero-day to Microsoft (patched March 2019) and to recommend network-based intrusion prevention, file-based detection, and IOC monitoring to defend against similar advanced persistent threats.

title: Budworm: APT Group Uses Updated Custom Tool in Attacks on Government and Telecoms Org | Symantec Enterprise Blogs
preprocessed: In August 2023, Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team identified the Budworm APT (aka LuckyMouse/APT27) deploying a novel variant of its exclusive SysUpdate backdoor (inicore_v2.3.30.dll) via DLL sideloading of the legitimate INISafeWebSSO app—an approach it has employed since 2018—to compromise a Middle Eastern telecom and an Asian government, harvesting credentials as its sole observed malicious activity. SysUpdate, in continuous development since 2020 (with a Linux counterpart spotted by Trend Micro in March 2023), offers service and process control, screenshot capture, drive reconnaissance, file operations, and arbitrary command execution, while Budworm further leveraged native and public tools—AdFind, Curl, SecretsDump, PasswordDumper—to map networks and exfiltrate hashes and plaintext credentials. Consistent targeting of high-value government and telecom sectors underscores Budworm’s intelligence-gathering motives; the group’s reliance on familiar toolsets and sideloading techniques suggests confidence in attribution resilience, yet the early interruption of this campaign highlights the effectiveness of vigilant detection of malformed INISafeWebSSO executions and the importance of monitoring for associated SHA256 IOCs to mitigate similar incursions.

title: MOVEit Vulnerabilities: What You Need to Know | Symantec Enterprise Blogs
preprocessed: Symantec has warned that extortion actors, notably the Clop ransomware operation (aka Snakefly/TA505/FIN11), have been exploiting a zero-day SQL injection vulnerability in the MOVEit Transfer web application (CVE-2023-34362) since May 27, 2023, enabling supply-chain attacks across multiple organizations; although first patched on May 31, additional vulnerabilities (CVEs pending) were disclosed on June 9. Attackers deploy a bespoke web shell, Lemurloot (detected as JS.Malscript!g1, Trojan.Gen.2, WS.Malware), to authenticate via hard-coded credentials, execute SQL statements to alter or delete database elements, exfiltrate records and Azure settings, and manipulate user accounts. With proof-of-concept code now public, secondary threat actors face elevated risk of exploitation and data theft. Clop has since threatened data leaks unless ransoms are paid, reflecting its shift from encryption to extortion. Symantec mitigations include file-based and ML detections, network-based attack signatures, and Data Center Security policy controls that harden MS SQL, IIS and sandbox environments to prevent web-shell deployment and unauthorized software execution.

title: Crambus: New Campaign Targets Middle Eastern Government | Symantec Enterprise Blogs
preprocessed: Between February and September 2023, Iran-linked espionage group Crambus (aka APT34/OilRig) staged an eight-month intrusion against a Middle Eastern government, compromising at least 12 machines and deploying backdoors and keyloggers on dozens more to steal credentials and sensitive files; initial access began with a PowerShell script (joper.ps1) on February 1, followed by repeated use of renamed Plink binaries (msssh.exe/plink.exe) to configure SSH port-forwarded RDP tunnels, modification of Windows firewall rules, and network drive mounts for lateral movement. Attackers executed netstat and batch scripts to enumerate connections, used Mimikatz on Domain Controllers to dump credentials, and introduced three novel malware families—Backdoor.Tokel (telecomm.exe) for arbitrary PowerShell execution with RC4-encrypted C2 in token.bin, Trojan.Dirps (virtpackage.exe) for directory enumeration and command execution, and Infostealer.Clipog (poluniq.exe) for keystroke and clipboard capture—alongside the PowerExchange PowerShell backdoor that logs into Exchange mailboxes and processes emails with “@@” in the subject to receive cf/uf/df commands for file execution and exfiltration. The campaign also leveraged living-off-the-land tools (netsh, Nessus scans targeting Log4j) and persistent services via remote scripts, culminating in extensive data exfiltration and credential theft, underscoring the need for vigilant log monitoring, Exchange mailbox auditing, hardened SSH/RDP controls, and timely patching to detect and disrupt similar long-running intrusions.

title: Equation: Advanced cyberespionage group has all the tricks in the book, and more | Symantec Enterprise Blogs
preprocessed: Symantec research reveals that the Equation group, a sophisticated cyberespionage actor active across multiple countries, employs a tiered infection chain beginning with reconnaissance Infostealer variants (Micstus/DoubleFantasy or Tripfant/TripleFantasy) to fingerprint and maintain backdoors on targeted systems, followed by deployment of modular multipurpose Trojans—initially Lassrv.B (EquationLaser), then Equdrug (EquationDrug), now GrayPhish/GrayFish—which leverage a stealthy bootkit and encrypted virtual file system in the Windows registry to subvert the OS boot process, while offering optional modules such as a firmware reprogramming component (detected as Packed.Generic.483) for persistence through disk reformatting. Complementary tools include the GroKey keylogger and the W32.Fanny worm, the latter using two zero-day exploits pre-dating and reused in Stuxnet to bridge air-gapped networks via infected USB drives. Defenders can counter Equation’s toolkit through Symantec/Norton signatures—Infostealer.Micstus, Trojan.Tripfant, Trojan.Grayphish, Trojan.Equdrug, Backdoor.Lassrv.B, Packed.Generic.483, Trojan.Grokey, W32.Fanny—and IPS rules (System Infected: Trojan Equation Activity), while monitoring for abnormal bootloader modifications, encrypted registry volumes, and unauthorized firmware changes to mitigate the group’s highly persistent and evasive espionage capabilities.

title: Equation: Advanced cyberespionage group has all the tricks in the book, and more | Symantec Enterprise Blogs
preprocessed: Equation, a highly resourced cyber-espionage group identified by Kaspersky Lab and tracked by Symantec, targets global organizations using a multi-stage infection chain that begins with reconnaissance/backdoor Trojans—Infostealer, Micstus (DoubleFantasy) and Tripfant (TripleFantasy)—to fingerprint systems and maintain access, then deploys modular, stealthy payloads such as Grayphish (a bootkit with an encrypted registry-based virtual file system) and its predecessor EquationDrug (Equdrug), plus the earlier Lassrv.B (EquationLaser), each supporting specialized modules including a rare HDD firmware reprogramming implant (detectable as Packed.Generic.483) that survives disk reformatting; the group further employs bespoke tools—Grokey keylogger and the W32.Fanny worm exploiting two zero-days later used by Stuxnet—to infiltrate air-gapped networks via USB and exfiltrate data. Symantec and Norton products currently detect these threats with AV signatures (e.g., Trojan.Grayphish, Trojan.Equdrug, W32.Fanny) and IPS rules, providing actionable defenses against Equation’s advanced stealth techniques, firmware-level persistence and sophisticated data exfiltration capabilities.

title: Fog Ransomware: Unusual Toolset Used in Recent Attack | Symantec Enterprise Blogs
preprocessed: In May 2025, a financially motivated group deployed Fog ransomware against an Asian financial institution after a roughly two-week dwell, leveraging a highly atypical toolset that blended legitimate and dual-use utilities with open-source pentesting frameworks to conduct discovery, exfiltration, lateral movement and persistence.  After gaining initial access—possibly via compromised Exchange Servers—the attackers installed GC2 implants that polled Google Sheets or SharePoint for commands (“whoami,” “ipconfig,” netstat, “upload,” “download,” “load,” “exit”), then used Stowaway to proxy and deliver the Syteca (formerly Ekran) employee-monitoring client to capture keystrokes and screen data.  They further spread laterally with PsExec and SMBExec, exfiltrated data using FreeFileSync, MegaSync and 7-Zip, and stealthily removed Syteca binaries and config files via PsExec.  On the day of encryption, Fog ransomware was deployed—continuing a trend since May 2024 of targeting VPN credentials and Veeam CVE-2024-40711—yet, unusually, a custom “SecurityHealthIron” service was created days later to maintain long-term access, suggesting espionage under the guise of ransomware.

title: Attackers Exploit MSDT Follina Bug to Drop RAT, Infostealer | Symantec Enterprise Blogs
preprocessed: In late May 2022, Symantec identified multiple threat actors exploiting the MSDT Follina bug (CVE-2022-30190) through ms-msdt URI-based RCE in Word/RTF documents that load a malicious HTML via Word’s remote template feature to launch msdt.exe, sdiagnhost.exe and ultimately PowerShell—bypassing the need for macros—to install a digitally signed AsyncRAT remote access Trojan that performs anti-analysis checks, collects hardware IDs, user names, execution paths and OS details, and maintains C&C communications, alongside parallel deployments of a browser infostealer targeting cookies and saved credentials in Firefox, Chrome and Edge. Symantec customers should apply Microsoft’s advisories or disable the ms-msdt handler, update Symantec Endpoint definitions (File-based-Downloader-Backdoor:Async, InfoStealer) and monitor for related IOCs to thwart these rapid, damaging campaigns.

title: Graphican: Flea Uses New Backdoor in Attacks Targeting Foreign Ministries | Symantec Enterprise Blogs
preprocessed: Between late 2022 and early 2023, the Chinese-affiliated APT15 (aka Flea/Nickel) executed a targeted espionage campaign against foreign ministries in the Americas—alongside a finance department, a regional products firm, and an outlier European victim—deploying a novel Backdoor.Graphican that abuses the Microsoft Graph API and OneDrive for dynamic C2, an evolution of its Ketrican/BS2005 malware. Graphican disables Internet Explorer 10’s first-run wizard, leverages a global IWebBrowser2 COM object to authenticate via Graph API, enumerates the “Person” OneDrive folder, decrypts its first subfolder name into the C2 address, generates a Bot ID from host attributes, registers with the server, and polls for commands to spawn shells, upload/download files, launch hidden processes, or run PowerShell with exfiltration. Concurrently, Flea rolled out updated and legacy Ketrican variants, living-off-the-land binaries, and open-source tools—EWSTEW for Exchange mail harvesting; Mimikatz, Pypykatz, Safetykatz; LaZagne; Quarks PwDump; SharpSecDump; K8Tools; EHole; and web shells such as AntSword, Behinder, China Chopper, Godzilla—while exploiting CVE-2020-1472 for privilege escalation. This persistent-access operation highlights Flea’s sustained evolution of custom tools for geopolitical intelligence gathering and introduces a C2 technique poised for adoption by other threat actors.

title: Grayfly: Chinese Threat Actor Uses Newly-discovered Sidewalk Malware | Symantec Enterprise Blogs
preprocessed: Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team has linked the newly discovered Sidewalk loader backdoor—an evolution of the Crosswalk/Backdoor.Motnug family—to Grayfly (aka GREF/Wicked Panda), a China-linked espionage group active since March 2017 that employs custom backdoors, Trojan.Chattak, Cobalt Strike, web shells and credential-dumpers against telecom, IT, media and finance targets in Taiwan, Vietnam, the US and Mexico; in a recent campaign they exploited public-facing Microsoft Exchange and MySQL servers via commodity and zero-day flaws to execute Base64-encoded PowerShell commands through certutil, install an ASPX web shell in the ClientAccess\ecp directory, deploy Sidewalk via installutil.exe, create persistence with WMIC-launched scheduled tasks, then run a custom Mimikatz variant (SHA256 b3eb783b017da32e33d19670b39eae0b11de8e983891dd4feb873d6e9333608d) to harvest credentials—all within about an hour before ceasing observable activity; three Chengdu 404 executives were indicted in 2020 for attacks on over 100 organizations, highlighting Grayfly’s persistence and underscoring the need to promptly patch Exchange and MySQL servers, monitor anomalous PowerShell and scheduled-task activity, and deploy IOC-based detection to block Sidewalk and related tools.

title: Log4j Vulnerabilities: Attack Insights | Symantec Enterprise Blogs
preprocessed: Following the December 9 disclosure of critical Log4j flaws (CVE-2021-44228 “Log4Shell,” CVE-2021-45046 and CVE-2021-45105), Symantec observed widespread exploitation via obfuscated jndi lookups over LDAP and RMI (with ${env}, ${lower}, ${::-} tricks) and secondary scans over IIOP, DNS, HTTP and NIS, delivering payloads from Muhstik botnet Java class files that drop ELF installers, XMRig miners via PowerShell, Java backdoors awaiting remote commands, reverse Bash shells and public threats including Dridex, Orcus RAT, Khonsari and Conti ransomware; between December 9–21, its IPS blocked 93 million Log4Shell attempts on 270 000 endpoints and 18 million on 60 000 servers—primarily targeting systems in the U.S. and U.K. and originating from the U.S., Germany, Russia, the U.K. and China—highlighting rapid global weaponization; actionable defenses include enforcing multi-layered DCS policies to prevent malware execution from temp or writable paths, sandboxing Java apps, restricting outbound LDAP/HTTP connections, whitelisting necessary proxy tools (*/curl, */wget), and updating detection rules to flag jndi:* patterns in web and Log4j logs for immediate alerting and mitigation.

title: Pegasus Spyware Takes Flight Again | Symantec Enterprise Blogs
preprocessed: In late 2021 Apple patched a zero-click iMessage vulnerability (CVE-2021-30860, “FORCEDENTRY”) exploited since February by NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware—sold to nation-states yet repeatedly abused against journalists and activists—to silently deliver maliciously crafted PDFs into iMessage’s sandbox, enabling arbitrary code execution to harvest messages, calls, location, passwords, microphone and camera data. Citizen Lab and Amnesty International identified infection URLs that Symantec WebPulse flagged in 1 of every 150,000 iOS devices, demonstrating that WebPulse–backed Symantec Endpoint Protection Mobile can intercept hidden iMessage fields, block command-and-control traffic, and quarantine zero-day payloads. Organizations are urged to deploy iOS 14.8+ patches and enforce layered mobile endpoint protection leveraging global URL intelligence to mitigate current and future Pegasus-style threats.

title: RansomHub: Attackers Leverage New Custom Backdoor | Symantec Enterprise Blogs
preprocessed: A Symantec analysis reveals that a RansomHub (Greenbottle) affiliate has introduced a bespoke multi‐function backdoor dubbed Betruger—masquerading as mailer.exe/turbomailer.exe—to consolidate screenshot capture, keylogging, file exfiltration, network scanning, privilege escalation and credential dumping into one payload, signaling a shift away from the typical use of publicly available tools; this innovation, deployed in several attacks since early 2024, coincides with RansomHub’s rapid rise to the most prolific RaaS operation by Q3 2024—driven by favorable affiliate revenue splits—and is accompanied by the use of BYOVD techniques (EDRKillshifter), exploitation of CVE-2022-24521 and CVE-2023-27532, and continued abuse of Impacket, Mimikatz, SystemBC, Rclone, Stowaway Proxy, ScreenConnect, Atera, Splashtop and TightVNC for lateral movement and exfiltration. Organizations should ingest the published IOCs for Betruger and related tools, apply critical Windows and Veeam patches, enforce least-privilege access, and enhance EDR monitoring to detect this unified backdoor and associated living-off-the-land behaviors.

title: Seedworm: Iranian Hackers Target Telecoms Orgs in North and East Africa | Symantec Enterprise Blogs
preprocessed: In November 2023, Iran-linked espionage group Seedworm (aka MuddyWater and subordinate to MOIS) launched a targeted cyber-espionage campaign against telecommunications organizations in Egypt, Sudan and Tanzania using its Go-based MuddyC2Go framework alongside both living-off-the-land and custom tools to maintain persistence, harvest credentials and exfiltrate data. Researchers observed a PowerShell-based MuddyC2Go DLL launcher named “vcruntime140.dll” sideloaded by the legitimate Java executable jabswitch.exe into csidl_common_appdata\javax, which read C2 URIs (“End” and “Status” values under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip) before invoking Invoke-WebRequest to contacts servers such as 95.164.38.99:443 and 45.150.64.39:443; the backdoor was executed via a scheduled task (“Microsoft\Windows\JavaX\Java Autorun”), while Impacket’s WMIExec, Revsocks (94.131.3.160:443), and SimpleHelp (146.70.124.102) were leveraged for lateral movement, SAM hive dumps, drive reconnaissance and remote administration alongside AnyDesk and a custom keylogger. This activity followed a prior Seedworm intrusion earlier in 2023 into at least one victim using SimpleHelp-driven PowerShell, proxy tools, LSASS dumping and JumpCloud deployment, confirming group attribution. Seedworm’s blend of custom C2 innovation and publicly available/proxy tools underscores the necessity for defenders to monitor for anomalous PowerShell invocations to suspect domains, unexpected Java sideloading, scheduled task creations, unauthorized SimpleHelp or AnyDesk services, Venom Proxy processes, and registry modifications in telecom-grade networks to detect and disrupt its persistent espionage operations.

title: Shuckworm Targets Foreign Military Mission Based in Ukraine | Symantec Enterprise Blogs
preprocessed: In February–March 2025, Russia-linked espionage group Shuckworm (aka Gamaredon/Armageddon) targeted a Western nation’s military mission in Ukraine using a multi-stage PowerShell-centric campaign initiated via an infected removable drive and malicious .lnk file. Obfuscated VBScript (~.drv) deployed through mshta.exe and wscript.exe created registry-named payloads: one performing WMI ping checks to mil.gov.ua before resolving dynamic C2 addresses via Teletype, Telegra.ph, t.me, check-host.net and Cloudflare tunnels (e.g., 107.189.19.218), and another altering Explorer registry keys to hide system files and propagate shortcuts across USB and network shares. The attackers then delivered an updated PowerShell infostealer (GammaSteel) alongside reconnaissance scripts that captured screenshots, systeminfo, process lists and host metadata, exfiltrating sensitive documents (*.docx, *.pptx, *.pdf) using PowerShell web requests with certutil-computed MD5 hashes and fallback cURL over Tor to mask origin. This campaign underscores Shuckworm’s shift from VBS to PowerShell, leveraging in-registry script storage and heavy obfuscation to evade detection, with indicators including anomalous UserAssist entries, unusual mshta/wscript invocations and atypical C2 resolution patterns.

title: Attackers Exploit Unpatched Windows Zero-Day Vulnerability | Symantec Enterprise Blogs
preprocessed: Attackers have been exploiting an unpatched Windows and Office zero-day vulnerability (CVE-2023-36884), disclosed by Microsoft on July 11, in highly targeted campaigns against government and defense organizations in Europe and North America; initial exploitation was documented by BlackBerry on July 8 when Storm-0978 (aka RomCom), a Russia-linked actor using the RomCom RAT with ties to the Hawker group and Cuba ransomware developers (and potentially to Industrial Spy ransomware operators), delivered malicious Word documents masquerading as Ukrainian World Congress materials to NATO Summit attendees, enabling remote code execution once opened. With no patch yet available, victims are urged to deploy all mitigations—leveraging Symantec’s email-, file-, network- and web-based protections (including WebPulse bad-reputation domain filtering), monitor the published IOC hashes, and prepare for Microsoft’s forthcoming monthly or out-of-cycle update—to prevent further compromise and forestall secondary ransomware or espionage operations.

title: Hackers Exploiting MS Excel Vulnerability to Spread Agent Tesla Malware
preprocessed: In a recently documented campaign by Zscaler ThreatLabz building on Fortinet FortiGuard’s earlier analysis, threat actors are reviving the 2017 Office Equation Editor vulnerability (CVE-2017-11882, CVSS 7.8) by embedding invoice-themed Excel attachments that, upon opening, launch an obfuscated VBScript to fetch a steganographically concealed Base64-encoded DLL (a tactic first detailed by McAfee Labs in September 2023) within a malicious JPG, inject it into RegAsm.exe, and deploy the .NET-based Agent Tesla keylogger/RAT for silent data harvesting and C2 communication. Parallel threats include the 8220 Gang’s exploitation of Oracle WebLogic CVE-2020-14883 (CVSS 7.2) to deliver cryptominers, an uptick in DarkGate MaaS activity targeting the technology sector via systematically rotated 50-60-day domains, and hospitality-sector phishing campaigns leveraging booking-related email lures to install RedLine and Vidar stealers, while “Insta-Phish-A-Gram” schemes harvest Instagram 2FA backup codes through bogus copyright infringement alerts. These activities highlight the persistent exploitation of legacy vulnerabilities, advanced steganographic evasion, and diversified phishing tactics, underscoring the imperative for organizations to promptly patch legacy Office and server exploits, monitor for anomalous DLL injections, enforce domain-based message authentication, and strengthen email filtering and user awareness to counter rapidly evolving threat actor strategies.

title: Iran-Linked BladedFeline Hits Iraqi and Kurdish Targets with Whisper and Spearal Malware
preprocessed: Since September 2017, the Iran-aligned BladedFeline subcluster of the OilRig APT has executed persistent cyber espionage against Kurdish and Iraqi government entities, initially compromising KRG systems and a regional Uzbekistan telecom provider via an internet-facing application vulnerability and social engineering to deploy the Flog web shell. ESET’s Q4 2023–Q1 2024 report documents the group’s evolving malware arsenal: the Shahmaran backdoor for remote file manipulation, the C#/.NET Whisper (aka Veaty) email-based implant, the DNS-tunneling Spearal and its optimized variant, Optimizer, the Slippery Snakelet Python implant for command execution and data exfiltration, and tunneling tools Laret and Pinar. BladedFeline leverages a malicious IIS module, PrimeCache—akin to OilRig’s RDAT—and the Hawking Listener early-stage implant to maintain stealthy access, systematically harvesting diplomatic and financial intelligence tied to KRG oil reserves and Western relations to further Iranian strategic objectives.

title: North Korean Hackers Spread Malware via Fake Crypto Firms and Job Interview Lures
preprocessed: North Korea–linked Contagious Interview actors have deployed three fake cryptocurrency consulting firms—BlockNovas LLC, Angeloper Agency and SoftGlide LLC—to lure candidates with bogus job interviews and video coding assessments, distributing the BeaverTail JavaScript stealer/loader that contacts lianxinxiao[.]com C2 to deliver the InvisibleFerret Python backdoor on Windows, Linux and macOS and, in some chains, the OtterCookie payload; they’ve also leveraged ClickFake Interview video lures to push FROSTYFERRET and GolangGhost, hosted a Hashtopolis password-cracking system on mail.blocknovas[.]com, and run a “Kryptoneer” crypto-wallet connector on attisscmo[.]com. Operating under aliases CL-STA-0240, DeceptiveDevelopment, Famous Chollima and others, the group obfuscated traffic via Astrill VPN, residential proxies and five Russian IP ranges masked by VPN/proxy/RDP layers from Khasan and Khabarovsk, used AI-generated personas across LinkedIn, Facebook, GitHub and more, and even advertised a senior software engineer role targeting Ukrainian professionals in December 2024. Their campaign enabled AnyDesk installation and led to at least one MetaMask compromise in September 2024; on April 23, 2025, the US FBI seized blocknovas.com, highlighting urgent needs to harden remote-hiring vetting, monitor anomalous C2 communications and enforce multi-factor authentication on crypto and recruitment platforms against DPRK’s evolving “Wagemole” salary-siphoning and potential DPRK–Russia infrastructure collaboration.

title: Chinese Hackers Exploited New Zero-Day in Barracuda's ESG Appliances
preprocessed: In late 2023, Chinese threat actor UNC4841 exploited a zero-day in Barracuda Email Security Gateway appliances (CVE-2023-7102) by embedding a specially crafted Microsoft Excel attachment that triggers arbitrary code execution in the Amavis scanner’s third-party Perl library Spreadsheet::ParseExcel, silently installing updated SEASPY and SALTWATER backdoors to achieve persistence and remote command execution without user interaction; Barracuda automatically deployed a security update on December 21, 2023, and a remediation patch for compromised appliances on December 22, while the underlying Spreadsheet::ParseExcel flaw (CVE-2023-7101, version 0.65) remains unpatched, requiring downstream mitigations. Mandiant’s investigation estimates that private and public sector organizations across at least 16 countries—and Google Cloud’s telemetry confirms targeting of high-tech, IT, and government entities in the U.S. and Asia-Pacific since November 30—have been impacted. This activity follows UNC4841’s earlier exploitation of CVE-2023-2868 and underscores the actor’s evolving tactics and persistence, signaling an elevated risk to similar appliance platforms and a need for continuous patch management, threat hunting for SEASPY/SALTWATER indicators, and heightened monitoring of Excel-based email threats.

title: EleKtra-Leak Cryptojacking Attacks Exploit AWS IAM Credentials Exposed on GitHub
preprocessed: Since at least December 2020, EleKtra-Leak—identified by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 researchers William Gamazo and Nathaniel Quist—has programmatically harvested AWS IAM credentials exposed on public GitHub repositories within four minutes of exposure, exploiting blind spots in GitHub’s secret scanning and AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantine policy; the adversary conducts account reconnaissance, blocklists victim accounts to deter analysis, configures security groups, then launches behind-VPN c5a.24xlarge EC2 instances from private, non-Marketplace AMIs to mine Monero, operating as many as 474 unique instances between August 30 and October 6, 2023, and fetching bespoke mining software via Google Drive. Evidence suggests overlap with a January 2021 cryptojacking campaign targeting unsecured Docker services using the same custom miner. Despite AWS’s two-minute quarantine response, the campaign maintains continuous fluctuations in compromised accounts, underscoring its rapid, large-scale cryptojacking impact. To mitigate risk, organizations must immediately revoke exposed API keys, remove them from GitHub, and audit repository cloning events for suspicious activity.

title: Microsoft Warns of New 'FalseFont' Backdoor Targeting the Defense Sector
preprocessed: Microsoft has identified a coordinated campaign by Iranian-linked APT33—also known as Peach Sandstorm, Elfin and Refined Kitten—targeting the Defense Industrial Base and adjacent sectors with a novel backdoor dubbed FalseFont first observed in November 2023; this implant provides operators with remote access, payload execution and data exfiltration via dedicated C2 servers, marking an evolution from the group’s February–July 2023 password‐spray operations against satellite, defense and pharmaceutical firms and continuing a decade-long focus on aviation and energy targets. Concurrently, Israel’s National Cyber Directorate attributed failed attacks on Ziv Hospital to Agrius and Lebanese Cedar crews employing a phishing lure around F5 BIG-IP CVE-2023-46747 (CVSS 9.8) to deploy Hatef and Hamsa wiper variants on Windows and Linux, which maintain constant Telegram communications to report wipe progress. Security teams should prioritize detection of FalseFont signatures, monitor for credential‐spray indicators, patch CVE-2023-46747 and watch for Telegram-based C2 traffic.

title: New JinxLoader Targeting Users with Formbook and XLoader Malware
preprocessed: In April 2023, threat actors began leveraging JinxLoader—a Go-based malware loader emblazoned with a League of Legends “Jinx” theme and sold on hackforums.net for $60/month, $120/year or a $200 lifetime fee—to deliver next-stage payloads Formbook and XLoader via password-protected RAR phishing emails impersonating Abu Dhabi National Oil Company; Unit 42 and Symantec’s late-November 2023 analysis detailed this multi-stage attack, its simple loader functionality and bespoke C2 login panel. At the same time, security researchers noted a spike in infections from the novice Rugmi loader carrying diverse info-stealers, ongoing DarkGate and PikaBot campaigns, and TA544 (aka Narwal Spider) deploying new IDAT Loader variants to install Remcos RAT or SystemBC. Stealer malware also advanced: Meduza Stealer version 2.2 now supports browser-based cryptocurrency wallets and enhanced credit-card extraction, while the newcomer Vortex Stealer exfiltrates browser data, Discord tokens, Telegram sessions, system information and sub-2 MB files—archiving data to Gofile/Anonfiles and broadcasting via Discord webhooks and Telegram bots—underscoring the need for rigorous email filtering, blocking of RAR attachments and Go-based loaders, strict endpoint controls and continuous network monitoring for anomalous C2 traffic.

title: Kimsuky Hackers Deploying AppleSeed, Meterpreter, and TinyNuke in Latest Attacks
preprocessed: Since at least 2019, the North Korea–affiliated APT group Kimsuky has conducted spear-phishing campaigns using malicious lure documents to deploy a potent mix of backdoors and RATs—most notably the Windows/Android DLL AppleSeed (aka JamBog), its Golang-based AlphaSeed variant (leveraging the chromedp library for DevTools-driven C2), Meterpreter, TightVNC and TinyNuke (Nuclear Bot)—to establish C2 via HTTP, SMTP or headless‐Chrome, drop additional payloads and exfiltrate files, keystrokes and screenshots; evidence shows some intrusions since October 2022 delivered both AppleSeed and AlphaSeed via a JavaScript dropper. Active for over a decade—initially targeting South Korean entities before expanding globally in 2017—and recently sanctioned by the U.S. for intelligence gathering to further North Korea’s strategic objectives, Kimsuky has also created fraudulent LinkedIn and GitHub personas to secure remote tech contracts, generating revenue and facilitating multi-pronged blockchain and cryptocurrency theft to evade sanctions and support regime priorities.

title: Critical Zero-Day in Apache OfBiz ERP System Exposes Businesses to Attack
preprocessed: A critical zero-day flaw (CVE-2023-51467) has been identified in Apache OfBiz’s login functionality—stemming from an incomplete patch for a prior high-severity RCE vulnerability (CVE-2023-49070, CVSS 9.8) tied to a deprecated XML-RPC component—that allows attackers to bypass authentication by sending empty or invalid USERNAME and PASSWORD parameters alongside “requirePasswordChange=Y,” effectively granting unauthorized access and enabling simple SSRF attacks against internal resources; discovered by SonicWall Capture Labs, the bug follows observations by The Shadowserver Foundation of active exploitation attempts against CVE-2023-49070, and SonicWall reports exploit traffic for CVE-2023-51467 spiking from 235 attempts on December 27, 2023, to 26,928 on December 29 and 3,129 on January 1, 2024, underscoring urgent need for organizations using OfBiz versions prior to 18.12.11 to upgrade immediately to mitigate further data exfiltration and system takeover risks.

title: New Rugmi Malware Loader Surges with Hundreds of Daily Detections
preprocessed: In late 2023, ESET telemetry recorded a surge from single‐digit to hundreds of daily detections of Win/TrojanDownloader.Rugmi—a three‐stage loader that fetches encrypted payloads, executes them from memory or disk, and delivers information stealers such as Lumma Stealer, Vidar, RecordBreaker (Raccoon Stealer V2) and Rescoms under a malware-as-a-service model (Lumma at $250/month or $20,000 for source code/resale rights). Evidence suggests Lumma’s code reused elements from Mars, Arkei and Vidar to enhance evasion, while distribution methods evolved from malvertising, fake browser updates and cracked VLC/OpenAI ChatGPT installers to abusing Discord’s CDN—using random and compromised accounts to entice targets with $10 or Discord Nitro in exchange for downloading a stealer-laden “iMagic Inventory” executable. Simultaneously, McAfee Labs disclosed a novel NetSupport RAT variant—spawned from legitimate NetSupport Manager—deployed by initial access brokers via obfuscated JavaScript that triggers PowerShell to retrieve remote-control and stealer modules, predominantly targeting U.S. and Canadian organizations. This rapid escalation of off-the-shelf loaders and RATs across diverse delivery vectors underscores an urgent need for enhanced endpoint hardening, vigilant network monitoring and proactive threat hunting to disrupt MaaS-driven campaigns.

title: Sea Turtle Cyber Espionage Campaign Targets Dutch IT and Telecom Companies
preprocessed: Sea Turtle, also known as Cosmic Wolf, Marbled Dust, Teal Kurma and UNC1326, has been conducting a stealthy, Türkiye-linked cyber espionage campaign since at least January 2017, recently targeting Dutch ISPs, telecom, IT-service and media providers as well as Kurdish websites via supply-chain and island-hopping attacks to harvest politically sensitive personal data and potential dissident communications. First detailed by Cisco Talos in April 2019 for state-sponsored DNS hijacking to redirect legitimate domain queries to attacker-controlled servers, the group elevated its upstream foothold tactics in late 2021 by exploiting known telecom and IT vulnerabilities across Armenia, Cyprus, Greece, Iraq and Syria, per Microsoft. Between 2021 and 2023 PwC observed deployment of “SnappyTCP,” a simple Linux/Unix reverse-TCP web shell (with and without OpenSSL/TLS) for persistence and C2, and Hunt & Hackett’s 2023 incident revealed credential-theft via a compromised cPanel account used to deploy SnappyTCP, tar and expose email archives publicly for direct exfiltration. Organizations should enforce strong password policies, 2FA, login-rate limiting, SSH monitoring and timely patching to mitigate this ongoing espionage threat.

title: Silent Skimmer: A Year-Long Web Skimming Campaign Targeting Online Payment Businesses
preprocessed: BlackBerry’s Research and Intelligence Team has uncovered “Silent Skimmer,” a year-long, financially motivated campaign by a Chinese-fluent actor exploiting Internet Information Services (IIS) vulnerabilities to breach online payment and PoS web applications across Asia-Pacific, North America and Latin America, achieving initial foothold before leveraging open-source and living-off-the-land tools for privilege escalation and executing a PowerShell-based RAT (server.ps1); this malware connects to geolocated VPS C2 servers to download additional utilities, deploy web shells and inject scrapers into checkout pages, stealthily harvesting payment data via reverse proxies and Cobalt Strike beacons. In parallel, Sophos detailed a “pig butchering” crypto scam using dating-app social engineering and liquidity-mining lures—no malware required—to trick victims into connecting wallets to malicious Ethereum contracts, netting actors millions; these findings highlight the urgent need for patching IIS, monitoring PowerShell and Cobalt Strike activity, enforcing least-privilege controls, detecting web shells, and training users against DeFi phishing.

title: SpectralBlur: New macOS Backdoor Threat from North Korean Hackers
preprocessed: Researchers have identified SpectralBlur, a new Mach-O backdoor targeting macOS and attributed to North Korean group TA444 (aka BlueNoroff), which shares core functionality with the KANDYKORN/SockRacket implant—file upload/download, remote shell execution via grantpt-driven pseudo-terminal, configuration updates, file deletion, hibernation and sleep—and exhibits advanced evasion techniques; in recent months, TA444 has increasingly fused RustBucket droppers and late-stage ObjCShellz payloads from Lazarus campaigns to deploy KANDYKORN variants, underscoring a strategic shift toward macOS infiltration of high-value cryptocurrency and blockchain targets. The initial SpectralBlur sample, uploaded to VirusTotal from Colombia in August 2023, highlights possible multi-developer reuse of requirements, and follows a surge from 13 to 21 newly discovered macOS malware families in 2023—a trend likely to accelerate in 2024—prompting defenders to monitor anomalous pseudo-terminal invocations, atypical grantpt calls and cross-chain dropper activity for early detection.

title: UAC-0050 Group Using New Phishing Tactics to Distribute Remcos RAT
preprocessed: Active since 2020, UAC-0050 has targeted Ukrainian and Polish entities with social-engineering phishing campaigns masquerading as legitimate organizations to deliver the Remcos RAT, and CERT-UA linked a February 2023 operation to the group; in recent months it mounted at least three phishing waves—one also deploying Meduza Stealer. Uptycs’s December 21, 2023 discovery of a malicious LNK file exposed an advanced infection chain: the LNK enumerates installed antivirus software before invoking mshta.exe to run “6.hta,” which launches a PowerShell script that unpacks secondary scripts and downloads word_update.exe and ofer.docx from new-tech-savvy[.]com. Upon execution, word_update.exe copies itself as fmTask_dbg.exe, establishes persistence via a Startup-folder shortcut, and uses unnamed Windows pipes between its process and a child cmd.exe to decrypt and launch Remcos RAT v4.9.2 Pro, enabling system reconnaissance and browser cookie and credential theft; this pipe-based interprocess communication demonstrates UAC-0050’s enhanced stealth to bypass EDR and antivirus defenses.

title: UAC-0099 Using WinRAR Exploit to Target Ukrainian Firms with LONEPAGE Malware
preprocessed: The threat actor UAC-0099, first profiled by CERT-UA in June 2023 for espionage-driven intrusions against Ukrainian state and media entities, has been observed deploying the VBS-based LONEPAGE malware via three phishing-borne chains—HTA attachments, self-extracting RAR archives, and specially crafted ZIP files exploiting WinRAR’s CVE-2023-38831 (CVSS 7.8)—to target Ukrainian employees at foreign organizations; in SFX attacks, an LNK shortcut masquerading as a WordPad-iconed DOCX summons triggers PowerShell to drop LONEPAGE, while the ZIP attack leverages the unpatched vulnerability (Deep Instinct identified samples dated August 5, 2023) to similarly execute malicious scripts, all of which spawn a scheduled task that calls back to C2 servers for follow-on payloads including keyloggers, credential stealers, and screenshot tools; during 2022–2023, CERT-UA confirmed dozens of compromised systems in Ukraine, underscoring the need for immediate patching of WinRAR, stricter email attachment filtering, and robust PowerShell execution controls to disrupt UAC-0099’s persistent espionage operations.

title: Russian Hackers Breach 20+ NGOs Using Evilginx Phishing via Fake Microsoft Entra Pages
preprocessed: Since April 2024, the Russia-affiliated threat actor Void Blizzard (aka Laundry Bear) has targeted over 20 NGOs and multiple government, defense, transportation, media and healthcare organizations across NATO member states, Western Europe, North America and Ukraine, initially leveraging password spraying and stolen credentials—likely purchased from cybercrime marketplaces—to access Exchange and SharePoint Online, enumerate Microsoft Entra ID via AzureHound, and exfiltrate large volumes of emails and files. More recently, the group shifted to adversary-in-the-middle spear-phishing using a typosquatted “micsrosoftonline[.]com” domain and an Evilginx-based phishing page delivered through malicious QR codes in forged European Defense and Security Summit PDF invitations, automating bulk data collection via Exchange, Microsoft Graph and Teams web client. Overlaps with Forest Blizzard, Midnight Blizzard and Secret Blizzard indicate coordinated Russian strategic espionage, and a September 2024 pass-the-cookie breach of a Dutch police account underscores their evolving cookie-theft capabilities—highlighting urgent needs for phishing-resistant MFA and hardened Entra ID configurations.

title: New Sneaky Xamalicious Android Malware Hits Over 327,000 Devices
preprocessed: McAfee Mobile Research Team uncovered Xamalicious, a new Android backdoor built with Xamarin that abuses accessibility permissions to harvest device metadata, query a C2 server for a second-stage payload, and dynamically inject an assembly DLL to perform unauthorized ad-clicking, app installs and other financially motivated actions; this threat has been embedded in 25 apps—ranging from horoscope and gaming to utility tools—on Google Play since mid-2020, amassing over 327,000 installations across Brazil, Argentina, the UK, Australia, the US, Mexico and Europe. To evade detection, Xamalicious encrypts all C2 traffic as JWE tokens (RSA-OAEP/128CBC-HS256), self-updates its APK to transform into spyware or a banking trojan, and links back to the Cash Magnet ad-fraud campaign; its use of non-Java frameworks like Xamarin underscores heightened obfuscation. Google Play Protect now blocks or auto-removes infected apps. Separately, a malicious WhatsApp-based phishing campaign in India distributes fake SBI APKs invoking SMS permissions to capture credentials, banking and identity data, then exfiltrates them for unauthorized transactions.

title: Urgent: New Chrome Zero-Day Vulnerability Exploited in the Wild - Update ASAP
preprocessed: Google has released Chrome 120.0.6099.129/130 updates to patch an actively exploited high-severity zero-day (CVE-2023-7024), a heap-based buffer overflow in the WebRTC framework that enables crashes or arbitrary code execution, discovered by TAG researchers Clément Lecigne and Vlad Stolyarov on December 19, 2023. This marks the eighth Chrome zero-day exploited in the wild this year—following type confusion flaws in V8 (CVE-2023-2033, CVSS 8.8; CVE-2023-2136, CVSS 9.6; CVE-2023-3079, CVSS 8.8; CVE-2023-4762, CVSS 8.8), a heap overflow in WebP (CVE-2023-4863, CVSS 8.8), a heap overflow in libvpx (CVE-2023-5217, CVSS 8.8) and an integer overflow in Skia (CVE-2023-6345, CVSS 9.6)—amid a record 26,447 CVEs disclosed in 2023, 115 of which have been weaponized by threat actors and ransomware groups using remote code execution, security-feature bypass, buffer manipulation, privilege escalation and input-validation flaws. Given WebRTC’s cross-browser support, impacts on Firefox and Safari remain under assessment. Administrators and end users should immediately upgrade Chrome for Windows, macOS and Linux and apply forthcoming patches for Chromium-based browsers (Edge, Brave, Opera, Vivaldi) to mitigate potential compromise.

title: CISA Flags Critical Ivanti vTM Vulnerability Amid Active Exploitation Concerns
preprocessed: CISA has added CVE-2024-7593, a critical (CVSS 9.8) authentication-bypass flaw in Ivanti Virtual Traffic Manager (vTM) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog amid evidence of active exploitation and a public proof-of-concept, enabling remote attackers to bypass the admin panel and create rogue administrative users; Ivanti released patches in August 2024 for vTM versions 22.2R1, 22.3R3, 22.5R2, 22.6R2 and 22.7R2, and Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies must remediate by October 15, 2024. This alert follows active exploitation of CVE-2024-8190 and CVE-2024-8963 against a limited number of customers, while Censys data reveals 2,017 exposed Ivanti Cloud Service Appliance instances (predominantly U.S.), underscoring the need for immediate patch deployment, asset inventory and monitoring for unauthorized admin activity to prevent network compromise.

title: New Octo2 Android Banking Trojan Emerges with Device Takeover Capabilities
preprocessed: Researchers at ThreatFabric have identified a new Android banking Trojan, Octo2—a direct descendant of Exobot (2016) and its Coper variant (2021)—now distributed across Europe (Italy, Poland, Moldova, Hungary) via trojanized APKs (Europe Enterprise com.xsusb_restore3, Google Chrome com.havirtual06numberresources, NordVPN com.handedfastee5) bound with Zombinder to masquerade as “necessary plugins.” Spawned after the public leak of Octo’s source code earlier this year, Octo2—attributed to the threat actor known as Architect/goodluck—introduces stabilized device takeover (DTO) capabilities for seamless remote actions, a DGA-based C2 framework to evade domain blocklists and takedowns, and enhanced obfuscation and anti-analysis techniques that enable invisible on-device fraud and interception of banking credentials. According to Team Cymru, Octo2 has transitioned to a Malware-as-a-Service model, offered at no extra cost to existing Octo1 customers, signaling imminent global adoption by cybercriminals. With no evidence of Google Play distribution, users are compromised via side-loading or social engineering, highlighting the urgent need for enterprises to enforce strict app-source policies, deploy advanced mobile threat defenses, and monitor anomalous behaviors to prevent unauthorized transactions and account takeovers.

title: Attackers Use Public Exploits to Throttle Atlassian Confluence Flaw | Threatpost
preprocessed: Over the Memorial Day weekend, Volexity researchers uncovered an OGNL injection zero-day RCE (CVE-2022-26134) in all supported Atlassian Confluence Server and Data Center versions, attributing attacks to public exploits that inject a JSP webshell (China Chopper) into internet-facing deployments for secondary access; upon disclosure they reported it to Atlassian, which issued an advisory the same day with no immediate update and prompted CISA to warn users, before releasing patched builds for versions 7.4.17–7.18.1 and a temporary file-based workaround a day later—yet tests by Horizon3.ai confirm unpatched instances remain trivial to compromise via a single HTTP GET, with GreyNoise observing more than 400 unique IPs throttling the flaw in 24 hours. Industry experts warn this source-code-level vulnerability enables full host takeover, lateral movement through critical business data and poses SolarWinds-scale supply-chain risks, underscoring the urgent need for rapid patching, code audits and strict access controls on Confluence environments.

title: CISA Urges Patch of Exploited Windows 11 Bug by Aug. 2 | Threatpost
preprocessed: CISA has added CVE-2022-22047—a high-severity (CVSS 7.8) elevation-of-privilege flaw in the Windows Client Server Runtime Subsystem used since Windows 7 through Windows 11 and Server 2008–2022—to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog and is urging federal agencies to install Microsoft’s July 5 Patch Tuesday update by August 2 after evidence emerged of in-the-wild exploitation; initially disclosed as a zero-day by Microsoft’s security team, the CSRSS bug enables adversaries who already hold local or physical access—or who gain remote code execution via malware or specially crafted Office/Adobe documents and macros—to escalate to SYSTEM privileges for lateral movement, although FortiGuard Labs rates the overall business threat as “medium” given the prerequisite foothold and available patch, while Trend Micro’s ZDI notes such elevation flaws are typically paired with a separate RCE vector and Microsoft has signaled future default blocking of VBA macros to mitigate this attack chain.

title: Microsoft Patches ‘Dogwalk’ Zero-Day and 17 Critical Flaws | Threatpost
preprocessed: In its massive August Patch Tuesday rollout—121 vulnerabilities (17 critical, 101 important), nearly triple last year’s volume—Microsoft patched CVE-2022-34713, an actively exploited two-year-old “Dogwalk” variant in the Windows Support Diagnostic Tool (MSDT) enabling low-complexity code execution via URL protocol (e.g., Word docs) through social engineering or physical access; CVE-2022-34715 in Windows Network File System (severity 8.5–9.8), the fourth consecutive month of critical remote unauthenticated code-exec fixes granting elevated privileges via crafted NFS calls; three Exchange Server elevation-of-privilege flaws requiring authentication and user interaction to exploit via phishing-lured visits; and CVE-2022-35804 in SMBv3.1.1 on Windows 11 (rated 8.8, “Exploitation More Likely” and potentially wormable unless SMBv3 compression is disabled). Researchers urge immediate patch deployment—especially for Dogwalk, NFS, SMB and Exchange—and note Dogwalk’s rediscovery following Follina (CVE-2022-30190) exploitation, while Adobe also addressed 25 CVEs across Acrobat, Reader, Commerce, Illustrator, FrameMaker and Premiere Elements.

title: Follina Exploited by State-Sponsored Hackers | Threatpost
preprocessed: Proofpoint researchers led by Sherrod DeGrippo have uncovered state-sponsored actors exploiting CVE-2022-30190 (Follina), a Microsoft Office remote code execution flaw in the Windows Support Diagnostic Tool (MSDT) invoked via URL protocol, in phishing campaigns since mid-April targeting U.S. and E.U. government workers; following Shadow Chaser Group’s April 12 discovery and Microsoft’s May patch, adversaries dispatched over 1,000 recruitment-themed emails promising a “20% increase” and urging recipients to open a Word attachment that launches a PowerShell script to detect virtualized environments, perform extensive reconnaissance across browsers, mail clients and file shares, zip collected data for exfiltration, and enable arbitrary code execution with user-level privileges to install malware, manipulate or delete data, and create accounts—activities indicative of a state-aligned nexus that underscore the urgency of rapid patch deployment, user training and network-level MSDT exploit mitigations.

title: Google Patches Chrome’s Fifth Zero-Day of the Year | Threatpost
preprocessed: In its latest stable‐channel update, Google patched CVE-2022-2856—a high‐severity “insufficient validation of untrusted input in Intents” flaw in Chrome’s Android deep‐linking that could enable arbitrary code execution—reported by Google TAG’s Ashley Shen and Christian Resell on July 19, alongside ten other fixes including critical CVE-2022-2852 (a use-after-free in FedCM, the Federated Credential Management API) disclosed by Google Project Zero’s Sergei Glazunov on Aug. 8; this marks Chrome’s fifth actively exploited zero-day this year, following February’s CVE-2022-0609 Animation component use-after-free exploited weeks earlier by North Korean actors, March’s CVE-2022-1096 and April’s CVE-2022-1364 V8 type-confusion bugs, and May/July’s CVE-2022-2294 WebRTC heap overflows. Google’s practice of withholding exploit details until patches are broadly deployed—endorsed by Tenable’s Satnam Narang—provides a critical buffer for defenders and downstream Chromium-based browsers (e.g., Edge, Linux distributions) to rapidly update and mitigate control-flow hijacks and remote code-execution risks.

title: Emerging H0lyGh0st Ransomware Tied to North Korea | Threatpost
preprocessed: Microsoft Threat Intelligence Center has attributed the emerging H0lyGh0st ransomware, active since June 2021 and tracked as DEV-0530, to financially motivated North Korean state-sponsored actors with ties to PLUTONIUM (DarkSeoul/Andariel), which has compromised small-to-mid-sized businesses—including manufacturers, banks, schools and event planners—across multiple countries since September 2021 by deploying custom SiennaPurple (C++ BTLC_C.exe) and SiennaBlue (Go-based HolyRS.exe, HolyLock.exe, BLTC.exe) families that encrypt Windows files with a .h0lyenc extension, use string obfuscation and public-key management, and enforce persistence via a scheduled task called “lockertask”; victims receive a ransom note delivered over a .onion portal demanding Bitcoin payment under double-extortion threats to publish stolen data if unpaid; between October 2021 and May 2022 MSTIC observed iterative Go-based SiennaBlue variants sharing core encryption and network/intranet connectivity functions, and in April 2022 the group rolled out its latest BTLC.exe, which hard-codes ServerBaseURL fallback credentials for network shares, uploads victim public keys to a C2 server, and encrypts all drive files—underscoring the need for defenders to monitor anomalous scheduled tasks, default-credential share connections, .onion traffic, and the appearance of .h0lyenc files to detect and disrupt this evolving threat.

title: ChromeLoader Browser Hijacker Provides Gateway to Bigger Threats | Threatpost
preprocessed: ChromeLoader, a resurging cross-platform browser hijacker detailed by Malwarebytes Labs and Red Canary, infects Windows via ISO files masquerading as cracked games or pirated media and macOS via DMG files containing installer scripts; once executed, it leverages PowerShell-encoded commands (including the shortened –e flag) to inject a malicious Chrome (or Safari) extension fetched via cURL and ZIP, and employs a .NET wrapper for Windows Task Scheduler (or shell scripts on macOS) to maintain persistence before deleting its own scheduled task to evade detection. After installation, victims experience untrusted, ad-laden search results and potential credential harvesting or spyware deployment, since this rare PowerShell-driven injection technique can be repurposed for higher-impact payloads. Researchers recommend users avoid pirated software, inspect Chrome’s “More Tools → Extensions” menu for suspicious add-ons, and administrators hunt for PowerShell processes invoking encodedCommand or spawning chrome.exe with appdata\local flags on Windows, as well as encoded sh/bash/zsh commands or installer scripts on macOS, to detect and mitigate infections before escalation.

title: Cybercriminals Are Selling Access to Chinese Surveillance Cameras | Threatpost
preprocessed: New research reveals that over 80,000 Hikvision cameras worldwide remain unpatched against the critical CVE-2021-36260 command-injection flaw (NIST score 9.8/10) disclosed last fall, allowing remote code execution and potential espionage by state-linked groups such as MISSION2025/APT41, APT10 and unknown Russian actors trading stolen credentials on dark-web forums; systemic deficiencies—default or hardcoded passwords, no auto-update mechanism, poor forensics and lack of security-by-design—have left devices in 100+ countries (including the U.S., despite an FCC “unacceptable risk” designation) continuously discoverable via Shodan or Censys and ripe for exploitation, underscoring the urgent need for organizations to inventory IoT assets, change default credentials, deploy available patches and improve visibility and update processes to mitigate geopolitical and operational impact.

title: APT Lazarus Targets Engineers with macOS Malware | Threatpost
preprocessed: North Korean APT Lazarus has launched “Operation In(ter)ception,” a macOS-focused cyberespionage campaign that lures engineering professionals with a fake Coinbase job posting and deploys a signed universal macOS executable (Intel and Apple Silicon) that drops three components—a decoy PDF (Coinbase_online_careers_2022_07.pdf), a FinderFontsUpdater.app bundle and a downloader named safarifontagent—before phoning home to a new, currently nonresponsive C2 at concrecapital[.]com/%user%.jpg. Identified by ESET in late July and using a February-2022 developer certificate for “Shankey Nohria” revoked by Apple on August 12, the malware mirrors a May sample but introduces fresh C2 infrastructure and was first uploaded from Brazil. A companion Windows variant, spotted by Malwarebytes on August 4, follows the same decoy routine. This marks another evolution in Lazarus’s longstanding impersonation tactics—previously targeting engineers via spear-phishing and defense-sector ruses—while the group simultaneously diversifies into cryptocurrency heists (prompting Tornado Cash sanctions) and VHD ransomware operations to fund the North Korean regime.

title: Evil Corp Pivots LockBit to Dodge U.S. Sanctions | Threatpost
preprocessed: Researchers at Mandiant Intelligence have identified UNC2165—the latest evolution of the U.S.-sanctioned Evil Corp—as leveraging the FakeUpdates infection chain to gain initial access, followed by deployment of LockBit ransomware to obscure attribution and monetize extortion efforts. After OFAC sanctions in December 2019 crippled Evil Corp’s ability to profit from Dridex and its WastedLocker strain, the group briefly resurfaced under PayloadBin (likely a WastedLocker rebrand) and used HTML redirectors in malicious Excel files, then adopted Hades ransomware with code overlaps to distance itself further. By aligning with LockBit’s RaaS model—already proven effective against high-profile victims such as Accenture and Bangkok Air—UNC2165 can blend in with legitimate affiliates, reduce development overhead, and bypass sanctions enforcement that deters U.S. entities from negotiating ransoms with known Evil Corp actors. This shift underscores the need for defenders to monitor FakeUpdates chains and LockBit activity for potential Evil Corp–linked intrusions and to enhance detection of rebranded ransomware variants despite attribution obfuscation tactics.

title: New Magniber Ransomware Targets South Korea, Asia Pacific | Threatpost
preprocessed: Researchers have identified a new ransomware strain dubbed Magniber—an affiliate of both the Magnitude exploit kit and Cerber ransomware—exclusively targeting users in South Korea and the Asia-Pacific region following Magnitude’s reemergence on October 15, 2017, after a brief hiatus during which its Cerber distribution waned. FireEye and Trend Micro findings reveal that Magniber leverages malvertising and IE memory corruption vulnerability CVE-2016-0189 to deliver a binary payload encrypted in reverse RC4 with 30-byte keys, unpacks it in memory, then executes an AES-128 encryption routine that renames files with a “.ihsdj” extension before self-deletion. It employs a GetSystemDefaultUILanguage check to exit on non-Korean systems and generates four callback URLs via a 19-character pseudorandom string to evade virtual machines. Organizations should prioritize patching IE CVE-2016-0189, deploy ad blockers and updated exploit kit defenses, and monitor for Magnitude EK activity in APAC environments.

title: Microsoft Releases Workaround for ‘One-Click’ 0Day Under Active Attack | Threatpost
preprocessed: Microsoft released a temporary registry-based workaround in June 2022 to mitigate an actively exploited zero-day RCE (CVE-2022-3019, “Follina”) in the Microsoft Support Diagnostic Tool (MSDT), which attackers in Russia, Tibet and Belarus have leveraged since mid-April to execute arbitrary code, install programs, manipulate data or create accounts at the privilege level of the calling application without requiring macros. Researchers from Shadow Chaser Group and Recorded Future traced the flaw to an April 2020 bachelor’s thesis and first spotted it on April 12, with Malwarebytes confirming the issue and a formal report submitted to Microsoft on April 21—though Microsoft initially downplayed the risk until renewed alerts from Japanese vendor Nao Sec and security analyst Kevin Beaumont. The interim fix—deleting the HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\ms-msdt registry key—disables URL-launched troubleshooters but disrupts system utilities and, according to experts, offers limited protection despite Office’s Protected View and Application Guard safeguards. With no official patch yet and all supported Windows and Office 2013–365 editions exposed, including lure campaigns impersonating the Central Tibetan Administration’s “Women Empowerment Desk,” organizations must implement the registry hardening, monitor for exploitation indicators and prepare for a comprehensive security update.

title: Fake Reservation Links Prey on Weary Travelers | Threatpost
preprocessed: Since 2018, financially motivated TA558 has relentlessly targeted travel and hospitality organizations—primarily in Latin America, North America, and Western Europe—beginning with CVE-2017-11882 exploits and macro-laced Word/PowerPoint documents and expanding to English-language lures before ramping up post-COVID phishing campaigns that deliver fake reservation emails containing URLs to ISO and RAR containers; victims who decompress these archives trigger an embedded .BAT file that executes a PowerShell loader to fetch follow-on RATs (AsyncRAT, Loda, RevengeRAT). After Microsoft disabled VBA and XL4 macros by default, TA558 jumped from five URL-based campaigns in 2018–2021 to 27 in 2022, leveraging reconnaissance, data theft, and distribution of downstream payloads with medium-to-high confidence of financial intent. Organizations and customers in the travel sector should enforce email filtering, URL and attachment inspection, macro restrictions, endpoint detection, and user awareness training to mitigate this evolving threat.

title: iPhone Users Urged to Update to Patch 2 Zero-Days | Threatpost
preprocessed: Apple has released emergency updates for iOS 15.6.1 and macOS Monterey 12.5.1 to remediate two actively exploited zero-day vulnerabilities—CVE-2022-32894, an out-of-bounds kernel write, and CVE-2022-32893, an out-of-bounds WebKit write—that allow attackers to execute arbitrary code with kernel privileges or via malicious web content in Safari and third-party iOS browsers, raising fears of Pegasus-style spyware campaigns by nation-state APTs leveraging these flaws; credited to an anonymous researcher, these bugs underscore the ongoing arms race between threat actors and vendors, as seen in Google’s concurrent Chrome patch for its fifth zero-day this year, and highlight the urgent need for users—especially high-value targets such as journalists and activists—to install updates immediately and for mobile app developers to implement additional security controls beyond OS defenses to mitigate future exploits.

title: Mitel VoIP Bug Exploited in Ransomware Attacks | Threatpost
preprocessed: CrowdStrike researchers in April 2022 uncovered that ransomware actors exploited a critical remote code execution flaw (CVE-2022-29499) in unpatched Linux-based Mitel MiVoice appliances (SA 100, SA 400 and Virtual SA) to gain initial access, plant malware and pivot laterally: the exploit chain began with an external HTTP GET to a “get_url” parameter in a PHP file (to bypass IP restrictions) followed by a device-originated GET that injected commands via a malicious URL, enabling an SSL-enabled reverse shell (using mkfifo and openssl_client) and deployment of a “pdf_import.php” web shell and the Chisel tunneling tool. Although the threat actors deleted evidence from the VoIP filesystem, CrowdStrike recovered the undocumented exploit, downloaded tools and anti-forensic measures. With some 21,000 MITEL devices worldwide still exposed (per Kevin Beaumont’s Shodan string “http.html_hash:-1971546278”), organizations are urged to apply Mitel’s April advisory patches for MiVoice Connect 19.2 SP3 and earlier, enforce strict network segmentation around perimeter devices, conduct threat modeling to detect anomalous GET requests, and prioritize timely firmware updates to thwart zero-day exploitation.

title: Elusive ToddyCat APT Targets Microsoft Exchange Servers | Threatpost
preprocessed: Since December 2020, the relatively new APT group ToddyCat has conducted multi-wave intrusion campaigns against high-profile government and military Microsoft Exchange servers in Asia and Europe, first targeting Taiwan and Vietnam via China Chopper-deployed web shells to drop a multi-stage chain that installs the Samurai passive backdoor on ports 80/443, uses obfuscated C# modules for arbitrary code execution, lateral movement and registry hijacking to load iiswmi.dll and a .NET loader, and in some cases launches the Ninja post-exploitation toolkit—which, like Cobalt Strike, offers HTTP-camouflaged command and control. From February to May 2021 the group scaled up by abusing the ProxyLogon vulnerability to compromise organizations in Iran, India, Malaysia, Slovakia, Russia and the UK, then post-May expanded its scope to desktops and additional government and military targets in Indonesia, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan. Independent telemetry from ESET (“Websiic”) and GTSC has partially mapped ToddyCat’s infection vectors and dropper delivery, though full chains and later stages remain undocumented. Researchers noted overlaps with Chinese-language groups using the FunnyDream Exchange backdoor against the same targets—sharing staging locations and directories—yet found no conclusive link, suggesting multiple APT interests. This campaign highlights the urgent need to patch Exchange servers, hunt for China Chopper web shells, monitor anomalous registry modifications and HTTP indicators, and enforce network segmentation to mitigate high-impact geopolitical espionage.

title: ZuoRAT Can Take Over Widely Used SOHO Routers | Threatpost
