preprocessed: Since April 2020, researchers at Black Lotus Labs have observed a sophisticated, likely state-sponsored multi-stage RAT dubbed ZuoRAT exploiting known SOHO-router vulnerabilities CVE-2020-26878/79 via a Python-compiled Windows PE referencing the ruckus151021.py proof-of-concept to harvest credentials and deploy its agent; initial delivery is staged from a benign-content VPS, followed by router-to-router proxy C2 infrastructure with periodic rotation to evade detection. In stage one, ZuoRAT fingerprints the router and adjacent LAN, captures packets, performs core dumps to extract credentials, routing tables and IP tables, then exfiltrates telemetry to C2. In stage two, the actor dynamically pushes auxiliary modules—approximately 2,500 embedded functions ranging from password spraying, USB enumeration and code injection to LAN enumeration and undetectable DNS/HTTPS hijacking—to maintain persistence and enable man-in-the-middle attacks. Black Lotus has confirmed roughly 80 compromised devices across Cisco, Netgear, Asus and others, highlighting the pandemic-driven rise of unpatched edge devices as low-visibility ingress points for prolonged network compromise and data exfiltration. To mitigate this ongoing threat, organizations should promptly patch affected routers, enforce firmware-integrity monitoring and scrutinize anomalous DNS, HTTPS and router-to-router traffic.

title: Ransomware Spotlight: Akira | Trend Micro (US)
preprocessed: Between April and August 2023, the newly emerged Akira ransomware group targeted 107 organizations—predominantly SMBs in North America (85.9%) and France (53.1% of detections), with additional impacts in the United States and Turkey—surging from just three recorded attempts in May to 508 in June; operators gain initial access via compromised VPN credentials (including exploitation of CVE-2023-20269 on Cisco ASA/FTD), employ third-party tools such as PCHunter, PowerTool, AdFind, Advanced IP Scanner and MASSCAN for defense evasion and discovery, dump credentials with Mimikatz and LaZagne, and establish persistence by creating new domain accounts, then move laterally via RDP, exfiltrate data through RClone, FTP clients (FileZilla, WinSCP), AnyDesk, Radmin, Cloudflare Tunnel, MobaXterm, RustDesk or Ngrok, and encrypt data using a hybrid ChaCha20/RSA scheme—avoiding system directories and common extensions, deleting shadow copies, and appending .akira to files before dropping akira_readme.txt—and to mitigate this threat organizations should prioritize patching and virtual patching of vulnerable VPN appliances, enforce multifactor authentication and least-privilege access, monitor anomalous use of administration and reconnaissance tools, implement comprehensive backup and recovery procedures, and deploy layered endpoint, network and email defenses with behavior-based detection.

title: Ransomware Spotlight: BlackCat | Trend Micro (US)
preprocessed: Trend Micro data shows BlackCat executed 39.3% of its 176 manufacturing detections against US targets and confirmed 173 leak-site compromises from December 2021 to September 2022—58.7% US-based—favoring finance, professional, legal, technology, energy, utilities, construction, and manufacturing sectors, with small (52%) and midsize (26%) businesses most targeted. Initial access was achieved via Exchange CVE-2021-26855/26857/26858/27065 exploits, ConnectWise RCE, and SSH key abuse. Execution leverages COBEACON to inject the Rust-based ransomware into ntoskrnl.exe, evading detection; defense evasion includes disabling AV, using AdFind/ADRecon/SoftPerfect, Process Hacker, Mimikatz, WMIC, Netstat, and LSASS credential dumping. Lateral movement exploits embedded PsExec, RDP, MobaXterm, and BITSAdmin transfers of zzz.exe/xxx.exe/yyy.exe/sv.exe. C2 communication uses Base64-encoded PowerShell with a Cobalt Strike SMB beacon over named pipes. Exfiltration employs ExMatter (upgraded September 2022), 7-Zip, Rclone, MEGASync, WinSCP, and FreeFileSync for double extortion. The payload defaces backgrounds, terminates backup/AV/DB/Internet/VM services, disables recovery (shadow copy deletion, safe-mode variant), and appends variable Sphynx extensions while avoiding critical directories and file types. BlackCat maps to MITRE ATT&CK T1190, T1078, T1562.001/009, T1003.001, T1021.002, T1486, T1490, T1489, T1048/T1567. Security teams should patch Exchange CVEs, secure MSP tools, enforce least privilege, segment networks, monitor PowerShell injections, and vet outbound file transfers to disrupt this evolving affiliate-driven operation.

title: Ransomware Spotlight: Clop | Trend Micro (US)
preprocessed: Clop ransomware, a TA505-sponsored RaaS strain appending the “.ClOP” extension, infects entire networks by compromising Active Directory servers and manipulating Group Policy for persistence, then uses phishing-delivered HTML attachments to drop the Get2 loader, which in turn pulls SDBOT, FlawedAmmyy RATs, Cobalt Strike beacons and TinyMet reverse shells for reconnaissance, lateral movement (via SMB exploits), and exfiltration (often using the DEWMODE web shell). Operators employ double and quadruple extortion—threatening to publish or auction stolen data on their Cl0p^_-Leaks site and targeting executives/customers—to coerce ransoms, driving average payments up 43% to $220,298 (median $78,398) in Q1 2021 after FIN11’s and FIN7’s twin zero-day campaigns against Kiteworks FTA (CVE-2021-27101/02/03/04) and Fortra GoAnywhere MFT, while in 2023 they exploited PaperCut CVE-2023-27350 to deploy Truebot and LockBit/Clop, then MOVEit CVE-2023-24362/CVE-2023-35036 and an unpatched SQL injection flaw to steal data without payloads. Trend Micro detections reveal a May 2023 surge (245 attempts), with top targets in banking, retail and healthcare across Türkiye, Canada, the US and large enterprises worldwide.

title: Malicious Actors Target Comm Apps such as Zoom, Slack, Discord | Trend Micro (US)
preprocessed: In Trend Micro’s midyear 2020 report, attackers pivoted to popular communication apps—Zoom, Slack, and Discord—exploiting increased usage from pandemic-driven remote work. Zoom-based campaigns evolved beyond nuisance Zoombombing to malware delivery via fake or compromised installers (Trojan.Win32.ZAPIZ.A, Backdoor.Win32.DEVILSHADOW.THEAABO) and bundling legitimate installers with RATs such as RevCode WebMonitor (Backdoor.Win32.REVCODE.THDBABO); ZAPIZ opens backdoor access on TCP port 5650 to steal usernames and machine names, while DEVILSHADOW executes malicious commands under the guise of Zoom. Extortion emails threatening release of hacked video footage further underscored attackers’ creativity. On Slack, the CRYPREN ransomware (Ransom.Win32.CRYPREN.C) encrypts multimedia and document files using a .encrypted suffix and uniquely leverages Slack webhooks to report victim machine names, user names, infected-file counts and timestamps to its C2. Discord-based attacks deliver AveMaria and AgentTesla via malicious spam—often posing as postal or invoice notifications—pointing to hxxps://cdn[.]discordapp[.]com/attachments/.../example.exe, facilitating remote access, keylogging and data exfiltration. These tactics exploit the trust and ubiquity of comms apps, blending into normal traffic and granting anonymity. Recommended defenses include obtaining software exclusively from official sources, avoiding unverified links or attachments, and confirming email legitimacy to block tampered installers and malicious payload delivery.

title: Ransomware Spotlight: Conti | Trend Micro (US)
preprocessed: Trend Micro observed over one million Conti ransomware attack attempts in the U.S. (Jan–Nov 2021), with the retail, insurance, manufacturing, telecommunications and healthcare sectors most targeted; operators—tied to Trickbot—gain initial access via BazarLoader phishing emails (Google Drive links) and exploitation of FortiGate flaws (CVE-2018-13379/13374) or Exchange ProxyShell, deploy Cobalt Strike, then perform reconnaissance (Whoami, Nltest, Net, ShareFinder), escalate privileges by harvesting domain-admin credentials or exploiting Zerologon (CVE-2020-1472) and PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-1675), and dump credentials using ProcDump and Mimikatz (mass-mimikatz, Rubeus, kerberoasting), “reg save,” Get-GPPPassword, SharpChrome and SeatBelt; they move laterally via EternalBlue, PSExec, scheduled tasks and remote-access tools (Atera, AnyDesk), evade defenses with automated batch scripts (GMER, PC Hunter, PowerShell) to disable security services, then execute ransomware via scheduled jobs or DontSleep.exe, exfiltrate data using Rclone (to Mega) or WinSCP, and encrypt files with ChaCha20/RSA-4096 while deleting shadow copies for double extortion; organizations should inventory assets, enforce least privilege, virtual-patch public-facing apps, monitor for Cobalt Strike and anomalous scheduled tasks or credential-dumping activities, deploy multilayered endpoint and network defenses, and maintain reliable backups.

title: Threat Recap: Darkside, Crysis, Negasteal, Coinminer | Trend Micro (US)
preprocessed: In the past weeks, Trend Micro researchers identified four major threat trajectories: Darkside, a newly emerged ransomware (Ransom.Win32.DARKSIDE.YXAH-THA) mimicking Maze/Nefilim by appending victims’ MAC addresses to encrypted files and threatening public data leaks based on corporate financial profiles while sparing medical, education, non-profit and government sectors; a Crysis/Dharma RaaS operator–released hacking toolkit named Toolbox bundling Mimikatz, NirSoft RDP PassView, Hash Suite Tools and reconnaissance utilities to lower operational expertise barriers and expand affiliate-driven deployments; targeted Negasteal/Agent Tesla campaigns (TrojanSpy.MSIL.NEGASTEAL.DYSGXT) exploiting CVE-2017-11882 via spoofed Krung Thai Bank emails to harvest credentials for web/FTP/SMTP exfiltration; and fileless Monero coinminer infections (Coinminer.Win32.MALXMR.THHADBO) clandestinely bundled with unofficial installers of TeamViewer, Rufus and YTD Video Downloader that drop obfuscated VBS scripts to fetch loaders from pastebin and monerohash.com:3333. These developments underscore the urgency for rigorous patch management, restricting downloads to official sources, robust email filtering and behavior-based endpoint defenses such as Apex One and XDR to detect script-based, RDP-harvesting and fileless intrusions early.

title: New APT Group Earth Berberoka Targets Gambling Websites With Old and New Malware | Trend Micro (US)
preprocessed: Trend Micro researchers have uncovered a new Chinese-speaking APT dubbed Earth Berberoka (aka GamblingPuppet) that targets online gambling websites on Windows, macOS and Linux by deploying both legacy (PlugX, Gh0st RAT) and novel malware, most notably a five-stage loader called PuppetLoader and a Go-based oRAT. PuppetLoader’s Stage 1 decrypts an initial payload with a flawed RC4 implementation (key “2726c6aea9970bb95211304705b5f595”), then stealthily hijacks the loading of a legitimate DLL (asycfilt.dll) via hooked NTDLL APIs (NtOpenFile, NtMapViewOfSection, RtlPushFrame/RtlPopFrame) to rebase and execute a malicious lz32.dll; Stage 2 drops marker files (CPuppetProcessFileSharer with GUID 78106D5F-CD1A-A8C4-A625-6863092B4BBA, Config.ini encrypted with “whk0q9ogev6ofg8d”), MSVCPX00.dll and BMP stagers; Stage 3’s BasicLoader scans Users\Public directories for 33×11-pixel BMPs containing encrypted payloads; Stage 4’s Core module logs activity via custom RC4-encrypted entries delimited by 0xAABBCCDD and supports -NoModuleLoadDLL and -LoadShellcode flags; and Stage 5’s MainConsole client written in C++ provides interactive shell, file upload/download, process listing, module installation and RDP enumeration over a custom RC4-encrypted UDP protocol with specific packet types (RemoteModuleCommandPacket, FileTransferContent_Packet, InstallModulePacket, etc.). Concurrently, oRAT droppers packaged as an Electron MiMi chat app and a macOS DMG carry AES-GCM-encrypted Go configurations enabling gateway or traffic-forwarder modes and expose HTTP(S)/QUIC routes (e.g., GET/POST /agent/info, /agent/upload) for direct code execution. This multivector, multiplatform campaign highlights the critical need to monitor anomalous DLL load behavior, bitmap steganography, flawed RC4/AES-GCM decryption routines and custom UDP or HTTP traffic on gambling infrastructures.

title: Operation Earth Kitsune: Tracking SLUB’s Current Operations | Trend Micro (US)
preprocessed: Trend Micro’s “Operation Earth Kitsune” report reveals that the SLUB threat actor recently pivoted from abusing Slack and GitHub to using an on-premise Mattermost instance—complete with five C&C servers and 15 user accounts—to coordinate a sophisticated watering-hole campaign against GNUBoard CMS sites (notably the Korean American National Coordinating Council domain), redirecting visitors to a weaponized proof-of-concept for CVE-2019-5782 (Chrome) that loads shellcode to fetch three backdoors (“1.jpg,” “2.jpg,” “3.jpg”) and exploiting CVE-2020-0674 (Internet Explorer) via a PowerShell loader (with optional LPE via CVE-2019-1458), alongside prior flaws CVE-2016-0189 and CVE-2019-1458; two new malware variants (dneSpy and agfSpy) extend system-information exfiltration and remote-control capabilities, underscoring the need for organizations to patch affected browsers, CMS platforms, audit Mattermost usage for unauthorized channels, and monitor for anomalous shellcode or PowerShell activity to disrupt SLUB’s evolving toolkit.

title: FOG Ransomware Spread by Cybercriminals Claiming Ties to DOGE | Trend Micro (US)
preprocessed: During our analysis of nine FOG ransomware samples uploaded between March 27 and April 2, Trend Micro found cybercriminals abusing references to the US Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) to troll users and distribute a ZIP-wrapped LNK file (“Pay Adjustment.zip”) via email phishing that, when clicked, executes a multi-stage PowerShell script (stage1.ps1) to retrieve a ransomware loader (cwiper.exe), a privilege-escalation exploit (ktool.exe leveraging Intel’s iQVW64.sys with hardcoded key “fd6c57fa3852aec8”), and additional PowerShell scripts (including lootsubmit.ps1 variants) that harvest system information—CPU, IP/gateway/MAC (via ARP and Wigle API), geolocation—and exfiltrate data to hxxps://hilarious-trifle-d9182e.netlify[.]app, embed political commentary and YouTube links, perform sandbox-evasion checks, decrypt embedded .flocked binaries in memory, drop dbgLog.sys logs and readme.txt ransom notes (with code-paste instructions and a QR-linked Monero wallet address), and encrypt files under the FOG ransomware family (detected as Win32.FOG.SMYPEFG); since January, FOG operators or impersonators have declared 100 victims (53 in February, 29 in March, 18 in January) across technology, education, manufacturing, transportation, business services, healthcare, retail, and consumer sectors, while Trend Vision One has blocked 173 FOG incidents among customers since June 2024, underscoring the need for proactive IoC monitoring (e.g., .flocked file creation, readme.txt drops, stage1.ps1 activity), network segmentation, diligent patching of drivers and applications, secure offline backups, and employee phishing awareness training to prevent financial loss and operational disruption.

title: Ransomware Spotlight: LockBit | Trend Micro (US)
preprocessed: Trend Micro’s investigation into the LockBit ransomware-as-a-service operation, tracked as intrusion set Water Selkie, reveals the group’s marketing of its lightning-fast AES-128 head-only file encryption (first 4 KB) with RSA-wrapped keys, deployed via versatile affiliate-driven campaigns that source initial access through phishing (T1566), CVE-2018-13379 Fortinet VPN exploits (T1190) and compromised RDP/VPN accounts (T1078), then execute payloads via PowerShell Empire, Meterpreter, scheduled tasks or signed binaries (T1059, T1218), evade defenses with Mimikatz, GMER, Process Hacker or disabled Windows Defender (T1562), discover network shares and AD servers (T1083, T1135), laterally propagate via SMB or Cobalt Strike (T1570), exfiltrate data using StealBit or cloud storage (T1567) and encrypt data for impact (T1486), often on weekdays (~78%). Between July 2021 and January 2022 LockBit attempts surged globally—chiefly the US, India and Brazil—targeting healthcare and education yet boasting 41 leak-site victims (Dec 2021–Jan 2022) primarily SMBs (65.9%) across North America, Europe and APAC. With a professional affiliate program fueling continuous innovation and predicted upticks in supply-chain attacks in 2022, organizations should implement comprehensive asset inventory, least-privilege access, regular patching (including Fortinet CVE-2018-13379), RDP/VPN lockdown, application allow-listing, multifactor authentication, offline backups and MITRE TTP monitoring to detect and disrupt LockBit activity.

title: Ransomware Spotlight: Magniber | Trend Micro (US)
preprocessed: In 2022 Magniber ransomware attacks accelerated from fewer than 20 monthly attempts in Q1 to a peak of 1,482 detections in September and 508 in December, with Trend Micro data showing Taiwan as the hardest-hit nation (204 attempts, ~76.1% of total), followed by South Korea (15), Australia (9), Turkey and Japan (6) and emerging targets beyond Asia; industry-wise education, government and manufacturing bore the brunt (987 detections), then healthcare and technology, with energy, transportation and real estate also affected. Attackers gain initial access via exploit kits and public-facing flaws—CVE-2016-0189, CVE-2018-8174, CVE-2019-1367, CVE-2020-0968, CVE-2021-26411, CVE-2021-40444, PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527) and CVE-2022-44698—delivering payloads through fake MSI and CPL installers, MSHTML/Regsvr32 proxy execution and Mark-of-the-Web bypass. They employ NtQuerySystemInformation for discovery, thread execution hijacking and process injection for defense evasion, UAC bypass via Fodhelper scripts that delete shadow copies, then encrypt files using AES per 1 MiB block and RSA-wrapped keys, inhibit recovery and append mutex-based extensions. Security teams should prioritize patching these CVEs, monitor anomalous Msiexec/Regsvr32 activity, script-based installers and registry modifications, and detect shadow-copy deletion or process injection to mitigate this streamlined yet potent ransomware chain.

title: Mispadu Banking Trojan Resurfaces | Trend Micro (US)
preprocessed: Trend Micro has identified a resurgence of the URSA/Mispadu banking Trojan (TrojanSpy.Win32.MISPADU) in spam campaigns targeting Spanish- and Portuguese-language systems—especially in Mexico, Spain and Portugal—by sending “overdue invoice” emails that coax users into downloading a ZIP containing an MSI installer with a triple-obfuscated VBScript. Once executed, the VBScript checks for Hyper-V, VirtualBox or VMware, aborts on non-target locale IDs (1034, 1046, 2058, 2070, 3082/58378) or a host named “JOHN-PC,” then deobfuscates to load an AutoIT injector which deploys a Delphi payload into memory. The Delphi binary presents fake banking overlays using legitimate bank logos and employs NirSoft’s WebBrowserPassView and MailPassView tools to harvest credentials and exfiltrate them via a large network of dynamic-DNS and IP-based endpoints (e.g., *.ddns.net, *.freedynamicdns.org, 87.98.137.173). IOC analysis—bolstered by CronUp Red Team findings—revealed dozens of malicious URLs and SHA-256 hashes (including Trojan.VBS.MISPADU.THIAHBO and AutoIt.MISPADO.THIADBO), demonstrating Mispadu’s sophisticated obfuscation, locale-based evasion and multi-stage loader methods. Organizations are urged to enforce strict email hygiene (block untrusted attachments, verify sender domains, scrutinize URLs and grammar) and deploy advanced email threat defenses such as Trend Micro™ Email Security and Deep Discovery™ Email Inspector to detect and quarantine this malware at the gateway.

title: Ransomware Spotlight: RansomEXX | Trend Micro (US)
preprocessed: Trend Micro’s analysis of RansomEXX activity from March 31, 2021 to March 31, 2022 reveals a predominantly human-operated ransomware campaign that hit the manufacturing sector hardest (followed by education and banking) with the highest attack attempts observed in the U.S., France, and Brazil—driven in part by a high-profile 2021 breach of a Taiwanese hardware manufacturer. Initial access is achieved via malspam delivering multi-stage payloads that leverage IcedID and TrickBot for footholds, deploy Cobalt Strike beacons and PyXie RAT for code execution and data exfiltration, use SMB to propagate a VATET loader for lateral movement, and employ Mimikatz and LaZagne for credential harvesting. Upon execution, RansomEXX evades defense by disabling tools (T1562.001), skipping encryption of critical Windows paths, file names, and extensions, and terminating hundreds of business and security processes to maximize impact (T1486, T1490), then encrypts data and demands ransom. Recommended mitigations include strict audit and asset inventory, hardened configurations and least-privilege access, macro and email sandboxing to block malspam entry, regular patching and virtual patching, multifactor authentication, advanced behavior-based detection (e.g., Trend Micro Vision One™), and continuous employee training and red-team testing to disrupt the ransomware kill chain and protect against future RansomEXX intrusions.

title: Ransomware Spotlight: Ransomhub | Trend Micro (US)
preprocessed: RansomHub, first reported in February 2024 and linked to the Knight ransomware family, gains initial access through spear-phishing voice scams with convincing American-accent callers and compromised VPN credentials, then leverages PsExec, PowerShell and Python scripts to harvest credentials (Mimikatz, LaZagne, SecretServerSecretStealer), discover remote systems, establish SSH sessions and exploit CVE-2023-27532 in Veeam Backup & Replication to dump database credentials. Operators maintain persistence by creating local administrative accounts and registry run keys, evade defenses with disableAV.bat (BAT.KAPROCHANDLER.A), the STONESTOP binary using the signed POORTRY driver, batch scripts that disable Windows Defender and purge AV registry entries, TDSSKiller, EDR Kill Shifter via BYOVD and IOBit Unlocker, then transfer encryptors via SFTP or an Impacket-based SMB spreader. They also automate vCenter interactions to enable and exploit ESXi SSH, reset host passwords and move laterally, while command and control is managed through Atera, Splashtop, AnyDesk, Ngrok, Screen Connect and Remmina, and data exfiltration is conducted using RClone. The ransomware employs ECDH and AES to encrypt files—appending a 32-byte master public key and requiring a 32-byte passphrase to decrypt its embedded configuration that specifies targeted file types, exclusions and service terminations. Since April 2024, Trend Micro observed at least 338 RansomHub victims across 58 countries—predominantly small educational enterprises in the U.S. and Malaysia—underscoring the need for hardened email defenses, credential monitoring, timely Veeam patching, isolated backups and robust EDR solutions.

title: Ryuk 2020: Distributing Ransomware via TrickBot and BazarLoader | Trend Micro (US)
preprocessed: Ryuk, first observed in August 2018 and now responsible for one-third of ransomware attacks in 2020, leverages initial access via TrickBot or Emotet infections and, since early 2020, BazarLoader (aka BazarBackdoor) droppers delivered through phishing emails with malicious attachments or links to free file-hosting sites; once inside, attackers use C&C servers to deploy backdoors and exploit vulnerabilities such as EternalBlue and Zerologon to move laterally and encrypt entire domains within hours, demanding average ransoms of US$1.3 million in Q1 2020. After a lull from May to September, Ryuk resurfaced with notable incidents—February’s US government contractor breach and late October attacks on three New York hospitals—underscoring the need to patch domain controllers, disable or firewall administrative shares, restrict PowerShell, enforce 3-2-1 backups and least-privilege file permissions, and enable behavior-based ransomware protection and agent self-protection on security platforms.

title: Ransomware Spotlight: TargetCompany | Trend Micro (US)
preprocessed: Since its emergence in 2021 and first detection on Trend Micro telemetry in March 2022, the TargetCompany ransomware group has launched 269 attempted attacks against 250 disclosed Trend customers—predominantly in Asia (notably India and Saudi Arabia)—while avoiding Kazakhstan, Russia, Qatar, and Ukraine, and focusing on manufacturing, retail, and telecommunications; their November 2022–May 2023 leak site lists 20 confirmed victims (mostly small businesses) across the Asia-Pacific, Europe, and Middle East in IT, manufacturing, apparel, and automotive sectors. Initial access vectors include exploitation of CVE-2019-1069 and CVE-2020-0618 RCE flaws, SQL Server xp_cmdshell abuse, and OneNote-based spam campaigns. Execution relies on WMIC-invoked PowerShell scripts to retrieve various payloads (TargetComp ransomware, Remcos backdoor, Negasteal, Snake Keylogger) and, since January 2022, reflective loading of a .NET downloader that decrypts and runs payloads in memory via XOR or inversion. For defense evasion, operators deploy GMER, PCHunter64 (YDArk.exe), Advance Process Termination, KILLAV, and killer.bat to disable AV and security services; discovery is achieved through network scans and Mimikatz credential dumping; lateral movement via RDP-based RCE; C2 evolved from an open Mallox directory to an Nginx-protected server. Impact involves ChaCha20 file encryption with keys generated by Curve25519 and AES-128, file extensions such as .mallox/.exploit/.avast and ransom notes titled “HOW TO RECOVER!!.TXT,” and potential data exfiltration. Their tactics span MITRE techniques T1190, T1059.001, T1047, T1562.001, T1003.001, T1071.001, T1486, and more. The group’s maturation—evidenced by reflective loading and possible RaaS adoption—underscores the urgency for organizations to enforce asset inventories, least-privilege access, prompt patching (or virtual patching), multifactor authentication, sandboxed email defenses, AI/ML-driven detection, regular backups, and continuous red-team testing to thwart this active threat.

title: Ransomware Spotlight: Trigona | Trend Micro (US)
preprocessed: Trend Micro first detected Trigona ransomware in July 2023—attacks peaked in August and ceased after its October leak-site shutdown—targeting Turkey (23.5%), the Philippines (19.6%), Brazil (13.7%), Germany and Thailand, with government entities accounting for 21.4% of SPN detections and technology, retail, FMCG and banking also hit; leak-site data revealed 33 victims (45.5% North America—50% US, 27.3% Europe—9.1% UK, 6.1% AU), over half SMBs and 18.2% finance firms. Operators exploited CVE-2021-40539 and brokered credentials for initial access, evaded defenses by dropping turnoff.bat and defoff.bat to kill AV, performed discovery with network/port scanners, harvested credentials via Mimikatz, moved laterally using Splashtop, LogMeIn, ScreenConnect, AnyDesk, TeamViewer and Cobalt Strike–dropped MHYPROTINST, and escalated privileges on MSSQL via CLR shell to deploy nt.exe. The payload encrypts files with AES and TDCP_rijndael—defaulting to the first 0x80000 bytes with ._locked appended unless /full is used—and supports numerous CLI flags (e.g., /r,/erase,/shdwn) on Windows and Linux. Effective defenses include vulnerability management, least-privilege administration, MFA, allowlisting, secure backups and AI-driven detection across email, endpoint, web and network using solutions like Trend Micro Vision One, Deep Discovery Email Inspector, Cloud One Workload Security and Apex One.

title: Ransomware Spotlight: Water Ouroboros | Trend Micro (US)
preprocessed: Water Ouroboros is a Ransomware-as-a-Service operation that exploits public-facing Oracle WebLogic vulnerabilities (CVE-2019-2725, CVE-2017-10271, CVE-2019-2729) or drive-by installers for initial access (T1190, T1189), then executes remote Windows commands (wmic.exe, bcdedit.exe, wbadmin.exe, vssadmin.exe) to delete backups and disable recovery (T1490, T1562.001) before encrypting fixed, removable and network drives via a Go-based custom routine that uses RTLGenRandom to generate a symmetric key, protects it with embedded RSA public keys (App_ExportKey), appends “.locked” (unless suppressed with –E), excludes over 60 file extensions, and accepts credentials (c {user}:{pass}), logging (–a), non-aggressive (–A) and size filters (–m). Victims find Contact Us.txt ransom notes pointing to a TOR payment site and Hive Leaks data-dump threat. Post-infection, actors maintain access via compromised admin accounts (T1078), disable security tools (PCHunter, ProcessHacker), dump credentials from registry hives (T1003.002), move laterally over RDP/SMB (T1021.001/002), discover assets via AdFind (T1595.002) and exfiltrate data over C&C (SharpRhino RAT/T1071.001, T1041). With 136 incidents in the US and notable impacts on construction, IT, manufacturing and healthcare SMBs, the campaign underscores the need for timely patching, hardened public-facing apps, least-privilege access, MFA, robust backups and advanced threat detection.

title: BladedFeline: Whispering in the dark
preprocessed: In 2024, ESET researchers uncovered a sustained cyberespionage campaign by the Iran-aligned APT group BladedFeline—active since at least 2017 against Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) and Iraqi government officials—that leverages an evolving toolset including the Shahmaran 64-bit backdoor, two reverse tunnels (Laret and Pinar), Whisper (an Exchange-based backdoor communicating via email attachments), a malicious IIS module dubbed PrimeCache bearing code similarities to OilRig’s RDAT backdoor, and supplementary implants such as the Flog webshell and Hawking Listener. Forensic analysis revealed early indicators on KRG systems—VideoSRV reverse shell (Sept 2017) and RDAT (Jan 2018)—consistent with OilRig’s operational patterns, leading to a medium-confidence assessment that BladedFeline operates as a subgroup of OilRig alongside Lyceum. The timeline spans initial KRG compromises in 2017–2018, Shahmaran deployment against diplomatic officials in early 2023, expansion to a telecommunications provider in Uzbekistan in March 2023, and the 2024 discovery of Whisper, Laret, Pinar, and PrimeCache across KRG, GOI, and Uzbek networks. BladedFeline’s tactics—native IIS module implantation, email-based C&C, reverse tunnels, and webshell exploitation—underscore the need to monitor Exchange mailbox activity for anomalous attachments, IIS module registrations (e.g., HttpModule.pdb), port listeners, and VirusTotal submitter IDs to detect and disrupt this persistent threat targeting strategic communications, oil-related infrastructure, and diplomatic data in the Middle East.

title: Shifting the sands of RansomHub’s EDRKillShifter
preprocessed: ESET’s 2024 analysis shows that in the wake of law-enforcement-led Operation Cronos and the collapse of LockBit and BlackCat, RansomHub emerged in February as the dominant RaaS operator—driving a 15 percent rise in leak-site victims even as overall ransomware payments fell 35 percent—and by November had eclipsed LockBit in cumulative victim postings. By tracing unique victim IDs and builder tool fingerprints, researchers linked RansomHub to established gangs Play, Medusa and BianLian and revealed that its multiplatform encryptor (Windows, Linux, ESXi) repurposes Knight source code and is protected by a unique 64-character password per sample. In May, operators added “EDRKillShifter,” a custom EDR killer that abuses at least two publicly known vulnerable drivers and uses password-encrypted shellcode to disable security products, all delivered via RansomHub’s web panel under the same affiliate-specific password model. Affiliates—who keep 90 percent of ransoms and enroll via recommendation, reputation proof or a refundable US $5 000 deposit—negotiate exclusively over Tor, post detailed ransom notes to victims, and benefit from free trial decryptions. Key mitigations include strict driver allow-listing, monitoring for anomalous driver loads, hardening EDR self-protection, blocking known Tor endpoints, and correlating builder requests and password probes to detect emerging RansomHub activity.

title: Operation RoundPress targeting high-value webmail servers
preprocessed: In Operation RoundPress, the Sednit group (aka APT28/Fancy Bear) has since 2023 employed spear-phishing emails embedding XSS exploits against high-value webmail portals—initially abusing CVE-2020-35730 in Roundcube and, from 2024, expanding to zero-day CVE-2024-11182 in MDaemon plus known flaws CVE-2023-43770 in Roundcube, CVE-2024-27443 in Zimbra, and an old XSS in Horde—to inject obfuscated SpyPress JavaScript that exfiltrates credentials, contacts and email content via HTTP POST, sets persistent Sieve-based forwarding rules and even bypasses two-factor authentication; predominantly targeting governmental and defense entities in Eastern Europe (notably Ukraine, Bulgaria and Romania) with additional victims in Africa, Europe and South America; these campaigns, attributed to Sednit with medium confidence through reusable domains and email addresses, underline the critical need to patch webmail software promptly, enforce robust email filtering, monitor C&C traffic and audit server-side mail rules.

title: Arid Viper poisons Android apps with AridSpy
preprocessed: ESET Research has uncovered five overlapping campaigns, active since 2022 and three still live, in which the Arid Viper APT (aka APT-C-23, Desert Falcons, Two-tailed Scorpion) has been distributing a three-stage Android spyware suite dubbed AridSpy via dedicated phishing sites (lapizachat[.]com, nortirchats[.]com, reblychat[.]com, plus inactive pariberychat[.]com and renatchat[.]com) impersonating messaging apps (LapizaChat, NortirChat, ReblyChat), a job-opportunities app and a Palestinian Civil Registry app; these trojanized versions of legitimate apps (StealthChat, Session, Voxer) require manual install from unknown sources and leverage a custom myScript.js downloader to fetch successive payloads from C2 servers, enabling dynamic code loading and evasion. The first-stage loader—documented by Zimperium in 2021—evolved in 2022 during a Qatar World Cup campaign (Kora442) into multistage AridSpy, with ESET detecting six infections in Palestine and Egypt beginning August 2023. Medium-confidence attribution to Arid Viper is based on targeting in its historic Middle East focus, reuse and obfuscation of the myScript.js indicator (first tied to the group by 360 Beacon Labs and FOFA), and telemetry pivoting. AridSpy’s capabilities center on remote data espionage—collecting contacts, messages, device metadata and location—and its modular architecture and third-party distribution model pose ongoing risks to Android users in high-value geopolitical regions.

title: BadBazaar espionage tool targets Android users via trojanized Signal and Telegram apps
preprocessed: ESET researchers uncovered two concurrent Android campaigns deploying trojanized Signal (Signal Plus Messenger) and Telegram (FlyGram) apps via Google Play, Samsung Galaxy Store and dedicated domains (signalplus[.]org, flygram[.]org), active since July 2020 (FlyGram) and July 2022 (Signal Plus), delivering the China-aligned GREF group’s BadBazaar espionage malware. Both apps are recompiled open-source clients embedding payloads that exfiltrate IMEI, phone number, MAC address, operator details, location, Wi-Fi information, Google account emails, call logs and contact lists, with FlyGram harvesting metadata and offering an optional Telegram backup feature—activated by at least 13,953 users—to siphon full backups (sans message content), while Signal Plus Messenger uniquely abuses Signal’s “link device” mechanism (C&C at signalplus[.]org:4332) to steal the Signal PIN and silently pair the victim’s device to the attacker’s Signal instance, enabling full conversation interception. ESET’s telemetry identified installations in over 20 countries, with FlyGram garnering over 5,000 installs and Signal Plus over 100 before Google removed them on May 23, 2023 (FlyGram was taken down after January 6, 2021), yet both remain on Samsung Galaxy Store. Attribution to the GREF cluster rests on shared code-signing certificates, unique class names, Chinese-localization checks and prior targeting of Uyghur and Turkic minorities, highlighting the necessity for rigorous store vetting, user verification of linked devices and real-time app integrity monitoring to thwart similar espionage threats.

title: Sponsor with batch-filed whiskers: Ballistic Bobcat’s scan and strike backdoor
preprocessed: ESET researchers uncovered the Iran-aligned APT35 (aka Ballistic Bobcat, Charming Kitten, TA453/PHOSPHORUS) deploying a novel Sponsor backdoor across at least 34 opportunistic victims—primarily Israeli organizations in sectors from automotive to telecommunications, plus medical targets in Brazil and the UAE—by scanning for and exploiting Exchange CVE-2021-26855 vulnerabilities since September 2021, wrapping up their CISA AA21-321A/PowerLess campaign before dropping Sponsor via innocuously named batch files that deploy configuration files (config.txt, node.txt) to disk, install a persistent Windows service (“SystemNetwork”/“Update”) when run with an “install” argument, then periodically RC4-decrypt and call back to embedded C2 relays, all while leveraging open-source tooling (Mimikatz, Chisel, GO Simple Tunnel, Plink, RevSocks and Merlin) for lateral movement and data exfiltration; ESET has catalogued five Sponsor versions through June 2022, underscoring Ballistic Bobcat’s modular, short-duration, narrowly targeted “Sponsoring Access” campaign and highlighting the need for Exchange patching, service and file monitoring for batch deployments, and detection of RC4-encrypted config lookups to disrupt ongoing espionage operations.

title: Evasive Panda leverages Monlam Festival to target Tibetans
preprocessed: Since at least September 2023, the China-aligned Evasive Panda APT (aka BRONZE HIGHLAND/Daggerfly) has conducted a dual-pronged cyberespionage campaign against the Tibetan diaspora by compromising both the Kagyu International Monlam Trust’s website and the official Monlam translation-software supply chain—first implanting obfuscated JavaScript into jquery.js on the festival site that verifies victims’ first three IP octets via an MD5 hash salted with “1qaz0okm!@#,” serves a faux “Aw, Snap!” error page to users in India, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Australia and the U.S., and lures them to download a malicious “certificate.exe” or “.pkg” downloader; that loader side-loads memmgrset.dll (http_dy.dll) to fetch a JSON config from update.devicebug[.]com and ultimately deploys the undocumented Nightdoor backdoor alongside the group’s modular MgBot implant, while a trojanized Monlam software installer (Windows autorun.exe abusing MonlamUpdate.exe for DLL side-loading of RPHost.dll, and macOS Mach-O downloaders) has delivered further downloaders and payloads—retrieved from tibetpost[.]net and a direct IP—to %TEMP%\default_ico.exe for additional Nightdoor and MgBot installation.

title: eXotic Visit campaign: Tracing the footprints of Virtual Invaders
preprocessed: In a targeted Android espionage campaign dubbed eXotic Visit (November 2021–December 2023), ESET researchers discovered threat actors tracked as Virtual Invaders distributing seemingly legitimate messaging apps via dedicated websites and low-install Google Play listings (0–45 installs per app, ~380 victims in Pakistan and India) that secretly bundle the open-source XploitSPY RAT enhanced with a custom native chat module, shared C&C infrastructure and admin panels, and iterative improvements including code obfuscation, emulator detection with fake C&C redirection, Firebase-delivered C&C addresses, and a secondary channel for exfiltrating files over 2 MB. These trojanized apps—WeTalk/ChitChat (Dec 2021), Dink Messenger (benign v1.0–1.2 then RAT-enabled v1.3 in June 2022), Telco DB (Aug 2022), Sim Info (Aug 2022), Alpha Chat (Nov 2022) and Defcom (June 2023)—harvest contacts, SMS, call logs, installed apps, Wi-Fi networks, GPS, camera/audio recordings, and intercept new-message notifications, while selectively listing and extracting user-specified files on command. ESET’s partnership with Google led to the removal of identified apps and ten additional XploitSPY-based samples, highlighting the need for rigorous app vetting, behavior-based detection of native libraries and dynamic C&C retrieval, and network defenses to block known C&C domains.

title: Android GravityRAT goes after WhatsApp backups
preprocessed: In August 2022, ESET researchers uncovered an updated Android GravityRAT variant deployed by the SpaceCobra threat group via trojanized versions of the open-source OMEMO Instant Messenger app—branded BingeChat (active) and Chatico (now inactive)—hosted on invitation-only sites to target specific victims. Upon launch, the malicious app requests typical messaging permissions, registers with hard-coded C2 subdomains (dev.androidadbserver[.]com, cld.androidadbserver[.]com, ping.androidadbserver[.]com), and exfiltrates call logs, contact lists, SMS, device info, location data and files matching extensions such as jpg, pdf, xml and, critically, WhatsApp encrypted backups (crypt12/crypt14/crypt18/crypt32), then deletes staged data to evade detection. Unlike prior versions, it also accepts three remote commands—DeleteAllFiles, DeleteAllContacts and DeleteAllCallLogs—enabling precise data destruction. ESET telemetry shows at least one India-based infection, confirming a narrowly targeted campaign that leverages legitimate chat functionality to surreptitiously harvest and purge sensitive information.

title: MoustachedBouncer: Espionage against foreign diplomats in Belarus
preprocessed: ESET researchers disclosed MoustachedBouncer, a Belarus-aligned cyberespionage group active since at least 2014 targeting foreign embassies in Belarus, employing two parallel malware frameworks: the email-based NightClub (SMTP/IMAP C2) and its 2020-onward successor Disco (Go/.NET) delivered via adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) at ISP level—likely leveraging Belarus’s SORM lawful interception—to redirect Windows captive portal checks to a fake Windows Update page. This page loads jdrop.js to prompt a malicious installer, which schedules SMB-delivered OfficeBroker payloads from attacker-injected Google Cloud IPs. Both frameworks support plugins for screenshots, audio recording and file theft. ESET observed compromises of embassies from four continents and assesses medium confidence in state alignment and low confidence in cooperation with Winter Vivern. Recommendations include out-of-band encrypted VPNs to thwart ISP-level interception.

title: NGate Android malware relays NFC traffic to steal cash
preprocessed: ESET researchers uncovered a novel crimeware campaign, active in Czechia since November 2023 and paused only by the arrest of a suspect in March 2024, in which attackers combined social engineering, phishing and Android malware to target clients of three Czech banks via deceptive SMS links to malicious progressive web apps (PWAs) and WebAPKs; after harvesting credentials, the attackers lured victims into installing NGate, a custom Android malware named for its incorporation of the open-source NFCGate tool, which relays NFC data from victims’ unrooted smartphones to an attacker’s rooted device, enabling the emulation of cloned payment cards and unauthorized ATM withdrawals (over 160,000 CZK recovered from just three recent victims, with likely higher overall losses), with a fallback tactic of illicit bank-to-bank transfers when the relay method fails.

title: OilRig’s Outer Space and Juicy Mix: Same ol’ rig, new drill pipes
preprocessed: ESET’s updated analysis consolidates OilRig APT (aka APT34) under a parent-subgroup structure and attributes two exclusive Israeli-targeted campaigns—Outer Space (2021) and Juicy Mix (2022)—to its Lyceum subgroup, revealing a repeatable playbook in which spear-phishing VBS droppers employing arithmetic and base64 obfuscation deliver C#/.NET first-stage backdoors (Solar then its enhanced successor Mango) as scheduled Earth/Venus-style tasks that communicate via compromised Israeli websites using HTTP(S) URIs with “rt=d”/“rt=u” flags, XOR-based JupiterX encryption and Base64, and leverage the SC5k downloader (via Microsoft Exchange Web Services API) to fetch additional payloads. Post-compromise, Lyceum deployed MKG Chrome/Edge credential dumpers, Windows Credential Manager stealers and OilRig’s DanBot, Shark, Milan and Marlin backdoors to exfiltrate browser data and credentials. Code overlaps with Out to Sea, DNSpionage and HardPass campaigns—namely the MKG dumper, upload/download URI conventions, obfuscation techniques and downloader structures—solidify attribution to the Iran-linked group. Defenders should hunt for VBS scripts with obfuscation patterns, anomalous scheduled task creation (30/40-second or 14-minute intervals), EWS-based C&C traffic to non-public domains, Solar.exe/Mango.exe binaries and SC5k indicators to disrupt these data exfiltration pipelines.

title: Rescoms rides waves of AceCryptor spam
preprocessed: In the second half of 2023, ESET telemetry recorded a dramatic uptick in AceCryptor CaaS operations — detections tripled from ~13,000 to over 42,000 endpoints and unique AceCryptor-packed Rescoms RAT incidents soared from under 100 to more than 32,000 — marking Rescoms’ debut as a primary payload. Unlike H1’s focus on Peru, Mexico and Egypt, H2 campaigns heavily targeted European companies, with Poland alone accounting for 26K+ attacks, followed by Ukraine, Spain, Serbia, Bulgaria and Slovakia. Adversaries employed typosquatted domains and abused previously compromised corporate mailboxes to send multi-language, B2B-styled emails containing ISO or 7z archives named “offer/inquiry,” which unpacked AceCryptor to deploy Rescoms for browser and email credential harvesting. Repeated use of identical binaries reduced unique sample counts (23K→17K) despite higher encounter rates, and embedded Rescoms license IDs linked the waves to a single actor. While the overall use of Danabot and RedLine Stealer with AceCryptor decreased by over 60%, other families like SmokeLoader, STOP ransomware and Vidar remained active. The operations aimed at initial access for further ransomware or data exfiltration, underscoring the critical need for strict email hygiene and advanced endpoint security.

title: You never walk alone: The SideWalk backdoor gets a Linux variant
preprocessed: ESET researchers have identified a Linux variant of the SparklingGoblin APT’s SideWalk backdoor—formerly tracked as StageClient and matching the Specter RAT—deployed in February 2021 against a Hong Kong university previously breached in May 2020, where it compromised print, email and student-schedule servers. SideWalk Linux features a C++-based modular architecture with ChaCha20 encryption (counter 0x0B), MD5 integrity checks, LZ4 compression and a five-thread execution model loading precompiled modules like TaskSchedulerMod and SysInfoMgr. It communicates over HTTP/HTTPS using gtsid/gtuvid parameters, resolves C&C via Google Docs and Cloudflare workers, and aligns with SparklingGoblin’s TTPs (Motnug and ChaCha20 loaders, CROSSWALK, Korplug/PlugX, Cobalt Strike). Shared ChaCha20 keys, identical network protocols and reuse of C&C address 66.42.103[.]222 provide high-confidence attribution, highlighting academic networks’ susceptibility to multi-stage, custom implant campaigns.

title: SwiftSlicer: New destructive wiper malware strikes Ukraine
preprocessed: ESET researchers have identified SwiftSlicer, a new Go-written destructive wiper attributed to the Sandworm APT, on a Ukrainian organization’s network on January 25 via malicious Group Policy, indicating full Active Directory compromise; detected as WinGo/KillFiles, SwiftSlicer deletes shadow copies and recursively overwrites files in %CSIDL_SYSTEM%\drivers, %CSIDL_SYSTEM_DRIVE%\Windows\NTDS and other drives with 4,096-byte random blocks before forcing a reboot. This deployment method mirrors earlier HermeticWiper and CaddyWiper attacks—CaddyWiper was used against Ukrinform—and follows a wave of RansomBoggs ransomware linked to Sandworm two months prior. Sandworm’s near-decade track record of disruptive campaigns against Ukrainian critical infrastructure includes BlackEnergy, GreyEnergy, the original Industroyer, and a thwarted Industroyer2 in April, underscoring the imperative to harden Active Directory, monitor Group Policy changes, and maintain secure, offline backups.

title: Operation Texonto: Information operation targeting Ukrainian speakers in the context of the war
preprocessed: In October 2023, a spearphishing campaign against a major Ukrainian defense company and an EU agency leveraged a spoofed Gmail sender (it.[redacted]@gmail.com) and look-alike OAuth URLs on login.microsoftidonline[.]com and choicelive149200[.]com to harvest Office 365 credentials, and forensic pivots revealed the same network infrastructure powering Operation Texonto’s two PSYOP waves in November and December 2023, which eschewed common channels like Telegram in favor of six attacker-owned domains (e.g., ua-minagro[.]com, minuaregionbecareful[.]com, uamtu[.]com) to disseminate PDF attachments misusing Ukrainian ministry logos to spread Russian propaganda themes of heating failures, energy blackouts, food scarcity and drug shortages; further pivots uncovered Navalny-themed domains targeting Russian dissidents and the reuse of the PSYOP mail server for Canadian pharmacy spam, a tactic long favored by Russia‐aligned threat actors, and although no direct code overlaps tie Texonto to known groups such as Callisto, the blend of credential phishing, disinformation, domain masquerading and infrastructure reuse supports a high-confidence attribution to a Russia-aligned operator conducting hybrid warfare against Ukrainian speakers and related targets.

title: WinorDLL64: A backdoor from the vast Lazarus arsenal?
preprocessed: ESET researchers have retrospectively identified WinorDLL64.dll—a backdoor payload for the Wslink loader (WinorLoaderDLL64.dll) first uncovered in 2021—that operates as an in-memory server using MemoryModule and is protected by Oreans Code Virtualizer; although the initial compromise vector remains unknown, sparse detections in Central Europe, North America and the Middle East and a South Korean VirusTotal submission triggered YARA alerts based on its unique filename. Communicating over the loader’s established AES-256-CBC encrypted TCP channel, WinorDLL64 implements at least 16 commands—including comprehensive system profiling, secure file exfiltration, overwrite and deletion, process and RDP session management, unrestricted PowerShell execution, directory compression for data theft, and connection latency measurement—facilitating reconnaissance, persistence and lateral movement. Low-confidence attribution to North Korea–aligned Lazarus (HIDDEN COBRA) derives from targeting of South Korean victims, shared VS2010 LTCG build signatures and code/behavior overlap with 2018 GhostSecret (FE887FCAB66D7D7F79F05E0266C0649F0114BA7C) and Bankshot implants; this underscores Lazarus’s organized, modular arsenal and highlights the need to detect anomalous in-memory loaders and encrypted session anomalies.

title: Analysis of two arbitrary code execution vulnerabilities affecting WPS Office
preprocessed: ESET researchers uncovered that South Korea–aligned APT-C-60 has been exploiting a zero-day arbitrary code execution flaw in WPS Office for Windows (CVE-2024-7262) via a malicious MHTML spreadsheet that embeds a hidden hyperlink using the ksoqing:// protocol handler to hijack promecefpluginhost.exe and load a remote DLL, dropping a custom SpyGlace/TaskControler.dll backdoor; root cause analysis of Kingsoft’s silent March 2024 patch for CVE-2024-7262 revealed remaining logic flaws, leading to discovery of a second exploit path (CVE-2024-7263) in the same plugin, both now fixed after a coordinated disclosure timeline spanning February to August 2024 with independent confirmation by DBAPPSecurity; leveraging MHTML’s img tag to download libraries to %localappdata%\Temp\wps\INetCache\ and abusing QLibrary::Load’s trailing-dot trick, attackers achieved one-click or even Explorer preview–triggered RCE against over 500 million users in East Asia, underscoring the urgency for organizations to apply Kingsoft’s August 2024 patches to mitigate further in-the-wild espionage.

title: FiveHands Ransomware Overview
preprocessed: On May 6, 2021, CISA disclosed that FiveHands ransomware actors exploited a zero-day VPN vulnerability for initial access, then used SoftPerfect Network Scanner for host discovery and PsExec to deploy ServeManager.exe (the NTRUEncrypt-based FiveHands payload) alongside SombRAT RAT, leveraging publicly available tools (RouterScan, grabff, rclone, s3browser) and PowerSploit modules for credential access, persistence, token manipulation, Kerberoasting, and exfiltration; once in place, FiveHands enumerated and deleted Volume Shadow Copies via WMI (T1490, T1047), encrypted recovery folders and user data (T1486), and dropped ransom notes across directories. The campaign caused direct financial losses (ransoms, legal fees, incident response, downtime, reputational harm) and exposed third-party partners. Mitigation hinges on patching/decommissioning unused VPN servers, enforcing MFA on remote and privileged accounts, maintaining up-to-date AV/OS, implementing robust backup and recovery routines, hunting for IoCs, and reinforcing employee training against phishing and malicious attachments.

title: An In-Depth Look at the Data Extortion Group, Karakurt
preprocessed: Karakurt, active since June 2021 and also known as Karakurt Team/Lair, has extorted over 40 small and midsize companies in North America and Europe by skipping encryption to steal data via brokered or stolen VPN credentials (often from unpatched devices without MFA), establishing persistence through service creation, AnyDesk or Cobalt Strike C2 beacons, and harvesting credentials with Mimikatz and PowerShell dumps of ntds.dit. They compress data with WinZip/7zip and exfiltrate via Rclone or SFTP to Mega.io, then threaten public leaks—backed by 11.6 BTC moved into Conti wallets and shared file-tree.txt artifacts—highlighting ties to Conti’s rebranding post–May 19, 2022 “shutdown.” The group’s pure data-extortion model renders backups ineffective, demanding that defenders deploy intrusion prevention systems, enforce VPN MFA, continuously monitor for unauthorized remote-management tools, and strengthen credential hygiene to foil initial access, lateral movement, and exfiltration.

title: An In-Depth Look at Lorenz Ransomware
preprocessed: Lorenz ransomware, emerging in 2021 and likely a rebranding of the .sZ40/ThunderCrypt family, has preyed on over 20 mostly small-to-mid-sized organizations in the US, China and Mexico—demanding $500K–$700K via a double-extortion scheme and posting stolen data on a Tor leak site—most notably compromising Germany’s defense contractor Hensoldt in January 2022 (exfiltrating 95% of files) before exploiting a Mitel MiVoice Connect VoIP RCE (CVE-2022-29499, CVSS 9.8) in September to gain a perimeter foothold; CrowdStrike observed operators deploying a reverse shell via “pdf_import.php,” renaming binaries to “memdump” for anti-forensics, then using Chisel over SSH-secured HTTP to tunnel into the environment. Arctic Wolf analysis indicates either an initial-access broker or in-house exploit capability, a month-long dwell before invoking cURL to download and execute the “wc2_deploy” script for SSL pipes (mkfifo/OpenSSL), followed by CrackMapExec dumping credentials via comsvcs and Out-Minidump LSASS memory, installation of FileZilla under compromised admin accounts, and encryption via BitLocker triggered by a “worm.txt” script on the domain controller—with all event logs wiped and encryption progress beaconed via HTTP POSTs. These TTPs underscore the critical need to monitor IoT devices in real time, maintain up-to-date inventories with device-role tagging, enforce robust patch management, and deploy zero-trust, SIEM, whitelisting and vulnerability-management controls; Avertium specifically advocates applying Mitel’s remediation script for CVE-2022-29499 to mitigate further exploitation.

title: New Iranian hacking group APT42 deploys custom Android spyware
preprocessed: Since at least 2015, Mandiant has identified APT42—an IRGC-linked Iranian state-sponsored threat actor also known as APT35—conducting over 30 spear-phishing operations across 14 countries against government officials, policymakers, journalists, academics and dissidents, evolving tactics from 2020 Oxford vaccinologist-themed pharmaceutical lures to 2021 fake interview requests using compromised U.S. media accounts for 37-day MFA-intercepting credential harvesting, and February 2022 phishes posing as a British news agency targeting political science professors; beyond credential theft via shortened URLs and PDF attachments directing victims to spoofed login portals, APT42 deploys custom Android spyware—spread via SMS links to messaging/VPN apps—to exfiltrate calls, SMS, audio recordings, images and GPS data in real time, while on Windows it employs lightweight custom malware for initial access, privilege escalation, reconnaissance, lateral movement through follow-on phishing, and persistence via scheduled tasks and registry keys; Mandiant further correlates APT42’s TTPs with November 2021 PHOSPHORUS BitLocker ransomware attempts against Fortinet FortiOS SSL VPN and unpatched Exchange servers, highlighting the group’s multi-platform espionage-to-ransom capabilities and real-world threat to high-value targets.

title: Hackers stole data undetected from US, European orgs since 2019
preprocessed: The Chinese state-backed APT41 group Winnti has since at least 2019 conducted Operation CuckooBees against technology and manufacturing firms across East Asia, Western Europe and North America, stealthily exfiltrating hundreds of gigabytes of intellectual property—including patents, blueprints and proprietary manufacturing data—via an infection chain that begins with exploiting known and zero-day ERP vulnerabilities and establishes persistence through an encoded WebShell, WinRM abuse, DLL side-loading (via IKEEXT and PrintNotify services) or a signed kernel rootkit. After recon with native commands run as scheduled tasks (‘systeminfo’, ‘net start’, ‘dir C:\’), Winnti performs credential dumping with ‘reg save’ and the MFSDLL.exe tool, moves laterally via scheduled task-launched batch files, and exfiltrates archives using a digitally-signed WinRAR wrapped in rundll32.exe. Cybereason’s discovery of the novel DEPLOYLOG 64-bit DLL, which hides payloads in Windows CLFS logs and deploys the reflective-loading WINNKIT rootkit (leveraging an expired BenQ signature to bypass DSE) with dual C2 channels, underscores the campaign’s sophistication and antivirus evasion. Given the group’s enduring activity despite DOJ indictments, defenders should ensure all software is patched, monitor network traffic for anomalous scheduled tasks and CLFS usage, and implement strict network segmentation to mitigate similar espionage operations.

title: Lyceum/Hexane Threat Group Uses Common Hacking Tactics
preprocessed: In August 2019 Dragos and SecureWorks detailed a protracted (since April 2018) campaign by the Lyceum/Hexane threat group targeting Middle East critical infrastructure with straightforward but effective tactics: initial password‐spraying and brute‐force attacks on corporate email accounts, followed by spear-phishing from compromised internal accounts to executives, HR and IT staff using malicious Excel macros that deploy the DanBot RAT; once inside, operators run PoshC2-sourced PowerShell scripts—Decrypt-RDCMan.ps1 to extract RDCMan-stored passwords and Get-LAPSP.ps1 to harvest Active Directory credentials via LDAP—enabling environment reconnaissance and lateral movement. Despite its reliance on common techniques rather than novel malware or zero-days, Lyceum’s persistence highlights the urgency of enforcing multi-factor authentication, disabling macros, monitoring for unauthorized PowerShell/PoshC2 activity and training high-value users to detect spear-phishing, thereby mitigating the group’s primary objective of information collection before any potential pivot into OT/ICS environments.

title: New 'Karakurt' hacking group focuses on data theft and extortion
preprocessed: Researchers at Accenture Security exposed Q3 2021 proliferation of Karakurt, a financially motivated data‐extortion group first identified in June 2021 upon registering two domains and launching a Twitter handle, which compromised over 40 primarily North American (95 percent) organizations across random sectors between September and November by sourcing or phishing VPN credentials for initial access, establishing persistence with Cobalt Strike beacons or AnyDesk, then harvesting administrator privileges via Mimikatz to evade EDR solutions; they compress stolen data with 7zip or WinZip and exfiltrate it to Mega.io using Rclone or FileZilla, foregoing ransomware encryption in favor of public leak threats, a low-overhead approach that can still cripple victims—underscoring the need for robust VPN credential management, continuous monitoring for living-off-the-land tools, and preventative controls to detect and disrupt such intrusions before data exfiltration.

title: Moses Staff hackers wreak havoc on Israeli orgs with ransomless encryptions
preprocessed: Since September 2021 the politically motivated Moses Staff group has launched ransomless encryptions against Israeli organizations, exploiting unpatched public-facing infrastructure—most notably vulnerable Microsoft Exchange servers—and leveraging off-the-shelf exploits to breach networks, then moving laterally via PsExec, WMIC, and PowerShell without deploying custom backdoors. Upon infiltration, the group deploys PyDCrypt, a custom variant built atop the open-source DiskCryptor tool, which generates unique symmetric keys per hostname using an MD5 hash and salt; however, Check Point researchers note that failed self-deletion of PyDCrypt payloads allows key recovery and decryption under certain conditions. Rather than seeking financial gain, Moses Staff focuses on maximum operational disruption by exfiltrating corporate secrets and posting stolen data across a Tor leak site, Twitter, and Telegram channels—tactics reminiscent of Pay2Key and BlackShadow—and may originate from Palestine based on VirusTotal submissions. The attacks have caused widespread system downtime and data exposure, prompting Check Point to advise immediate patching of known vulnerabilities on public-facing servers, enhanced monitoring for lateral-movement utilities, and rapid retrieval of PyDCrypt samples to facilitate decryption.

title: US and UK expose new malware used by MuddyWater hackers
preprocessed: US and UK agencies (CISA, FBI, CNMF, NCSC-UK and NSA) issued a joint advisory detailing how the Iranian-backed MuddyWater group—active since at least 2017 and linked to Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security in January 2022—has expanded its arsenal beyond PowGoop, Canopy/Starwhale, Mori and POWERSTATS to include a new Python backdoor dubbed “Small Sieve” and a PowerShell backdoor that encrypts C2 channels; these tools target telecom, defense, local government and oil and gas organizations across Asia, Africa, Europe and North America, maintain persistence via custom string and traffic obfuscation (hex byte-swapping plus an obfuscated Base64 routine) over the Telegram Bot API via HTTPS, and facilitate lateral movement and data exfiltration, underscoring the need for defenders to monitor anomalous Telegram API calls, obfuscated Base64 traffic and encrypted PowerShell sessions.

title: Global Salt Typhoon hacking campaigns linked to Chinese tech firms
preprocessed: Since at least 2021, the Chinese state-linked APT group Salt Typhoon—supported by Sichuan Juxinhe Network Technology Co. Ltd., Beijing Huanyu Tianqiong Information Technology Co., and Sichuan Zhixin Ruijie Network Technology Co. Ltd., which supply cyber products and services to China’s Ministry of State Security and PLA—has conducted global cyber-espionage against government, telecommunications, transportation, lodging and military networks, notably breaching U.S. carriers (AT&T, Verizon, Lumen) to exfiltrate text messages, voicemails and law-enforcement wiretaps, infiltrating U.S. and Canadian telcos via unpatched Cisco IOS XE vulnerabilities to establish GRE tunnels and steal configurations, and executing a nine-month 2024 compromise of a U.S. Army National Guard network to harvest admin credentials and config files. Their primary tactic exploits widely known, fixed edge-device flaws—CVE-2024-21887 (Ivanti Connect Secure command injection), CVE-2024-3400 (Palo Alto PAN-OS GlobalProtect RCE), CVE-2023-20273 & CVE-2023-20198 (Cisco IOS XE auth bypass/privilege escalation) and CVE-2018-0171 (Cisco Smart Install RCE)—to gain router access, modify ACLs, enable SSH on nonstandard ports, deploy GRE/IPsec tunnels, abuse Cisco Guest Shell for persistence, capture TACACS+ traffic, and deploy custom Golang SFTP tools (“cmd1,” “cmd3,” “new2,” “sft”). A 13-nation advisory warns that compromised edge devices and trusted provider interconnects facilitate lateral movement into core targets. Recommended mitigations include urgent patching, device hardening, configuration monitoring, disabling unused services (Cisco Smart Install/Guest Shell), restricting management interfaces to secure networks, enforcing SSHv2/SNMPv3 and proactively hunting for known-vulnerability exploitation to thwart further espionage.

title: SnapMC hackers skip file encryption and just steal your files
preprocessed: Researchers at NCC Group have identified SnapMC as a new rapid-strike extortion group that eschews file encryption in favor of pure data theft, leveraging the Acunetix vulnerability scanner to pinpoint and exploit unpatched PrintNightmare LPE, Telerik UI for ASPX.NET RCE and SQL-injection flaws in VPN and web-server applications, then running SQL export scripts, compressing stolen CSVs with 7zip and exfiltrating them via the MinIO client—all within 30 minutes—before delivering standard extortion emails. By making data theft the primary leverage, SnapMC renders backup-based recovery moot and heightens the risk that victims who pay ransoms will face repeated extortion or public data sale, as seen with Sodinokibi, Netwalker, Mespinoza and Conti, and echoed by Coveware’s advice never to pay. Effective defenses include prompt patching of known CVEs, deploying well-configured web application firewalls around vulnerable services like Telerik and maintaining rigorous vulnerability management to thwart this growing threat.

title: FrostyGoop’s Zoom-In: A Closer Look into the Malware Artifacts, Behaviors and Network Communications
preprocessed: In July 2024, evolving from an early-year attack on a Ukrainian municipal energy provider disclosed by Ukraine’s CSSC, the Russian-linked OT malware FrostyGoop (aka BUSTLEBERM) exploited an obscure Go-based Modbus TCP library, goccy’s go-json encoder/decoder and an open-source ‘queues’ execution controller—delivered via compromised MikroTik routers or internet-exposed OT devices—to issue bespoke Modbus read/write commands that disrupted heating services to over 600 apartment buildings for two days in sub-zero conditions. FrostyGoop accepts JSON or command-line arguments to configure operation codes, addresses, counts, values and timing, includes a PEB BeingDebugged flag check for anti-analysis, and our telemetry reveals 1,088,175 Modbus TCP devices exposed from Sept. 2–Oct. 2, 2024 (6,211,623 total), including 32 ENCO control devices with Telnet-accessible TCP/23 in Romania and Ukraine. Concurrently, we identified a co-occurring Golang sample, go-encrypt.exe, using AES-CFB to encrypt/decrypt JSON files—likely for concealing FrostyGoop configs—that first appeared with task_test.json on Oct. 10, 2023. These insights highlight the need for ICS-centric detection—signatures for the unique Modbus library and JSON schema, monitoring for PEB debug checks and encrypted JSON usage—and rigorous network segmentation to mitigate the growing OT threat.

title: Jumpy Pisces Engages in Play Ransomware
preprocessed: Unit 42’s investigation reveals that North Korean state‐sponsored group Jumpy Pisces (aka Andariel/Onyx Sleet) gained initial access to a corporate network in May 2024 via a compromised user account, deployed a customized Sliver C2 beaconing to 172.96.137[.]224/americajobmail[.]site and their bespoke DTrack infostealer across hosts via SMB, and leveraged Impacket’s secretsdump.py, Mimikatz dumps (KB0722.log), a custom RDP account tool and a trojanized browser‐data stealer for credential harvesting, lateral movement and persistence; this activity continued until early September when the same account and toolset were abused—using TokenPlayer for Windows token abuse, PsExec for privilege escalation and EDR sensor removal—to facilitate Play ransomware (Fiddling Scorpius) deployment, marking the first observed collaboration (affiliate or initial access brokerage) between Jumpy Pisces and Play ransomware and signaling a shift from espionage to broader ransomware operations that could target victims globally, underscoring the imperative for defenders to treat Jumpy Pisces activity as a precursory ransomware threat and to deploy mitigations such as Cortex XDR, Advanced WildFire, Advanced URL Filtering and Advanced DNS Security.

title: Lynx Ransomware: A Rebranding of INC Ransomware
preprocessed: Following the sale of INC ransomware source code in March 2024 and its initial appearance in August 2023, researchers in July 2024 uncovered Lynx ransomware, a Windows-only, C++-based RaaS variant that shares ~48% of INC’s functions (70.8% among common routines) and has been deployed against U.S. and U.K. retail, real estate, architecture, financial and environmental service firms via phishing, malicious downloads and underground forums; employing AES-128-CTR and Curve25519 Donna for encryption with a .lynx extension, it conducts double-extortion by exfiltrating victims’ data (published on lynxblog[.]net under a policy excluding governments, hospitals and non-profits) before encrypting all files by default—killing processes, encrypting network shares and hidden disks, deleting shadow copies and backups, leveraging the Restart Manager API to target in-use files, and printing a OneNote report—then dropping a README.txt ransom note; this evolution of RaaS underscores the need for organizations to adopt robust cybersecurity measures, including anti-phishing training, backup hardening, dynamic and behavioral detections via Palo Alto Networks’ Cortex XDR Anti-Ransomware and Advanced WildFire, and vigilant monitoring of Indicators of Compromise such as published SHA256 hashes to mitigate high-profile, code-reused ransomware campaigns.

title: Magic Hound Campaign Attacks Saudi Targets
preprocessed: Since mid-2016, a persistent espionage campaign dubbed Magic Hound has targeted Saudi energy, government and technology organizations using spear-phishing emails linking to weaponized Word and Excel documents with malicious macros that invoke PowerShell to download shellcode-based payloads via open-source modules like Magic Unicorn and deliver Metasploit’s Meterpreter, Pupy RAT and custom IRC bots. Infrastructure pivoting around “gerry knight” metadata and chrome-up[.]date domains revealed over fifty samples—including MagicHound.Rollover (document loader), Fetch (executable loader that writes c:\temp\rr.exe and creates autorun registry keys using an AES-encrypted “agkrhfpdbvhdhrkj” key), DropIt (base64 blob dropper/binder), Retriever (downloader) and Leash (IRC backdoor)—hosted on diverse VPS providers and overlapping with Rocket Kitten’s MPK bot IP. The campaign’s evolving multi-stage toolset, domain spoofing (ntg-sa[.]com, mol.com-ho[.]me) and obfs3-obfuscated communications underscore its sophistication and persistent intelligence impact.

title: Threat Assessment: WastedLocker Ransomware
preprocessed: Unit 42 has observed a sharp rise in post-intrusion WastedLocker ransomware attacks by the Evil Corp group—already known for Dridex—against large U.S. organizations in sectors from manufacturing to legal services, with initial compromise typically via ZIP files masquerading as legitimate updates that deploy a SocGholish JavaScript loader to profile systems and invoke PowerShell-based Cobalt Strike payloads; attackers then leverage WMI and PsExec for lateral movement, identify high-value and backup systems, elevate privileges, disable Windows Defender, delete shadow copies, install WastedLocker as a service, and encrypt files using a “.<victim_name>wasted” extension while appending ransom notes (“.<victim_name>wasted_info”) with contact addresses on ProtonMail, Airmail and others. Palo Alto Networks’ WildFire, Cortex XDR (anti-ransomware and behavioral threat protection), NGFW DNS signatures and AutoFocus tagging detect and prevent WastedLocker activity; organizations are urged to implement robust, off-site backup strategies and hardened cybersecurity controls to mitigate this high-impact targeted ransomware threat.

title: Unveiling Void Manticore: Structured Collaboration Between Espionage and Destruction in MOIS - Check Point Blog
preprocessed: Check Point Research has revealed that Void Manticore, an Iranian MOIS–affiliated threat actor operating under personas “Homeland Justice” for its 2022 Albania campaign and “Karma” for 2023–2024 Israel attacks, conducts coordinated espionage and destructive wiping operations by collaborating with Scarred Manticore (Storm-0861), which exploits CVE-2019-0604 via Foxshell and Liontail to dwell for over a year and exfiltrate emails (using LionHead), before handing victims to Void Manticore (Storm-0842) to deploy custom Windows and Linux wipers—CI Wiper, CL Wiper, partition-table LowEraser and the BiBi Wiper—thereby corrupting files and obliterating partition tables; the repetition of tactics across regions underscores a systematic, state-sponsored influence and destruction playbook and highlights the need for defenders to patch legacy SharePoint flaws, monitor for public-tool usage, implement immutable backups and share threat intelligence.

title: Chinese APT group Winnti stole trade secrets in years-long undetected campaign
preprocessed: Security researchers at Cybereason uncovered that since at least 2019 a Chinese state-sponsored APT group known as Winnti (also tracked as APT41, Barium, Wicked Panda, Axiom) has been running “Operation CuckooBees,” a multi-year, multi-stage espionage campaign targeting technology and manufacturing firms across Asia, Europe and North America to steal hundreds of gigabytes of trade secrets. The attackers exploited both known and zero-day RCE flaws in a popular ERP platform to deploy JSP web shells, enabled WinRM for persistence, dumped registry-stored credentials to move laterally via scheduled tasks, and used a sophisticated loader chain—Spyder Loader (disguised as SQLite3 DLL), STASHLOG (which hides payloads in Windows’ proprietary CLFS logs), SPARKLOG (which extracts and side-loads PRIVATELOG via DLL hijacking for SYSTEM privileges), and DEPLOYLOG (which abuses Transactional NTFS to overwrite dbghelp.dll and hijack the AMD K8 kernel driver)—to install WINNKIT, a kernel-level rootkit signed with a stolen BenQ certificate that hooks TCP/IP at the NIC to receive commands for shell execution, file enumeration, SOCKS5 proxy, RDP and process control, all while evading detection for years.

title: ICS malware FrostyGoop disrupted heating in Ukraine, remains threat to OT worldwide
preprocessed: Dragos researchers, in collaboration with Ukraine’s CSSC, unearthed FrostyGoop—an ICS-specific malware first spotted in April and used in January to disrupt central heating in over 600 Lviv apartment buildings—marking the first known malware to leverage Modbus TCP for read/write operations on operational technology. Attackers gained initial access in April 2023 by exploiting a MikroTik router vulnerability, deployed a webshell on the router’s web server, and maintained persistence via Tor and L2TP tunnels to Moscow-based IPs. After spending months conducting reconnaissance, they extracted credentials by dumping the SAM registry hive in December, then directly issued scripted Modbus commands—read from a JSON configuration file—to publicly exposed ENCO heating controllers, even downgrading firmware to disable monitoring and force inaccurate measurements that halted heating services for nearly two days amid subzero temperatures. This incident underscores the threat posed by internet-exposed ICS devices—over 46,000 globally using Modbus—and highlights poor network segmentation, unpatched ICS CVEs, and the ease with which FrostyGoop’s protocol-agnostic payload can be repurposed against diverse industrial controllers, necessitating immediate network segmentation, firmware monitoring, and patch management in OT environments.

title: Iranian APT group uses previously undocumented Trojan for destructive access to organizations
preprocessed: Moses Staff, an Iran-linked APT active since September 2021, has conducted politically motivated sabotage campaigns—initially against Israeli organizations and later targets in India, Germany, the U.S., Italy, Chile, Turkey and the UAE—by exploiting known public-facing server vulnerabilities (e.g., Microsoft Exchange), moving laterally with PsExec, WMIC and PowerShell, and deploying a two-stage destructive toolkit: a Python-based loader (PyDCrypt) that installs a custom DiskCryptor variant (DCSrv) to encrypt files and disrupt operations without ransom demands, and, as newly documented by Cybereason, the StrifeWater RAT masquerading as calc.exe to establish early footholds, harvest system metadata (machine name, OS version, CPU architecture, user privileges, time zone), execute commands, capture screens, maintain persistence via scheduled tasks, and download auxiliary modules before self-removal—all while communicating with hard-coded C2 IPs, URLs and domain names—to evade detection; organizations should urgently patch exposed servers, monitor anomalous calc.exe and scheduled-task activity, and enhance EDR rules to detect PyDCrypt, DCSrv and StrifeWater behaviors to thwart data exfiltration and infrastructure damage.

title: WastedLocker explained: How this targeted ransomware extorts millions from victims
