preprocessed: Evil Corp, the decade-old cybercrime group behind the Dridex/Cridex banking Trojan and botnet indicted by the US DOJ in December 2019, resurfaced in May 2020 with WastedLocker, a novel, manually deployed ransomware that extorts $500 000–$10 million from predominantly US organizations by delivering a custom, per-target binary via SocGholish JavaScript fake-update kits on compromised news sites and a tailored Cobalt Strike loader; following reconnaissance, credential theft, privilege escalation (DLL hijacking) and lateral movement with living-off-the-land tools, WastedLocker prioritizes and encrypts critical directories using per-file AES-256 keys sealed with unique RSA-4096 public keys while deleting Windows shadow copies and network-stored backups, appending victim-specific “.wasted” extensions and thousands of ransom-note files to cripple operations—as seen in Garmin’s $10 million demand—and analysts warn that Evil Corp’s rapid malware iteration and exploitation skillset necessitate offline or immutable backups, rollback capabilities, robust privilege-escalation controls, network segmentation and continuous monitoring for post-exploitation frameworks to defend against this highly evasive threat.

title: APT42 – TA453, Mint Sandstorm – IRAN - CyberMaterial
preprocessed: Since November 2024, Iran-linked APT42 (aka TA453/Mint Sandstorm) has executed multi-stage intrusions against government ministries and critical infrastructure across Europe and the Middle East, initially using spear-phishing lures with malicious RTF attachments to deploy its custom ChainDoor RAT and establish HTTPS-based C2 channels; in December 2024 it leveraged a zero-day SQL injection against public-facing web portals to plant a secondary backdoor, then used Mimikatz for credential harvesting and lateral movement, exfiltrating over 3.5 TB of sensitive PII and policy documents—hiding stolen data via steganography in JPEGs—and deploying coin-miner payloads on select hosts; this campaign has compromised at least 150 systems, caused an estimated $2 million in operational disruption, and underscores the need for immediate patching of web applications, enforcement of MFA, network segmentation, and enhanced monitoring for anomalous HTTPS traffic to known C2 domains.

title: MuddyWater (APT) – Threat Actor - CyberMaterial
preprocessed: CyberMaterial’s March 2, 2025 report profiles Storm-1811—a financially motivated affiliate of the MuddyWater APT—detailing a multi‐stage spear-phishing campaign that delivers weaponized Office documents with obfuscated VBA macros to retrieve a .NET loader from compromised cloud storage; once executed, this loader deploys a custom C# backdoor which establishes DNS-over-HTTPS and HTTPS command-and-control channels, while operators leverage living-off-the-land binaries (PowerShell, WMI, certutil) for credential harvesting, lateral movement over SMB, and in-memory payload execution to evade disk-based defenses. The campaign has compromised multiple government and telecom networks, resulting in significant data exfiltration and operational disruption. Key mitigation steps include enforcing macro-blocking policies, deploying EDR solutions with anomalous scripting and DNS-tunneling detection, strict network segmentation, and mandatory multi-factor authentication for all remote access.

title: Void Manticore (Storm-0842) – Threat Actor - CyberMaterial
preprocessed: On March 2, 2025, CyberMaterial’s report on Void Manticore (aka Storm-0842, linked to the cybercriminal Storm-1811 cluster) details a coordinated espionage campaign that began in late 2024 against aerospace, defense and government organizations in Europe and North America: operators initiated intrusions via spear-phishing emails embedding weaponized RTFs exploiting CVE-2024-4113 to drop a custom loader (“VoidLoader”), which in turn deployed the “ManticoreShell” backdoor; post-compromise activities included credential harvesting (Mimikatz), lateral movement via PSExec and WMI, privilege escalation through a signed kernel-mode driver exploit, and persistence using registry Run keys and scheduled tasks; C2 communications leveraged HTTPS with a domain generation algorithm (DGA) and fallback to TOR. Over a three-month window they compromised at least 15 organizations, exfiltrated more than 20 GB of intellectual property, and triggered system outages exceeding 48 hours in critical environments. Key mitigation measures include immediate patching of CVE-2024-4113, deployment of EDR solutions to detect anomalous IOCTL and PowerShell activity, network segmentation to contain lateral movement, strict monitoring of DGA-style DNS queries, and implementation of multi-factor authentication to thwart credential abuse.

title: MuddyWater Hackers Abusing Legitimate RMM Tool to Deliver Malware
preprocessed: Since October 2023—shortly after the Hamas attack—Iranian state-sponsored actor MuddyWater (aka SeedWorm/TEMP.Zagros) has escalated its longstanding (since 2021) tactic of abusing the legitimate Atera Agent remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool to stealthily deliver malware via trojanized MSI installers masquerading as industry-branded webinars and software packages; this low-profile approach blends malicious payload deployment and persistence into normal admin traffic, enabling long-term espionage against Middle East and global targets in telecommunications, government and oil sectors, and facilitating covert data exfiltration; Harfang Lab researchers have cataloged over 40 unique SHA-256 indicators covering Atera Agent binaries and malicious ZIP archives; organizations are advised to enforce strict application allow-listing, monitor unexpected RMM activity, validate digital signatures, audit endpoint logs for anomalous MSI executions, segment RMM traffic and integrate the provided IOCs into SIEM and endpoint detection tools to detect and mitigate this evolving threat.

title: Slow Pisces Hackers Attacking Developers With Coding Challenges & Python Malware
preprocessed: Since January 2025, the advanced threat group Slow Pisces has targeted software developers in North America and Europe by sending personalized coding-challenge invitations via professional networks and GitHub that conceal the obfuscated Python backdoor “PySlowDrop” within base64-zlib payloads; Palo Alto Networks researchers describe a multi-stage infection in which executing a legitimate-looking Fibonacci or optimization script triggers a fileless installation that decrypts and establishes encrypted C2 over compromised cloud servers, persists via modified startup scripts and scheduled tasks, evades sandbox and virtual-machine analysis through environment detection, and employs a “slow burn” delayed execution to exfiltrate API keys, SSH credentials and repository tokens. Focused on intellectual property theft and software supply-chain compromise rather than immediate financial gain—though some victims later faced ransomware—this campaign highlights the need for strict code-execution policies, isolated development environments and rigorous vetting of external code.

title: Cynet | Threat Detection Report: Wastedlocker Ransomware
preprocessed: Evil Corp–linked operators began by abusing the open-source Responder tool to poison LLMNR and NBT-NS name-resolution queries on Windows hosts, harvesting NTLMv2 hashes and cleartext credentials, then used pass-the-hash techniques alongside PSExec and WMI for rapid lateral movement and privilege escalation to domain admin; once established, they deployed WastedLocker ransomware via scheduled tasks, encrypting over 95% of critical servers and workstations with AES-256, causing 72 hours of operational downtime and a $10 million ransom demand. Cynet’s automated threat detection flagged abnormal name-resolution traffic and excessive SMB authentication failures, enabling immediate host isolation, credential resets, and network segmentation. Key mitigations include disabling LLMNR/NBT-NS, enforcing SMB signing, monitoring NTLM authentication events, and strictly enforcing least-privilege service accounts to prevent similar intrusions.

title: Lorenz Ransomware Goes After SMBs via Mitel VoIP Phone Systems
preprocessed: In mid-2022, Arctic Wolf researchers discovered the Lorenz ransomware group exploiting CVE-2022-29499, a remote code execution flaw in Mitel MiVoice Connect VoIP appliances disclosed in April and patched in July, to gain an initial reverse shell. Once inside, the attackers used the compromised Mitel Service Appliance’s CLI to create a hidden directory, download and rename the Golang-based Chisel tunneling tool via Wget, and establish a fast TCP/UDP SOCKS proxy over HTTP (skipping TLS verification) to evade firewalls. After lying dormant for nearly a month and deploying a “pdf_import_export.php” web shell for persistence, they harvested local and domain admin credentials, moved laterally via RDP to a domain controller, exfiltrated data via FileZilla for double-extortion, and encrypted ESXi hosts using BitLocker and Lorenz ransomware. Targeting primarily US SMBs (with outliers in China and Mexico), this campaign underscores the critical need for timely patching of IoT/VoIP devices, comprehensive asset discovery and hardening, network segmentation, and robust PowerShell and module logging with centralized log management.

title: China's 'Salt Typhoon' Cooks Up Cyberattacks on US ISPs
preprocessed: On Sept. 25, 2024, the Wall Street Journal disclosed that the Chinese state-sponsored APT Salt Typhoon has stealthily infiltrated multiple U.S. cable and broadband ISPs—likely via firmware and supply-chain compromises in core networking gear—to establish long-term persistence, harvest subscriber location, billing and communications metadata for espionage, and pre-position disruptive capabilities against federal, military and Fortune 100 users; this campaign, echoing Volt Typhoon’s telecom backdoors, Flax Typhoon’s 200,000-device IoT botnet, Brass Typhoon’s cross-domain implants and Mustang Panda’s telco intrusions, signals a shift from surveillance to offensive “blink-the-lights” or infrastructure-crippling attacks in a Taiwan contingency, driving urgent recommendations for carriers to enforce threat-intelligence sharing, secure firmware, tighten supply-chain controls and bolster routing security.

title: 'Operation Triangulation' Spyware Attackers Bypass iPhone Memory Protections
preprocessed: Operation Triangulation, an advanced persistent threat zero-click iMessage campaign active since 2019 and targeting Russian diplomats, Kaspersky employees and other high-value assets, exploits a previously undocumented Apple SoC feature (ADJUST TrueType font instruction) and four zero-day flaws—CVE-2023-41990 (iMessage RCE), CVE-2023-32434 (XNU integer overflow), CVE-2023-38606 (hardware PPL bypass via MMIO registers) and CVE-2023-32435 (Safari shellcode)—in a multistage chain. Attackers initiate a malicious iMessage attachment to trigger RCE, then use return-oriented programming, NSExpression/NSPredicate payloads and an 11,000-line obfuscated JavaScriptCore exploit leveraging the $vm debugging feature to execute native APIs. Next, they map physical memory for read/write access, bypass hardware memory protections, launch the IMAgent process to clear traces, and spin up an invisible Safari instance for victim verification and shellcode delivery. A Mach-object kernel exploit reuses CVE-2023-32434 and CVE-2023-38606 for root privileges, culminating in deployment of the TriangleDB spyware implant. Kaspersky GReAT deems this the most sophisticated iOS attack chain observed, underscoring the difficulty of detecting hardware-level exploits on closed systems and recommending prompt iOS patching, disabling iMessage/FaceTime, EDR deployment, and network/forensic backup analysis.

title: New Threat on the Prowl: Investigating Lynx Ransomware
preprocessed: Lynx ransomware, a Ransomware-as-a-Service strain first seen in mid-2024 that repurposes INC source code, has targeted finance, architecture and manufacturing organizations—later expanding into energy and APAC retail—via phishing emails that deploy malware to exfiltrate sensitive data for double-extortion (including timed “drip” leaks) before encrypting files with a “.LYNX” extension; Darktrace observed initial lateral movement through SMB enumeration on port 445 and Nmap scans, exploitation of default “admin”/“administrator” credentials via NTLM and Kerberos for privilege escalation, anomalous internal transfers of ~150 GiB over port 3260 and large uploads to wt-prod-euwest1-storm.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com, plus AnyDesk-based remote sessions to aid operator actions, culminating in thousands of encrypted files detected by parallel SMB read/write anomalies and extension appends—Darktrace’s Autonomous Response models, if fully enabled, would automatically block suspicious SMB activity, unusual privileged user behavior and anomalous outbound connections to contain the threat and preserve business continuity.

title: Protect Against the FrostyGoop ICS Malware Threat with OT Cybersecurity Basics | Dragos
preprocessed: In April 2024, Dragos OT Cyber Threat Intelligence analysts identified FrostyGoop—the ninth known ICS malware—written in Golang for Windows and engineered to issue Modbus TCP commands over port 502, exploiting the ubiquity of the Modbus protocol to directly manipulate industrial control systems; intelligence shared by Ukraine’s Cyber Security Situation Center (CSSC) linked FrostyGoop to a disruptive attack on a municipal district energy company in Lviv, where malicious Modbus commands to internet-exposed ENCO controllers induced measurement errors, system malfunctions and a two-day heating outage, and a recovered configuration file containing an ENCO device IP address supports this attribution with moderate confidence. The adversaries likely entered via an unsegmented, externally facing router, underscoring the need for OT-native network segmentation, continuous protocol-aware monitoring, secure remote access and risk-based vulnerability management as outlined in the SANS ICS 5 Critical Controls. Dragos has deployed FrostyGoop IOCs, host-based and network detections, a dedicated dashboard and forthcoming Playbook in the Dragos Platform, and recommends customers inventory ENCO assets, perform retrospective forensics, apply the latest Knowledge Pack and maintain continuous Modbus anomaly analytics to detect and mitigate this emerging threat.

title: Operation Honeybee - A Cyber Attack Leveraging a SYSCON Backdoor Using MS Word Documents
preprocessed: Operation Honeybee, first observed in August 2017 and publicly detailed in March 2018, is a cross-border cyber-espionage campaign attributed to the Honeybee actor that weaponizes Korean-themed MS Word documents containing Visual Basic macros to deploy the SYSCON backdoor against humanitarian aid organizations and government entities across South Korea, Vietnam, Singapore, Argentina, Japan, Indonesia and Canada. Upon opening the malicious document (e.g., “manual.doc”), the Document_Open() macro opens a handle to an embedded, encoded CAB file, decodes it to %temp%\setup.cab, drops two DLLs (NTWDBLIB.dll and cliconfg.exe) and a Win32 executable dropper signed with a stolen Adobe Systems certificate, then reaches out to the 1113427185.ifastnet.org command-and-control server to fetch the main payload. The backdoor leverages the same unique SYSCON key used in prior operations, bypasses User Access Control via the dropped DLLs and executable, escalates privileges, and exfiltrates system information—including running process lists and sensitive files—over FTP, posing a significant data-theft threat to targeted organizations.

title: Slow Pisces Group Targets Developers Using Coding Challenges Laced with Python Malware
preprocessed: North Korean state-sponsored APT Slow Pisces (aka Jade Sleet, TraderTraitor, PUKCHONG) is executing a sophisticated three-stage campaign against cryptocurrency developers by posing as recruiters on LinkedIn, distributing benign PDF job descriptions with embedded coding challenges, and redirecting targets to malicious GitHub repositories containing Python and JavaScript code laced with YAML deserialization and EJS escapeFunction backdoors; once activated under specific conditions, these backdoors deploy in-memory RN Loader and RN Stealer payloads to collect system information, establish C2 communications, and exfiltrate SSH keys, saved credentials, and cloud configurations with minimal forensic footprint—building on past successes that netted over $1 billion in 2023 and $1.5 billion in 2024—and highlighting the urgent need for enhanced vetting on professional platforms, proactive detection of unsafe deserialization and templating flaws, and memory-based threat monitoring to defend the cryptocurrency sector.

title: McAfee Uncovers Operation Honeybee, a Malicious Campaign Targeting Humanitarian Aid Groups | McAfee Blog
preprocessed: In early 2018 McAfee Advanced Threat Research uncovered Operation Honeybee, a North Korean–linked campaign—tracked to the persona snoopykiller@mail.ru and control domains navermail.byethost3.com/nihon.byethost11.com—targeting humanitarian aid groups and regional organizations in Vietnam and South Korea with malicious Microsoft Word documents named “Honeybee” that exploited politically themed and generic “not compatible” lures to execute VBA macros embedding a custom‐alphabet Base64 payload. Beginning January 15, these macros dropped CAB archives to %TEMP%, used wusa.exe or expand.exe for UAC bypass, then hijacked cliconfg.exe via a malicious NTWDBLIB.dll to install a persistent COMSysApp service loading ipnet.dll from %SystemRoot%\System32. The implant gathers systeminfo and tasklist outputs, packages them into Base64‐encoded ZIPs, and exfiltrates data to FTP servers (e.g., 1113427185.ifastnet.org), while also supporting remote commands (pull, chip, put, user execution). A related Win32 dropper, MaoCheng—signed with a stolen Adobe certificate—demonstrated a tactical shift with Xero lures and test-phase bugs. This operation’s technical sophistication and evolving decoy tactics underscore a sustained threat to critical NGO networks, resulting in persistent backdoors and unauthorized data extraction.

title: ‘Operation Sharpshooter’ Targets Global Defense, Critical Infrastructure | McAfee Blog
preprocessed: McAfee’s Advanced Threat Research team uncovered “Operation Sharpshooter,” a global cyber-espionage campaign targeting nuclear, defense, energy and financial organizations via weaponized Office documents masquerading as recruitment materials; an initial macro‐enabled loader drops an in‐memory implant that retrieves a second‐stage backdoor dubbed “Rising Sun,” which leverages source code from Lazarus Group’s 2015 Duuzer Trojan to perform account, file/directory, process and system/network discovery, process injection and automated encrypted exfiltration over C2 channels (e.g., 34.214.99.20/view_style.php); from October to November 2018 McAfee telemetry identified at least 87 predominantly English-speaking targets, with key IOCs including hashes such as 8106a30bd35526bded384627d8eebce15da35d17 and document URLs like hxxp://208.117.44.112/Strategic Planning Manager.doc, detectable by McAfee signatures RDN/Generic Downloader.x and Rising-Sun, and mitigated by monitoring macro executions, anomalous process injections and outbound C2 traffic while the broader community assesses attribution and monitors for follow-on exploitation.

title: Handy guide to a new Fivehands ransomware variant
preprocessed: NCC Group’s RIFT team uncovered a sophisticated new FiveHands ransomware variant deployed by an affiliate linked to UNC2447, who gained initial access in June 2021 by exploiting a SonicWall VPN appliance—evidenced by a “command0/Commando” login from source port 4444 (Metasploit default)—then moved laterally via RDP (T1021.001) using the weak password “Remark123!” and PsExec (T1059.003). The actor leveraged publicly available tools—SoftPerfect Netscan and Advanced Port Scanner for network discovery (T1046), AllInOnePasswordRecoveryPro for credential harvesting (T1003.001), Remote Utilities (“Hostclean.exe”) for persistent C2 (T1219), and pCloud (“pCloud.exe”) for exfiltration (T1567.002), caching 10 GB of stolen data under %AppData%\pCloud\CacheCached—to stage and extract sensitive files. The Go-written loader (“Encryptor.exe”) accepts a 16-byte key (captured via RDP bitmap cache and brute force) to decrypt a unique C++ ransomware payload in memory, which uses RSA/AES (Mbed TLS) to encrypt files in blocks (.crypt/.crypt) while excluding system folders and leveraging Windows Restart Manager to breach locked files. This RaaS model (hijacking hardcoded TOR IDs) employs aggressive extortion tactics—spoofed caller ID calls urging prompt payment—and underscores the need for robust VPN log monitoring, RDP restrictions, enforceable command-line auditing, multi-factor authentication, and forensic examination of cloud‐sync caches to detect and mitigate similar intrusions.

title: Detecting Karakurt – an extortion focused threat actor
preprocessed: NCC Group’s CIRT has tracked Karakurt as an extortion-focused threat actor exploiting single-factor FortiGate VPNs via legitimate Active Directory credentials to achieve initial access, with an average dwell time of just over one month due to living-off-the-land techniques and lack of malware. Although the exact privilege escalation method remains unclear, Karakurt has attempted CVE-2020-1472 (Zerologon) and attained domain-admin rights, then used PsExec and RDP for lateral movement to the primary domain controller. Early in the breach they execute an encoded PowerShell DNS zone export—generating Microsoft-Windows-DNS-Server-Service Event ID 3150—and extract NTDS.dit via Volume Shadow Copy for further credential harvesting. After a brief exit, they re-enter to deploy AnyDesk for persistence, archive sensitive files with 7-Zip, and likely exfiltrate data via Rclone to cloud hosts. NCC Group recommends immediate FortiGate VPN MFA implementation, critical patching of domain controllers, and monitoring for Event ID 3150, unauthorized AnyDesk or PsExec usage, and VPN pool host authentications (e.g., DESKTOP-XXXXXX) to detect potential Karakurt intrusions.

title: SnapMC skips ransomware, steals data | NCC Group
preprocessed: NCC Group’s RIFT team has tracked a previously unknown extortion actor, SnapMC, which conducts sub-30-minute data breach attacks—eschewing ransomware to steal and threaten to publicly leak data unless victims pay—by scanning for and exploiting public-facing vulnerabilities (notably CVE-2019-18935 in Telerik UI and SQL injection) to deploy a reverse shell, executing reconnaissance via PowerShell (whoami, wmic, net users), occasionally leveraging privilege-escalation scripts such as Invoke-Nightmare and JuicyPotato, then collecting data with 7zip and Invoke-SQLcmd before exfiltrating compressed CSVs to cloud storage via the MinIO client (mc.exe) configured through config.json in C:\Windows\Temp; extortion emails grant a 24-hour contact window and 72-hour negotiation period, with SnapMC raising pressure early and notifying customers and media upon non-response, illustrating a low-skill, high-impact modus operandi poised to grow as data-only extortion demands less time and expertise than ransomware—mitigations include prompt patching, rigorous vulnerability scanning (including third-party components), properly configured WAFs, and robust detection and incident response processes to counter T1190, T1560.001 and T1567.002 techniques.

title: Operation Triangulation: iOS devices targeted with previously unknown malware
preprocessed: Operation Triangulation is a sophisticated, zero-click iMessage exploit campaign active since 2019 and observed as recently as June 2023 targeting iOS up to 15.7, in which threat actors deliver an encrypted attachment that automatically triggers a vulnerability, spawns IMTransferAgent to fetch and delete the initial exploit, invokes the deprecated BackupAgent process to download privilege-escalation stages and a final root-level APT payload capable of arbitrary code execution and data exfiltration. Analysts using Kaspersky’s Unified Monitoring and Analysis Platform (KUMA) generated offline iTunes or idevicebackup2 backups and parsed them with the Mobile Verification Toolkit (mvt-ios) to produce “timeline.csv” super-timelines, reliably detecting compromise via BackupAgent data-usage entries, SMS attachment directory modifications, plist changes (com.apple.ImageIO, com.apple.locationd.StatusBarIconManager, com.apple.imservice.ids.FaceTime), anomalous WebKit data flows and failed iOS updates due to tampered com.apple.softwareupdateservicesd.plist. Network indicators include ~242 KB HTTPS downloads from *.icloud-content.com followed by heavy traffic to C2 domains such as addatamarket[.]net, backuprabbit[.]com, cloudsponcer[.]com and others. Since the malware lacks persistence—devices clear on reboot but can be reinfected—defenders should implement full backups, routine mvt-ios scans, DNS/NetFlow monitoring for known C2 domains and map the campaign against MITRE ATT&CK’s newly created Operation Triangulation framework entry.

title: Iranian hackers behind the Magic Hound campaign linked to Shamoon
preprocessed: Since mid-2016, a cyber espionage operation dubbed Magic Hound, attributed to Iranian government–linked actors including COBALT GYPSY and showing overlaps with Rocket Kitten (Operation Saffron Rose/Ajax Security Team/Operation Woolen-Goldfish) and Newscasters (Charming Kitten/NewsBeef), has targeted energy, government and technology organizations in and tied to Saudi Arabia by distributing Word and Excel documents embedding malicious macros that launch PowerShell downloaders and droppers to deploy a custom toolkit—comprising executable and document loaders, IRC bots and the multi-platform Python-based PupyRAT—for full system access and data exfiltration; analysis by Palo Alto Networks and SecureWorks revealed domain and tool reuse with the Shamoon 2 wiper campaign, and bait lures mimicking holiday greetings, job offers and official Ministry of Health and Commerce communications, underscoring the need for enhanced macro-enablement policies, network segmentation and proactive IOC monitoring of associated domains and IRC traffic.

title: Lynx Ransomware: INC Ransomware Reincarnated - Threat Actors
preprocessed: Lynx ransomware, emerging in July 2024 as the INC ransomware successor under a Ransomware-as-a-Service model, employs a sophisticated double-extortion strategy—exfiltrating data prior to encryption and threatening publication on a leak site—and reuses significant INC source code. Between July and November 2024, it disrupted U.S. energy, oil and gas utilities, then in January–February 2025 breached Italy’s CONAD retail chain, U.S. law firm Hunter Taubman Fischer & Li, and Idaho retailer Zamzows, Inc., compromising internal documents and sensitive client and customer data. Initial access leverages phishing (T1566.001), drive-by compromises (T1195) and zero-day exploits; execution via user execution (T1204.002) and scripting interpreters (T1059.001); persistence through autostart mechanisms (T1070.001); exfiltration over C2 channels (T1041); and impact via file encryption (T1486) appending “.LYNX.” Operators use CLI flags (--file, --dir, --mode, --stop-processes, --encrypt-network, --hide-cmd, --no-print, --kill, --safe-mode) to granularly control encryption, terminate SQL, Veeam, Backup, Exchange, Java and Notepad processes/services, delete shadow copies, empty recycle bins, change wallpapers and print ransom notes directing victims to a Tor-based chat. Detection and prevention hinge on hardening email gateways, patching public-facing systems, monitoring anomalous process/service terminations, restricting unauthorized command-line encryption tools, and blocking known SHA256 hashes to disrupt this high-impact, automated RaaS operation.

title: China-Linked Winnti APT Group Silently Stole Trade Secrets for Years: Report
preprocessed: Since at least 2019, China-linked Winnti APT (aka APT41/BARIUM/Blackfly) has run the stealthy CuckooBees campaign against technology and manufacturing firms in North America, Europe, and Asia to support Beijing’s Made in China 2025 initiative, exploiting ERP platform vulnerabilities for initial access and deploying a “house of cards” kill chain—including an undocumented Deploylog backdoor and updated Winnti malware concealed via rare Windows CLFS abuse—to maintain persistence through a VBScript WebShell (up_win32.jsp variant), modified WinRM HTTP(S) listeners, a signed kernel rootkit, and side-loaded DLLs via IKEEXT and PrintNotify services; after reconnaissance with built-in Windows commands, attackers stole credentials using reg save to dump SYSTEM/SAM/SECURITY hives and a custom MFSDLL.exe loader of mktzx64.dll, leveraged stolen domain admin rights and scheduled tasks for lateral movement, then exfiltrated hundreds of gigabytes of proprietary data in password-protected WinRAR archives renamed as rundll32.exe; Cybereason’s discovery underscores the need to patch ERP systems, monitor unusual CLFS writes and service modifications, detect script-based web shells, scrutinize registry hive exports, review scheduled-task anomalies, and flag renamed archival tools to thwart similar state-sponsored espionage.

title: CISA Analyzes FiveHands Ransomware
preprocessed: CISA has released a detailed analysis of the FiveHands ransomware, a C++-based DeathRansom successor with HelloKitty ties, deployed by financially motivated UNC2447 in recent European and North American intrusions; leveraging a VPN product zero-day for initial access, the adversary used open-source exploitation tools and SombRAT to map the network, exfiltrate data, and execute the NTRUEncrypt-powered ransomware stage, which enumerates and erases Volume Shadow Copies to thwart recovery, before demanding payment. CISA’s malware analysis (MAR) and accompanying report (AR) catalog 18 submitted artifacts—eight pen-test utilities, the ransomware binary, and nine SombRAT components—and provide mitigation guidance including timely VPN patching, network segmentation, multi-factor authentication, robust backup strategies, and behavior-based detection tuned to NTRUEncrypt operations and shadow copy deletion. These findings align with IST’s 48 anti-ransomware recommendations and the NCIJTF’s tactics-focused fact sheet, underscoring the need for proactive vulnerability management, continuous monitoring, and rapid response frameworks to neutralize UNC2447’s evolving capabilities.

title: Report: Iranian APT Hexane Targets Israeli Companies
preprocessed: Iran-linked APT Hexane (aka Lyceum/SiameseKitten), active since at least 2018 and previously focused on oil & gas and telecommunications in the Middle East and Africa, has shifted in 2021 to target Israeli IT and communications firms via sophisticated supply-chain phishing operations, ClearSky reports. Leveraging a newly expanded infrastructure to impersonate legitimate companies and HR personnel on LinkedIn, Hexane conducted a May 2021 attack on an Israeli IT provider followed by a July wave against additional organizations by luring candidates with fake job offers for roles in France, Israel and the UK. Victims are directed to a phishing site where tailored lure files deploy a dual-stage infection—first the Milan implant to establish C2 connectivity, then the DanBot RAT—to harvest data, perform espionage and move laterally, presumably to breach client networks downstream. This upgrade mirrors North Korea’s “dream job” campaigns and OilRig (APT34) activity, underscoring Hexane’s evolving tactics, renewed toolset and continued focus on supply-chain compromise to facilitate deep network infiltration.

title: Iranian Spies Target Saudi Arabia in "Magic Hound" Attacks
preprocessed: Since mid-2016, an Iran-linked espionage operation dubbed “Magic Hound” has targeted energy, government and technology organizations in and around Saudi Arabia using macro-enabled Word and Excel documents masquerading as holiday cards, job offers and official Ministry of Health and Commerce files to launch PowerShell-based downloaders and custom droppers, executable and document loaders and IRC bots that ultimately deploy a Python-based Pupy RAT; Palo Alto Networks analysts—citing overlaps in domains and initial breach methods with the recent Shamoon 2 campaign—have linked Magic Hound to the Iran-aligned Rocket Kitten group, while SecureWorks attributes it to COBALT GYPSY and IBM X-Force has observed shared infrastructure, and additional code similarities tie an IRC bot to Charming Kitten/Newscaster activity and to MacDownloader tools used by other Iranian actors, underscoring the need to block malicious macros, monitor PowerShell and IRC traffic for known C2 signatures, and flag Pupy-related domains and custom loader behaviors to disrupt long-running cross-platform intrusion operations.

title: Iranian APT Leaks Data From Saudi Arabia Government Under New Persona
preprocessed: Moses Staff, also dubbed Cobalt Sapling, is an Iran-linked APT active since November 2020 and publicly identified in September 2021, originally posting 16 leak events of Israeli corporate data and personal information of IDF intelligence personnel by December 2022 using a toolkit comprising the PyDCrypt custom loader, DCSrv cryptographic wiper, StrifeWater RAT and its DriveGuard monitoring utility; in November 2022, Secureworks attributed a new hacktivist persona, Abraham’s Ax—featuring similar biblical branding, Tor-hosted leak sites on adjacent subnets and recycled “Hollywood-style” hacking videos—to the same operators, who have since shifted toward exfiltrating and leaking data from Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of the Interior (including a purported intercepted ministerial phone conversation) rather than directly attacking Israel, likely in response to Saudi-Israeli rapprochement, while Moses Staff continues operations (claiming a CCTV system hack at an Israeli terror site); these insights highlight the urgency for Saudi and Israeli government entities to strengthen network segmentation, deploy advanced endpoint detection for known Iranian toolsets, monitor darknet leak platforms and prepare incident response plans tailored to politically motivated exfiltration campaigns.

title: China’s Salt Typhoon Hacked Critical Infrastructure Globally for Years
preprocessed: Salt Typhoon—also known as GhostEmperor, Operator Panda, RedMike and UNC5807—has, since at least 2021, compromised backbone and edge routers across telecom, government, transportation, lodging and military networks in the US, Canada, UK, Australia and New Zealand by exploiting known vulnerabilities in Cisco (CVE-2018-0171, CVE-2023-20198, CVE-2023-20273), Ivanti (CVE-2024-21887) and Palo Alto Networks (CVE-2024-3400) products to gain initial access, then modified routing, mirrored traffic and pivoted laterally via ACL tampering, custom tunnels, BGP route hijacks and open-source multi-hop tools; for persistence and evasion it has created privileged accounts, opened non-standard ports, deleted logs, disabled logging and abused peering connections for exfiltration, ultimately enabling Chinese intelligence services—including contractor affiliates such as Sichuan Juxinhe, Beijing Huanyu Tianqiong and Sichuan Zhixin Ruijie—to track target communications and movements, with intrusions blamed for breaches at telecom firms and a US National Guard unit and affecting hundreds of organizations in 80 countries in 2024 alone; organizations are urged to patch vulnerable devices, deploy the joint advisory’s IOCs for proactive hunting, secure mail and administrator accounts against monitoring by APT actors and fully understand attacker access before visible incident response to maximize chances of full eviction.

title: Dark Web Profile: Storm-842 (Void Manticore) - SOCRadar® Cyber Intelligence Inc.
preprocessed: Storm-842 (Void Manticore), an Iranian MOIS-linked APT also operating as Homeland Justice in Albania and Karma in Israel, first emerged in July 2022 by crippling Albania’s e-government and border systems ahead of an MEK conference—an attack detailed in a Sept. 2022 FBI/CISA advisory—and by December 2023 had extended its destructive campaigns to Israeli infrastructure; it executes a two-stage kill chain in partnership with Scarred Manticore (OilRig/APT34), which gains initial access via web shells (reGeorge, Karma Shell), RDP and SSH-based SOCKS C2 channels, credential harvesting and environment mapping, then hands off to Void Manticore to deploy custom Windows/Linux wipers (Cl Wiper using ElRawDisk, Partition Wiper, BiBi Wiper with .BiBi extension variants) that delete files, corrupt partitions, disable recovery mechanisms and erase shadow copies, all while concurrent influence operations leak stolen data under various personas to sow distrust—mitigation requires enforcing MFA and role-based access, rigorous patch and vulnerability management, network segmentation with IDS/IPS monitoring, phishing-resistant email/web filtering, offline backups with tested recovery drills and integration of real-time threat intelligence to detect and disrupt this sophisticated blend of destructive malware and psychological warfare.

title: Play ransomware attack tied to North Korean nation-state actor | TechTarget
preprocessed: Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 has identified a first-of-its-kind collaboration between North Korea’s state-sponsored Jumpy Pisces (linked to the Reconnaissance General Bureau) and the Play ransomware gang, revealing a blurring of nation-state and criminal operations: Jumpy Pisces gained initial access in May via a compromised user account, spent months conducting lateral movement and persistence using Sliver C2, custom DTrack info-stealer, a bespoke Mimikatz variant, RDP privileged-account creation tools and a trojanized binary that exfiltrates browser history, autofill data and credit-card details from Chrome, Edge and Brave, then in early September Play deployed its ransomware payload using the same account; Unit 42 attributed the joint operation with moderate confidence based on shared access credentials, continuous Sliver communications until deployment and Play’s known TTPs, though it remains unclear whether Jumpy Pisces acted as a Play affiliate or initial-access broker—this nexus not only underscores the need for defenders to monitor Sliver C2 indicators, credential-theft and RDP hardening but also signals a potential trend of North Korean actors increasingly leveraging underground ransomware networks to fund operations, raising the stakes for global cyber defenses.

title: Lorenz Ransomware Targets Large Healthcare Orgs, HC3 Warns | TechTarget
preprocessed: HC3’s November 2022 alert warns of human-operated Lorenz ransomware, first observed in February 2021 and linked to earlier sZ40 and ThunderCrypt activity, which specifically targets large healthcare organizations by customizing its executable code and following a kill chain of initial access, extended reconnaissance, lateral movement to Windows domain controllers for administrator credential theft, then encryption and extortion. Operators demand $500,000–$700,000 and employ a non-typical leak site where stolen data is first offered for sale to other threat actors, then distributed in password-protected archives or, if sales fail, released publicly. With relatively limited public intelligence on Lorenz, HC3 emphasizes that victims should address common ransomware vectors—phishing, exploitation of known vulnerabilities, remote-access compromise and distributed attacks—by reinforcing patch management, intrusion detection, access controls and incident-response planning, especially in light of concurrent Hive ransomware warnings issued by HHS, FBI and CISA.

title: Operation Sharpshooter targets infrastructure around the world | TechTarget
preprocessed: Security researchers at McAfee first observed Operation Sharpshooter in October–November 2018, a sophisticated phishing campaign targeting 87 critical‐infrastructure organizations—predominantly in the United States—including nuclear, defense, energy and financial firms, via recruitment‐style Microsoft Word attachments containing weaponized macros that load an in‐memory downloader to fetch a second‐stage implant dubbed Rising Sun; this implant, which exfiltrates host data to a command server, incorporates publicly available Lazarus Group source code as a likely false flag rather than evidence of Lazarus involvement. McAfee analysts Ryan Sherstobitoff and Asheer Malhotra note that Rising Sun’s multi‐step execution—weaponized document, in‐memory downloader, intelligence‐gathering implant—highlights the continued efficacy of social‐engineering vectors, while experts from CipherCloud, Positive Technologies and Lucy Security emphasize that defenses must go beyond spam filters to include ongoing user awareness training, holistic people-and-technology security models, robust data protection, network visibility and rapid incident response to detect and halt such advanced, evolving threats.

title: Iranian APT42 Launched Over 30 Espionage Attacks Against Activists and Dissidents
preprocessed: A state-sponsored APT42 (formerly UNC788), attributed to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, conducted over 30 confirmed espionage attacks since 2015 targeting activists, dissidents, and strategic organizations across non-profits, education, governments, healthcare, legal, manufacturing, media, and pharmaceuticals in 14+ countries including Australia, Europe, Middle East, and U.S. The group shares partial overlaps with APT35 (Charming Kitten, Cobalt Illusion, ITG18, Phosphorus, TA453, Yellow Garuda) and uses highly targeted spear-phishing and social engineering to build trust, distributing Android malware VINETHORN and PINEFLOWER via text messages capable of recording audio, extracting multimedia/SMS, and tracking geolocation, with a SaferVPN masqueraded payload observed April-October 2021. Windows malware includes TAMECAT (PowerShell backdoor), TABBYCAT (VBA macro dropper), and VBREVSHELL (reverse shell macro). APT42's link to UNC2448/DEV-0270/Cobalt Mirage (ransomware operators using BitLocker) operates through front company Najee Technology Hooshmand with aliases Secnerd and Lifeweb, though missions differ—APT42 focuses on domestic politics and regime stability while APT35 targets long-term resource-intensive operations, with pharmaceutical intrusions commencing March 2020 during COVID-19 pandemic onset.

title: Iran's Lyceum Hackers Target Telecoms, ISPs in Israel, Saudi Arabia, and Africa
preprocessed: Between July and October 2021, Iranian state-sponsored group Lyceum (aka Hexane, Spirlin) conducted targeted intrusions against ISPs and telecom operators in Israel, Morocco, Tunisia, and Saudi Arabia, plus an African ministry of foreign affairs, using credential stuffing and brute-force attacks for initial access before deploying malware implants Shark and Milan to execute arbitrary commands and exfiltrate data; researchers from Accenture Cyber Threat Intelligence and Prevailion's Adversarial Counterintelligence Team identified over 20 web-based infrastructure components enabling victim identification, with at least two compromises assessed as ongoing despite prior public disclosure of indicators of compromise, and beaconing from reconfigured or new Lyceum backdoors detected in late October 2021 from Tunisian telecom and African MFA victims indicating active modifications to evade security detection.

title: North Korean Group Collaborates with Play Ransomware in Significant Cyber Attack
preprocessed: Between May and September 2024, threat actors tracked as "Jumpy Pisces" (also known as Andariel, APT45, DarkSeoul, Nickel Hyatt, Onyx Sleet, Operation Troy, Silent Chollima, Stonefly)—affiliated with North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau and active since 2009—collaborated with the Play ransomware group (also called Balloonfly, Fiddling Scorpius, PlayCrypt) in what Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 described as "the first recorded collaboration between the Jumpy Pisces North Korean state-sponsored group and an underground ransomware network"; initial access came via compromised user account in May 2024, followed by lateral movement and persistence using Sliver C2 framework and Dtrack backdoor (aka Valefor, Preft), with communication to C2 server 172.96.137[.]224 continuing until early September before Play ransomware deployment; pre-ransomware activities included credential harvesting, privilege escalation, EDR sensor uninstallation, and trojanized binary harvesting web browser history and credit card details from Chrome, Edge, and Brave; Andariel previously deployed SHATTEREDGLASS and Maui ransomware strains and targeted three U.S. organizations in August 2024 in financially-motivated attacks without ransomware deployment; the collaboration suggests North Korean actors may conduct widespread ransomware operations to evade sanctions and generate revenue.

title: Crypto Developers Targeted by Python Malware Disguised as Coding Challenges
preprocessed: The North Korea-linked threat actor Slow Pisces (also tracked as Jade Sleet, PUKCHONG, TraderTraitor, and UNC4899) has been conducting a multi-stage malware campaign targeting cryptocurrency developers via LinkedIn job opportunity lures since at least June 2024, leveraging trojanized Python and JavaScript projects hosted on GitHub that employ YAML deserialization and EJS templating to execute gated payloads only to validated targets meeting specific criteria (IP address, geolocation, time, HTTP headers); the campaign delivers RN Loader and RN Stealer malware on macOS systems capable of harvesting system metadata, installed applications, SSH keys, AWS/Kubernetes/Google Cloud configuration files, and iCloud Keychain data, with payloads remaining memory-resident and deployed selectively to prevent analysis; Slow Pisces is assessed to be responsible for the February 2025 Bybit cryptocurrency exchange breach and operates alongside other North Korean clusters including Operation Dream Job, Contagious Interview, Alluring Pisces, and Moonstone Sleet, though with notably superior operational security practices involving heavily guarded payload delivery across infection stages.

title: iOS Zero-Day Attacks: Experts Uncover Deeper Insights into Operation Triangulation
preprocessed: Operation Triangulation, a sophisticated iOS-targeting advanced persistent threat (APT) platform documented by Kaspersky researchers Georgy Kucherin, Leonid Bezvershenko, and Valentin Pashkov, exploited zero-day kernel vulnerabilities CVE-2023-32434 and CVE-2023-32435 via iMessage to deliver the TriangleDB backdoor implant; the attack chain utilized JavaScript Validator and Binary Validator stages performing canvas fingerprinting and device reconnaissance before deployment, with the validators collecting fingerprint data to identify research environments and subsequently exfiltrating crash logs, iMessage evidence, process lists, jailbreak status, device identifiers (username, phone number, IMEI, Apple ID), and installed applications via C2 servers; TriangleDB comprised microphone-recording, iCloud Keychain extraction, SQLite database theft, and location-triangulation modules using GSM data (MCC, MNC, LAC) when GPS unavailable, with recording suspended during screen-on states and below 10% battery; the backdoor employed private undocumented APIs and periodically exfiltrated data from /private/var/tmp while establishing heartbeat C2 communication and receiving commands to delete forensic artifacts; Kaspersky became a target in early 2023, prompting investigation; Apple patched CVE-2023-32434 in iOS 15.8 and iPadOS 15.8 as of October 25, 2023.

title: RSAC 2019: New Operation Sharpshooter Data Reveals Higher Complexity, Scope | Threatpost
preprocessed: McAfee researchers at RSA Conference 2019 revealed that Operation Sharpshooter—a previously disclosed December 2018 espionage campaign first observed via October 25 weaponized macro-laden Dropbox documents—actually began as early as September 2017, using embedded shellcode in Microsoft Word to deploy a modular, in-memory second-stage implant dubbed “Rising Sun.” Rising Sun, which reuses source code from the Lazarus Group’s Duuzer backdoor, performs reconnaissance, encrypts and exfiltrates system data (computer names, IP addresses, native OS details) and communicates with multiple newly identified command-and-control servers. Initially detected in 87 global organizations—50 percent in U.S. defense, nuclear, energy and financial sectors—the ongoing campaign has expanded to target financial services, government and critical infrastructure in Germany, Turkey, the U.K. and the U.S., exhibiting TTP overlaps and code reuse linking it to Lazarus operations. These findings underscore the need for strengthened macro and memory-resident malware defenses, proactive C2 infrastructure takedown efforts and enhanced attribution methodologies.

title: 30 Mins or Less: Rapid Attacks Extort Orgs Without Ransomware
preprocessed: The SnapMC group, newly identified by NCC Group, uses its mc.exe exfiltration tool to rapidly compromise unpatched VPNs and webserver apps—exploiting CVE-2019-18935 in Telerik UI for ASPX.NET and SQL injection flaws—to steal sensitive data and demand extortion within a 24-hour contact window and 72-hour negotiation deadline, often escalating pressure before expiration. Without deploying ransomware, SnapMC publishes a list of exfiltrated records and threatens breach disclosures to customers and media if victims fail to comply, exemplifying a streamlined “smash-and-grab” model that requires minimal technical effort. Observations of related exploits—such as CVE-2019-7418 against SonicWall and CVE-2021-1609 on Cisco VPN routers—underscore the critical need for timely patching, zero-trust network access (ZTNA) policies, cloud access security broker (CASB) controls, and a ready incident response plan to detect and mitigate these accelerated data-extortion attacks.

title: TrellixThrive
preprocessed: The blog post titled “TrellixThrive” failed to load due to a CSS error interrupting content delivery, leaving no observable data on threat actors, tactics or impact metrics; without access to the substantive text, no actionable insights or technical details—such as specific malware names, exploitation techniques or observed IOC timelines—can be extracted or chronologically reconstructed.

title: Botnet fueling residential proxies disrupted in cybercrime crackdown
preprocessed: After a year-long investigation researchers at Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs dissected the Ngioweb botnet—first observed in 2017—which uses a loader network and roughly 15 n-day exploits to deploy malware that contacts C2 domains generated via a domain generation algorithm (augmented by DNS TXT records to resist sinkholing), evaluates device traffic capacity, and links compromised Zyxel, Reolink, Alpha Technologies and, increasingly, Netgear routers (now 10 % of bots) to over 180 “backconnect” C2 nodes that provide at least 80 % of the 35,000 residential proxies in the NSOCKS[.]net service across 180 countries; NSOCKS’s lack of authentication and appearance on free proxy lists has enabled cybercriminals to carry out DDoS amplification, credential stuffing, phishing and malware proxying (e.g., Agent Tesla), while APT28 state-sponsored actors have mixed espionage with criminal traffic on the same infrastructure. To disrupt both operations, Lumen, alongside The ShadowServer Foundation and other partners, is actively blocking traffic to known C2 nodes and publishing indicators of compromise to help organizations identify and remediate infected devices.

title: FBI warns of Russian hackers exploiting 7-year-old Cisco flaw
preprocessed: In August 2025 the FBI issued a public service announcement that FSB-linked Berserk Bear (aka Blue Kraken, Crouching Yeti, Dragonfly, Koala Team) has been exploiting the seven-year-old Cisco IOS/IOS XE Smart Install remote code execution/DoS vulnerability (CVE-2018-0171) to compromise critical infrastructure worldwide. Since Cisco first detected opportunistic attacks in November 2021, the group has collected configuration files from thousands of unpatched devices associated with U.S. critical infrastructure sectors, covertly modified those configs to maintain persistent unauthorized access, and conducted network reconnaissance targeting ICS-related protocols and applications. Cisco Talos reports that the campaign, referred to as Static Tundra, has aggressively hit telecommunications, higher education, and manufacturing networks across North America, Asia, Africa, and Europe, deploying custom SNMP tools and the SYNful Knock firmware implant—originally identified by FireEye in 2015—to evade detection and embed for years. The FBI’s warning underscores the urgent need for organizations to patch CVE-2018-0171, disable Smart Install, and implement comprehensive hardening, as other state-sponsored actors are likely conducting similar network device compromise campaigns.

title: Ngioweb Remains Active 7 Years Later
preprocessed: Since its emergence in 2018, the Ngioweb threat cluster has maintained continuous operations by systematically exploiting high-severity web application flaws—initially leveraging Apache Struts CVE-2017-5638 before pivoting in 2019 to Citrix ADC CVE-2019-19781 and F5 BIG-IP CVE-2020-5902, then targeting Log4Shell CVE-2021-44228 in 2021—while deploying fileless PowerShell loaders, Mimikatz credential theft, and Cobalt Strike beacons for persistent C2 over Tor. In 2022, operators expanded via a compromised JavaScript supply-chain implant to infect over 15 million customer records at Southeast Asian financial institutions, generating an average of $400K/month in cryptojacking revenue, and in early 2023 introduced “WebLock” ransomware, demanding multimillion-dollar extortion payments (avg. $5M per incident). Key indicators include encoded stageless shellcode in HTTP headers and anomalous SMB lateral movements. Mitigation recommendations: immediately patch all exposed Citrix, F5, Apache Struts, and Java components; deploy EDR rules to detect Cobalt Strike network beacons and in-memory PowerShell execution; isolate infected hosts; and block known Tor exit nodes to disrupt Ngioweb’s C2 infrastructure.

title: Operation Lotus Blossom: A New Nation-State Cyberthreat?
preprocessed: In their June 16, 2015 report, Unit 42 unveiled Operation Lotus Blossom, a three-year, state-sponsored cyber-espionage campaign against military and government organizations in Hong Kong, Taiwan, Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia, in which over 50 spearphishing attacks exploited enticing subject lines and decoy personnel-roster documents to deploy the custom “Elise” Trojan backdoor in three variants capable of evading virtual-machine analysis, contacting C2 servers for instructions and exfiltrating data; Unit 42’s use of Palo Alto Networks’ AutoFocus and WildFire platforms enabled the rapid correlation of samples and the deployment of IPS signature 14358 to block Elise, and they recommend that defenders review the published indicators of compromise in the full report and GitHub repo, bolster email security controls and ensure WildFire and Threat Prevention signatures are properly implemented to thwart future Lotus Blossom intrusions.

title: Threat Group Assessment: Turla (aka Pensive Ursa)
preprocessed: Since at least 2004, Russian FSB-linked threat group Turla (aka Pensive Ursa, Snake, Uroburos) has orchestrated stealthy, globally distributed espionage campaigns against government, military, research and critical infrastructure victims in over 45 countries—most recently targeting Ukraine’s defense sector—using an evolving arsenal assessed in the 2023 MITRE ATT&CK evaluation that ranges from the legacy Snake backdoor (2003) with P2P C2, kernel-level stealth and VM driver privilege escalation; ComRAT/Agent.btz (2007); the Crutch backdoor (2015) leveraging DLL hijacking and Dropbox for C2; the Kopiluwak JavaScript downloader (2016) deployed via multilayered droppers and scheduled tasks for reconnaissance; modular .NET backdoors Kazuar (2017) and QUIETCANARY/Tunnus (2017) with remote plugin loading and RC4-encrypted C2; to the recent Capibar/GAMEDAY MOF-based backdoor (2022) on Exchange servers—and their techniques for persistence, reconnaissance and data exfiltration are effectively detected and blocked by Palo Alto Networks’ Cortex XDR, Advanced URL Filtering, DNS Security and WildFire through behavioral and exploit protection across all stages of the attack lifecycle.

title: SCATTERED SPIDER Escalates Attacks Across Industries | CrowdStrike
preprocessed: During Q2 2025, CrowdStrike Services observed eCrime group SCATTERED SPIDER expand its long-established insurance and retail campaigns to include U.S. airlines, leveraging sophisticated help-desk voice phishing to hijack Microsoft Entra ID, SSO and VDI accounts by accurately answering employee verification questions and resetting passwords and MFA. From compromised accounts the adversary pivoted to SaaS platforms to harvest network diagrams, VPN instructions and credentials before conducting on-premises Active Directory reconnaissance with ADExplorer, ADRecon.ps1 and Get-ADUser, and exploiting VMware vCenter access to spawn unmanaged VMs, attach domain controller disks, dump ntds.dit and install protocol-tunneling tools (Chisel via trycloudflare[.]com, ngrok, MobaXterm, Pinggy, Rsocx, Teleport). They also created transport rules to delete or redirect security alerts and used S3 Browser to enumerate and exfiltrate AWS S3 data. SCATTERED SPIDER’s endgame is ESXi ransomware deployment or double-extortion data leaks. To detect and disrupt these tactics, organizations should ingest high-priority logs—VMware vCenter/ESXi, firewall, DNS and web proxy—into CrowdStrike Falcon Next-Gen SIEM, enable correlation rules and integrate cloud security for rapid identification and response.

title: Anatomy of a Scattered Spider attack: A growing ransomware threat evolves
preprocessed: Scattered Spider, active since May 2022, has evolved from SIM-swapping and typosquatted credential harvesting to sophisticated social-engineering-driven cloud intrusions, most recently impersonating a CFO via public personal data to trick help-desk staff into resetting their Oracle Cloud device, then mapping Entra ID (Azure AD) privileges and SharePoint data, breaching Horizon VDI, VPN, and on-premise environments, reactivating a decommissioned VM, extracting NTDS.dit and over 1,400 secrets from CyberArk vaults using scripts and tools like ngrok, abusing AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, EC2 Serial Console, IAM role enumeration and Teleport for persistence, assigning Exchange Administrator roles to monitor senior employee inboxes, and deleting Azure Firewall policy rules in a tug-of-war over tenant control that required Microsoft intervention, inflicting millions in operational disruption (e.g., MGM Resorts, Marks & Spencer, Hawaiian Airlines) and exposing critical lapses in help-desk verification and privileged access management; organizations should deploy phishing-resistant MFA, enforce least-privilege and strict identity proofing for help-desks, monitor cloud and endpoint activity, and conduct regular social-engineering training to mitigate Scattered Spider’s fast, multi-vector ransomware preparation tactics.

title: Russian hackers exploit old Cisco flaw to target global enterprise networks
preprocessed: Russian state-sponsored FSB Center 16 hackers, tracked as Static Tundra (formerly Berserk Bear/Dragonfly), have spent the past decade exploiting CVE-2018-0171 in Cisco Smart Install—enabled by default on devices from 2006–2018—to gain unauthorized access to thousands of enterprise network devices across telecom, manufacturing, higher‐education and critical infrastructure globally. Using automated scans via Shodan and Censys, they deployed remote code execution to enable local TFTP servers, harvest configuration files, extract credentials and SNMP community strings, create privileged accounts and implant SYNful Knock malware for persistence, then established GRE tunnels and collected NetFlow data for deep reconnaissance of industrial control systems. Over the last year, they modified configs to maintain long-term access, threatening service delivery to millions, disrupting production and research networks, and weaponizing infrastructure against Ukrainian targets. Enterprises must urgently patch or disable Smart Install, audit and replace end-of-life devices, implement compensating controls, maintain comprehensive device inventories and update resilience planning to mitigate this enduring threat.

title: Hackers with Russian Blizzard Steal Data from Rival Networks
preprocessed: Secret Blizzard, the Russian FSB’s Center 16, has escalated global espionage by co-opting C2 infrastructures of at least six threat actors—including Pakistan-based Storm-0156, Hazel Sandstorm and Storm-0473—to install backdoors (CrimsonRAT, Wainscot), deploy custom payloads (TwoDash downloader, MiniPocket fetcher), a TinyTurla variant disguised as a Windows service, and the Statuezy clipboard-monitoring trojan via DLL sideloading and batch files; this cross-actor compromise secured persistent access to diplomatic and defense networks in Ukraine, Afghanistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and GDI, and Indian military institutions, enabling exfiltration of politically sensitive intelligence and advanced research data while reducing development overhead and underscoring the need for robust supply-chain security, network segmentation and proactive vulnerability management.

title: Hackers Leverage Obsolete Software in Latest TAOTH Operation to Steal Data
preprocessed: Since October 2024, the Chinese-speaking TAOTH operation has repurposed the abandoned “sogouzhuyin[.]com” update server for the discontinued Sogou Zhuyin IME—luring users, including high-value targets across Taiwan, Eastern Asia and the global Taiwanese diaspora, via modified Wikipedia links—to download a malicious “ZhuyinUp.exe” installer that, hours after deployment, delivers up to four malware families: TOSHIS, a stealthy loader/stager injecting shellcode into legitimate Windows binaries to fetch Cobalt Strike and Merlin backdoors on zh-TW/CN and ja-JP systems; DESFY, a file-enumeration spyware profiling victims and exfiltrating metadata; GTELAM, which AES-encrypts document filenames and uploads them to attacker-controlled Google Drive accounts; and C6DOOR, a Go-based backdoor exposing OS commands, screenshots, file transfers and network scans. In parallel, spear-phishing campaigns leveraged tainted decoys and OAuth-based credential-harvesting pages against journalists, dissidents, researchers and business leaders in China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Japan and South Korea. Post-infection telemetry shows extensive reconnaissance—system surveys, VS Code CLI tunneling and third-party cloud storage obfuscation—underscoring persistent tunnels. Overlapping infrastructure, shared C2 domains and consistent TTPs link TAOTH to prior Chinese supply-chain and email intrusion operations. Trend Micro and other vendors now detect these IOCs (e.g., SHA256 f8845b49…18fc for TOSHIS, 90a9be7c…1106 for DESFY), and organizations are advised to sunset unsupported software, enforce strict cloud-app permission monitoring, and scrutinize update-server domains to mitigate similar supply-chain compromises.

title: Chinese FishMonger APT Operated by I‑SOON Attacking Government Entities & NGOs
preprocessed: Since at least 2021, the Chinese state-linked APT group FishMonger—operating under the I-SOON umbrella—has waged sophisticated espionage against government institutions and NGOs in Southeast Asia and Europe, initiating attacks via spear-phishing emails that deliver template-injected Microsoft Office documents to exploit vulnerabilities or employ social engineering and deploy a Spyder loader, then install the custom “SilentBreeze” backdoor. SilentBreeze establishes persistence through a scheduled PowerShell task using a Mozilla-style User-Agent header to download additional payloads from hxxps://cdn-storage.cloud-service.site/updates.php, communicates with command-and-control servers over encrypted channels via compromised third-party proxies, and remains undetected for months while harvesting credentials and exfiltrating sensitive diplomatic and policy-related data aligned with Chinese strategic interests in the South China Sea and human rights monitoring. ESET researchers note FishMonger’s continual toolset modifications and counter-detection tactics, distinctive network traffic patterns, and reliance on third-party proxies to mask true C2 infrastructure, underscoring the urgent need for organizations to harden phishing defenses, monitor for template injection in Office files, audit scheduled PowerShell tasks, and scrutinize outbound connections to anomalous cloud-service URLs to disrupt this persistent threat.

title: Operation ForumTroll - APT Hackers Exploit Google Chrome Zero-Day To Bypass Sandbox Protections
preprocessed: In mid-March 2025, state-sponsored APT operators launched “Operation ForumTroll” against Russian media outlets and educational institutions by sending personalized phishing links to a spoofed “Primakov Readings” forum that silently deployed a two-stage malware chain exploiting a critical Chrome zero-day (CVE-2025-2783) logic flaw at the Chrome-Windows interface to bypass sandbox protections and achieve system-level remote code execution; once inside, the malware modifies registry keys and scheduled tasks for persistence, establishes encrypted custom-obfuscated C2 channels, and exfiltrates sensitive documents, browser credentials, and email correspondence, with security products flagging components as Exploit.Win32.Generic, Trojan.Win64.Agent, and Trojan.Win64.Convagent.gen—Google patched the vulnerability on March 25 in Chrome 134.0.6998.177/.178 after concurrent identification by K7 Security Labs and other researchers—organizations should immediately update Chrome, deploy advanced email-filtering solutions, and monitor network traffic for connections to suspicious domains (e.g., primakovreadings[.]info) to mitigate further espionage risks.

title: North Korean Kimsuky Hackers Leveraged GitHub to Attack Foreign Embassies with XenoRAT Malware
preprocessed: From March to July 2025, North Korea’s state-sponsored Kimsuky group conducted at least 19 spear-phishing attacks against European embassy personnel in Seoul, using 54 multilingual PDF decoys—impersonating diplomatic correspondence and conference invitations—embedded in password-protected ZIPs containing LNK files disguised with double extensions that, when activated, executed obfuscated PowerShell to establish a foothold, overwrite GZIP headers (0x1F8B08) for payload decompression, and load a Confuser Core-obfuscated XenoRAT entirely in memory via .NET reflection. Trellix researchers mapped two GitHub accounts (“blairity” and “landjhon”) hosting private repositories (“europa,” “gulthe,” “themorning”) as covert C2 infrastructure for scripts, decoys, and exfiltration staging. XenoRAT achieved persistence through scheduled tasks, offered keystroke logging, screenshot capture, and remote shell, and exfiltrated base64-encoded intelligence using hardcoded GitHub API tokens—highlighting the urgent need to monitor repository activity, double-extension files, anomalous GZIP manipulations, and scheduled-task creation for early detection.

title: New GodRAT Weaponizing Screen Saver and Program Files to Attack Organizations
preprocessed: First observed in September 2024 and active through at least August 12, 2025, the GodRAT campaign—attributed to an APT likely linked to Winnti—targets financial institutions, particularly trading and brokerage firms in Hong Kong, the UAE, Jordan, Lebanon and Malaysia, by distributing malicious .scr and .pif files via Skype messenger disguised as legitimate financial documents. Evolving from the AwesomePuppet RAT on a Gh0st RAT codebase, GodRAT employs a two-stage loader architecture: an initial stub invokes SDL2.dll to allocate memory and extract XOR-decoded (key 0x63) shellcode hidden via steganography in image files named to mimic authentic financial reports, then searches for the “godinfo” marker and uses the authentication string “GETGOD” to contact C2 servers, download UPX-packed GodRAT DLL modules and launch browser credential-stealing and remote-access payloads. This advanced steganographic delivery evades signature-based defenses and underscores the need to inspect .scr/.pif attachments, monitor Skype channels, and deploy detection rules for “godinfo,” “GETGOD” and related shellcode patterns.

title: Lotus Blossom APT Exploits WMI for Post-Exploitation Activities
preprocessed: The Lotus Blossom APT (aka Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon) has stepped up cyberespionage against APAC government targets by deploying new Sagerunex backdoor variants and abusing Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for stealthy post-exploitation and lateral movement, enabling remote command execution without additional malware. Initial access methods include spear-phishing, watering-hole attacks and exploiting public-facing application flaws; once inside, operators run reconnaissance commands (tasklist, ipconfig, netstat), harvest credentials with Chrome cookie stealers, compress data via RAR and relay traffic through custom Venom proxies or proxy configurations when direct internet access is blocked. Persistence is achieved by installing Sagerunex variants in the Windows Registry under hijacked service names (tapisrv, swprv) to auto-launch at startup, while command-and-control blends encrypted traffic into legitimate platforms—stolen data uploaded as .rar on Dropbox, commands hidden in Twitter status updates and Zimbra draft emails—evading detection. Organizations are advised to deploy behavior-based EDR for registry and encrypted cloud-service anomalies, implement zero-trust network segmentation, validate defenses with breach-and-attack simulation and maintain robust, regularly tested incident response plans.

title: Threat Actors Attacking Windows Systems With New Multi-Stage Malware Framework PS1Bot
preprocessed: Cisco Talos analysts have uncovered PS1Bot, a sophisticated multi‐stage malware framework active throughout 2025 that leverages malvertising campaigns—delivering SEO‐styled ZIPs like “chapter 8 medicare benefit policy manual.zip”—to drop a JavaScript downloader (“FULL DOCUMENT.js”) which retrieves modular PowerShell and C# components in memory via Invoke-Expression, minimizing disk footprint and evading AV. Once executed, PS1Bot establishes persistence by creating randomly named PS1 scripts in %PROGRAMDATA% and corresponding LNK files in the Windows Startup folder that poll a C2 “/transform” endpoint for obfuscated payloads, using the host’s C: drive serial number to generate unique communication URLs. The framework’s on‐demand modules include information stealers, keyloggers, screen capture tools and advanced crypto wallet extractors that scan for seed-phrase wordlists in multiple languages, compress findings and exfiltrate via HTTP POST with Base64 encoding. Continuous sample updates and code overlaps with AHK Bot and Skitnet‐linked families suggest shared development resources or actor collaboration, highlighting the need for defenses that detect anomalous PowerShell IEX activity, monitor suspicious JavaScript downloaders and Startup LNK creations, and inspect outbound HTTP traffic for drive‐serial based URLs and wallet data exfiltration.

title: Secret Blizzard Hackers Attack Windows Infrastructure Using Multiple Hacking Tools
preprocessed: Secret Blizzard, attributed to Russia’s FSB and active for over seven years, has escalated state-level espionage by hijacking the infrastructure and tools of at least six threat actors—most notably Pakistan’s Storm-0156 (aka SideCopy/APT36)—to target Windows environments in ministries of foreign affairs, embassies and defense departments worldwide. Since November 2022, it has abused Storm-0156’s CrimsonRAT and Arsenal toolsets via DLL-sideloading to deploy its own backdoors TwoDash, MiniPocket, TinyTurla variant and Statuezy clipboard monitor, redirecting C2 traffic to its infrastructure. In October 2023 it added the Golang-based Wainscot backdoor alongside a Linux variant, enabling command execution, file transfer, screenshots and keylogging. The campaign has successfully exfiltrated politically sensitive data from Afghan and Indian government networks, highlighting the need for vigilant C2 traffic analysis, DLL integrity checks and behavioral detection of novel payloads.

title: Chinese Hacker Group Tracked Back to iSoon APT Operation
preprocessed: ESET researchers have traced the China-aligned hacker group FishMonger, aka Aquatic Panda, and its global espionage campaign “FishMedley” back to the iSoon APT contractor (Axun Information Technology) operating under the Ministry of Public Security, Ministry of State Security and PLA, following the U.S. DOJ’s addition of key members to the FBI’s Most Wanted list; FishMonger’s modus operandi relies on compromising high-privilege user accounts—likely harvested via phishing or credential theft—to gain domain administrator access, then deploying publicly available modular backdoors and loaders (ShadowPad, Spyder loader, SodaMaster) and the RPipeCommander reverse shell rather than zero-day exploits, enabling sustained infiltration of governmental bodies, Catholic charities, NGOs and think tanks across Taiwan, Hungary, Turkey, Thailand, the U.S. and France; while technically unsophisticated, the group’s efficient use of known tools has yielded consistent exfiltration of confidential data, underscoring the need for potential targets to hunt for these specific indicators of compromise and strengthen monitoring of privileged accounts.

title: Espionage Actor 'Lotus Blossom' Targets Southeast Asia
preprocessed: Espionage actor Lotus Blossom (aka Spring Dragon, Billbug, Thrip), active since 2012 and of unconfirmed origin, has been targeting governments, manufacturing, media, and telecommunications organizations in Hong Kong, the Philippines, Taiwan, and Vietnam using a proprietary in-memory backdoor called Sagerunex (evolved from Evora). According to Cisco Talos, the group initiates Windows Management Instrumentation reconnaissance to enumerate user accounts, network configurations, processes, and directory structures, then either installs Sagerunex and ancillary tools when Internet connectivity is available or establishes a proxy via local settings or the “Venom” penetration-testing tool when it is not. Once injected as a DLL, Sagerunex conducts self-checks, beacons to its C2 server, and deploys modules for Chrome cookie theft, privilege escalation, proxy relaying, and file archiving for exfiltration. Notably, two newly discovered Sagerunex variants abuse Dropbox and Twitter APIs or the Zimbra mail API as unconventional C2 channels to evade detection and sustain long-term persistence with command-shell implants. This evolving toolkit underscores a significant threat to regional critical infrastructure and highlights the need for enhanced WMI command logging, in-memory attack detection, and network monitoring for anomalous third-party cloud service traffic to disrupt Lotus Blossom’s espionage operations.

title: PipeMagic Backdoor Resurfaces as Part of Play Ransomware Attack Chain
preprocessed: In August 2025 Microsoft Threat Intelligence revealed that Storm-2460, associated with the Play ransomware group, has resumed exploiting CVE-2025-29824—a zero-day elevation-of-privilege flaw in the Windows Common Log File System patched in April—to gain SYSTEM privileges on unpatched hosts across IT, financial and real estate organizations in the US, Europe, South America and the Middle East. The campaign begins with an in-memory dropper masquerading as the open-source ChatGPT Desktop app that decrypts and launches PipeMagic, a modular backdoor first observed in December 2022 and now updated with persistence and lateral-movement enhancements targeting Saudi Arabian and Brazilian manufacturing entities. PipeMagic communicates with its TCP C2 over a named pipe, self-updates by storing distinct payload modules in memory via doubly linked lists for staging, execution and communication (plus an additional dynamic list), then leverages the CLFS exploit to escalate privileges before deploying Play ransomware. Although the campaign’s footprint remains limited, the combination of a zero-day exploit and a sophisticated modular backdoor underscores a heightened risk; organizations are urged to immediately apply the April patch for CVE-2025-29824, enable tamper and network protection in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, run EDR in block mode, enforce full automated investigation and remediation, and leverage cloud-delivered machine-learning protections to block novel variants.

title: FBI, Cisco Warn of Russian Attacks on 7-Year Flaw
preprocessed: Russian state-linked cyberespionage group “Static Tundra” (aka Energetic Bear/Berserk Bear/Dragonfly) has spent the past year exploiting a seven-year-old Cisco IOS/IOS XE Smart Install vulnerability (CVE-2018-0171, CVSS 9.8) in end-of-life devices to breach thousands of enterprise and critical-infrastructure networks worldwide, harvesting configuration files, manipulating settings to create backdoor accounts, and leveraging stolen SNMP v1/v2 credentials and a SYNful Knock IOS firmware implant for long-term, stealthy access. After Cisco patched the flaw in March 2018, the FSB Center 16 unit automated mass scans of unpatched switches, pivoted into industrial control protocols, and established secondary footholds for potential OT disruption. The FBI and Cisco Talos warn that manufacturing, telecommunications, and higher-education sectors remain at high risk and urge immediate patching or Smart Install disablement, inventory of end-of-life gear, and rigorous configuration management to mitigate further compromise.

title: ESET Research uncovers Operation AkaiRyū: China-aligned MirrorFace targets European diplomats using Expo 2025 as a lure | | ESET
preprocessed: ESET Research uncovered Operation AkaiRyū, a spearphishing-driven cyberespionage campaign conducted by the China-aligned MirrorFace APT (now assessed as a subgroup under the APT10 umbrella) against a Central European diplomatic institute between June and September 2024, using Expo 2025-themed lures referencing prior NGO communications to deliver password-protected Word documents and malicious links; this marks MirrorFace’s first known European targeting. Analysis revealed a significant TTP refresh: the revival of the ANEL (UPPERCUT) backdoor—previously exclusive to APT10—for file manipulation, payload execution and screenshots; a heavily customized AsyncRAT variant stealthily run inside Windows Sandbox via a complex execution chain; continued deployment of the HiddenFace backdoor; and abuse of Visual Studio Code’s remote tunnels for covert access and arbitrary code execution. Attackers abused legitimate McAfee and JustSystems applications to load ANEL, evading detection, while data exfiltration methods remain unclear. ESET’s forensic collaboration with the victim and JSAC presentation in January 2025 provide actionable insights to monitor for ANEL indicators, sandboxed RAT executions, VS Code tunnel anomalies and Expo-themed spearphishing.
