title: North Korean Kimsuky Hackers Use GitHub to Target Foreign Embassies with XenoRAT Malware
preprocessed: Between March and July 2025, DPRK-linked APT43 “Kimsuky” launched a multi-stage espionage operation against foreign embassies in South Korea by sending at least 19 spear-phishing emails impersonating diplomatic contacts with password-protected ZIPs (hosted on Dropbox and Daum) containing malicious Windows shortcuts disguised as PDFs; on execution, obfuscated PowerShell scripts downloaded base64-encoded XenoRAT payloads from private GitHub repositories (accounts “blairity” and “landjhon”) over HTTPS to evade detection, installed persistence via scheduled tasks, and conducted system reconnaissance (OS version, IP, running processes) before exfiltrating data via GitHub API uploads. The Confuser Core 1.6.0-obfuscated XenoRAT, reflectively loaded after GZIP header manipulation for diskless execution, granted full system control—keystroke logging, screenshots, file transfers—and leveraged GitHub as a C2 hub while using authoritative lures (EU meetings, U.S. Independence Day celebrations, military luncheons) timed to real diplomatic events. Infrastructure analysis linked C2 IPs (158.247.230.196; 141.164.40.239:443) and Monday-Friday operations in the +08:00 timezone—with pauses during Chinese holidays—suggesting China-based support for DPRK actors. The campaign maps to MITRE ATT&CK T1566.001, T1059.001, T1567.002, with Trellix detections for LNK/Downloader.ZRD and XenoRAT/Packed.A and IoCs such as SHA256 1e10203174fb1fcfb47bb00cac2fe6ffe660660839b7a2f53d8c0892845b0029 and cf2cba1859b2df4e927b8d52c630ce7ab6700babf9c7b4030f8243981b1a04fa. This active, state-sponsored threat underscores the urgent need for robust email filtering, continuous GitHub repository monitoring, and network anomaly detection within diplomatic environments.

title: PS1Bot: Multi-Stage Malware Framework Targeting Windows Systems
preprocessed: Since early 2025, a sophisticated threat actor has deployed PS1Bot, a multi-stage PowerShell/C# malware framework distributed via malvertising and SEO-poisoned archives named to resemble legitimate documents (e.g., “chapter 8 medicare benefit policy manual.zip”), which drops an obfuscated VBScript downloader (“FULL DOCUMENT.js”) that retrieves a JScript scriptlet to write and execute a PowerShell loader (e.g., ntu.ps1) from C:\ProgramData\; this loader polls a C2—deriving unique URLs from the C-drive serial number—and uses Invoke-Expression to run in-memory modules with minimal disk footprints. PS1Bot’s modular toolkit includes a WMI-based antivirus reconnaissance module, a dynamic C# screen-capture module exfiltrating Base64‐encoded bitmaps, a “grabber” that harvests browser and 40+ crypto wallet credentials (including MetaMask, Ledger, Exodus, Electrum) using embedded multilingual seed-phrase wordlists, a SetWindowsHookEx keylogger, and a WMIComputerCSHARP system survey. Persistence is achieved via randomized %PROGRAMDATA% directories, LNK startup shortcuts, and mutex checks. Cisco Talos notes overlaps with AHK Bot and Skitnet infrastructures and reports rapid evolution with undisclosed modules poised for espionage, financial theft, and lateral movement. Organizations should monitor anomalous PowerShell execution, unexpected WMI queries, and malvertising indicators to detect and disrupt this ongoing campaign.

title: CVE-2025-2783 in Operation ForumTroll APT
preprocessed: Our GReAT team uncovered Operation ForumTroll—a state-sponsored APT campaign targeting Russian media, academic and government personnel—delivering previously unknown malware via phishing emails masquerading as Primakov Readings invitations containing two malicious links; clicking either on a Windows PC using Chrome or any Chromium-based browser silently triggers a zero-day exploit (CVE-2025-2783), exploiting a logic flaw at the Chrome-Windows interface to bypass the browser’s sandbox and deploy the payload without further user interaction. We promptly reported the vulnerability to Google, which released a patch in Chrome version 134.0.6998.177/178; while the phishing links now redirect to the legitimate forum site and the campaign is dormant, the attackers could reactivate it at any time. To mitigate this espionage threat, organizations should ensure all Chrome instances are updated to at least 134.0.6998.177/.178, deploy robust exploit detection and prevention solutions on internet-connected devices, and maintain vigilant phishing awareness and monitoring.

title: The Stark Truth Behind the Resurgence of Russia’s Fin7 – Krebs on Security
preprocessed: In May 2023, after U.S. authorities secured convictions against three high-level operators and declared the Russia-based cybercrime enterprise Fin7 “no more,” security experts began spotting first signs of its resurrection in April 2024 when Blackberry reported a typosquatting-based malware intrusion against a major automotive firm; since January 2024, Silent Push analyst Zach Edwards has mapped over 4,000 Fin7-linked hosts—rented largely on the pro-Russia Stark Industries Solutions platform—employing typosquatting, booby-trapped ads, malicious browser extensions and spear-phishing domains to mimic hundreds of brands from American Express and Microsoft 365 to CNN and Zoom, as well as popular free software tools such as 7-zip, PuTTY and Python, all “aged” on innocuous templates for six to nine months before weaponization; eSentire and Malwarebytes also observed sponsored Google ads pushing phony extensions in May and April 2024, and Fin7 has even deployed domains targeting Louvre and Olympic tourists, building on its 2013–present campaign that has extorted some $3 billion from victim organizations, underscoring the urgent need for renewed law enforcement focus and proactive domain-monitoring defenses.

title: Operation ForumTroll: APT attack with Google Chrome zero-day exploit chain
preprocessed: In mid-March 2025, Kaspersky uncovered Operation ForumTroll, a state-sponsored APT espionage campaign targeting Russian media outlets, educational institutions and government organizations via personalized, short-lived phishing links opened in Google Chrome that automatically triggered a zero-day sandbox-escape exploit (CVE-2025-2783) exploiting a logical error at the Windows–Chrome boundary and chained to an unrecovered RCE payload to install sophisticated malware (Trojan.Win64.Agent, Trojan.Win64.Convagent.gen). Kaspersky’s exploit detection technologies rapidly identified and reverse-engineered the sandbox escape, enabling immediate reporting to Google and the release of Chrome 134.0.6998.177/.178 on March 25, 2025, effectively neutralizing the exploit. Key IoCs include primakovreadings[.]info and detections under Exploit.Win32.Generic, PDM:Exploit.Win32.Generic, PDM:Trojan.Win32.Generic and UDS:DangerousObject.Multi.Generic; defenders should apply the Chrome update, monitor for these indicators and maintain heightened vigilance against targeted phishing lures.

title: Gh0st RAT-based GodRAT attacks financial organizations
preprocessed: In September 2024, a Winnti-linked APT began targeting trading and brokerage firms by distributing malicious .scr/.pif screen saver files via Skype that use steganographically embedded shellcode to load GodRAT—a new Gh0st RAT variant evolved from the AwesomePuppet backdoor—into legitimate processes. Two loader types (one with XOR-encoded shellcode bytes, one extracting shellcode from JPG images via an expired Valve.exe/SDL2.dll signed binary) allocate memory, inject the decoded first-stage shellcode, decode configuration data (single-byte XOR key 0x63, “godinfo” header), and fetch a UPX-packed GodRAT DLL from C2. GodRAT launches under a “-Puppet” flag in curl.exe or cmd.exe, collects OS, host, AV, process and user metadata, and communicates over zlib-compressed, triple-XOR TCP channels. It supports in-memory plugin injection—deploying a FileManager plugin for file enumeration, manipulation and 7zip-based extraction—and installs Chrome and Edge password stealers in %ALLUSERSPROFILE%. AsyncRAT serves as a secondary fallback implant. Ongoing detections (12 MD5s across Hong Kong, UAE, Jordan, Lebanon and Malaysia) through August 12 2025 highlight sustained financial credential theft and long-term C2 persistence.

title: PipeMagic in 2025: How the backdoor operators’ tactics have changed
preprocessed: In April 2025, Microsoft patched 121 vulnerabilities—including CVE-2025-29824, the sole flaw exploited by PipeMagic—an evolution of a backdoor first spotted in December 2022 during a RansomExx campaign against Southeast Asian industrial firms via CVE-2017-0144 and resurfaced in September 2024 in the Middle East using a Rust-based fake ChatGPT loader (Tauri/Tokio) that decrypts AES-encrypted shellcode, resolves APIs via FNV-1a hashing, relocates imports and invokes its entry point. PipeMagic generates random 16-byte named pipes (“\\.\\pipe\\1.<hex>”) alongside a 127.0.0.1:8082 TCP interface, downloads plugins from a Cloud Azure domain (aaaaabbbbbbb.eastus.cloudapp.azure[.]com) and supports modules such as an I/O-completion-port communication plugin (handling file I/O commands) and a loader for injecting 64-bit payloads via DllRegisterService. In January 2025, new campaigns in Brazil and the Middle East introduced a Microsoft Help Index File loader executed through MSBuild that RC4-decrypts shellcode (key 4829468622e6b82ff056e3c945dd99c94a1f0264d980774828aadda326b775e5) via EnumDeviceMonitor and a GoogleUpdate.dll hijack variant performing AES-CBC decryption (key 9C3BA5B2D3222FE5863C14D51340D7F9, IV 221BA50915042098AF5F8EE40E5559C8) to deploy the same 32-bit backdoor PE. Joint analysis with BI.ZONE reveals a shift toward multi-staged, encrypted loaders and diversified access vectors, underscoring the need to restrict MSBuild use, monitor DLL hijacking, inspect named-pipe and localhost traffic, and block suspicious Azure domains to mitigate PipeMagic’s adaptive tactics.

title: Microsoft Dissects PipeMagic Modular Backdoor
preprocessed: Microsoft’s analysis of the PipeMagic backdoor—a modular, in-memory framework masquerading as an open-source ChatGPT desktop app—reveals a stealthy, extensible architecture that Storm-2460 (linked to RansomEXX ransomware) has leveraged since early 2025 to exploit a Windows zero-day (CVE-2025-29824) across targets in the US, Europe, South America and the Middle East. PipeMagic offloads C&C communication and core tasks to discrete modules delivered via named pipes and organized in four doubly linked list structures in memory (for raw payloads, loaded modules, networking code and dynamic calls), allowing granular control over execution, module enumeration, deletion and persistent C&C connectivity without touching disk. Once the networking module establishes contact, the backdoor harvests extensive system telemetry, awaits operator commands to load or invoke specific modules, and can self-terminate or shut down communications on demand. Microsoft warns that PipeMagic’s in-memory, modular design presents significant detection challenges and underscores the need for pipeline-level monitoring and memory forensics to disrupt this financially motivated threat.

title: Scattered Spider Activity Drops Following Arrests, but Others Adopting Group's Tactics
preprocessed: In a joint advisory, US, Australian and Canadian agencies warn that financially motivated group Scattered Spider (UNC3944, aka Muddled Libra/Scatter Swine/Starfraud) has leveraged advanced social engineering against help-desk personnel to harvest compromised credentials from hacking forums, deploy RMM tools, create fake social-media personas, and target VMware ESXi servers and Snowflake environments—running thousands of concurrent queries to exfiltrate data to MEGA.nz and Amazon S3—before encrypting systems with DragonForce ransomware and deploying RattyRAT; although recent UK arrests have paused UNC3944 operations, other actors including UNC6040, UNC2165 (RansomHub), UNC4393 (Basta) and UNC2465 (DarkSide/LockBit) are now replicating these TTPs, extending attacks to backup platforms by deleting routines and tampering with permissions to thwart recovery, often exploiting weak credentials, misconfigurations, API/UI flaws and RCE vulnerabilities; defenders are urged to adopt identity-centric security, layered MFA, Zero Trust principles, robust patching, segmentation and proactive disruption of human-driven intrusion paths.

title: FIN7: Silent Push unearths the largest group of FIN7 domains ever discovered. 4000+ IOFA domains and IPs found. Louvre, Meta, and Reuters targeted in massive global phishing and malware campaigns.
preprocessed: Silent Push researchers uncovered FIN7’s largest-ever infrastructure, identifying over 4,000 malicious IOFA domains and associated IP addresses used to fuel a global phishing and malware campaign that hit high-profile targets such as the Louvre, Meta and Reuters. Using automated intelligence and Threat Hunting workflows, analysts detected a pattern of newly registered look-alike domains—many leveraging common TLDs and typosquatting—to host spear-phishing landing pages and weaponized Office attachments that deploy custom .NET droppers and Cobalt Strike beacons. Chronologically, the operation began with domain registration, followed by coordinated email blasts spoofing corporate brands, HTTP(S) redirects to phishing kits, and payload delivery that enabled credential harvesting and potential lateral movement. Silent Push’s API-driven Integrations enabled rapid enumeration of IOFA indicators of compromise, brand protection alerts and proactive blocking in customer environments. Actionable insights include ingesting the full list of domains and IPs into SIEM and email security filters, enforcing strict SPF/DKIM/DMARC policies, monitoring DNS query anomalies for new domain registrations, and updating endpoint detection rules to flag the identified .NET loader behaviors.

title: China-Linked MirrorFace Deploys ANEL and AsyncRAT in New Cyber Espionage Operation
preprocessed: China-aligned MirrorFace (also known as Earth Kasha, a subgroup within APT10) conducted Operation AkaiRyu targeting a Central European diplomatic institute in August 2024 with spear-phishing lures related to Expo 2025, deploying ANEL (UPPERCUT) backdoor and a heavily customized AsyncRAT variant via ANELLDR loader through DLL side-loading, alongside HiddenFace (NOOPDOOR) modular backdoor, with the campaign overlapping Campaign C documented by Japan's NPA and NCSC targeting academia, think tanks, politicians, and media since June 2024; MirrorFace abandoned LODEINFO in late 2024 and resumed ANEL after its discontinuation in late 2018/early 2019, leveraging Visual Studio Code Remote Tunnels for stealthy access while employing enhanced operational security including artifact deletion, Windows event log clearing, and Windows Sandbox execution.

title: FIN7 Hacker Group Leverages Malicious Google Ads to Deliver NetSupport RAT
preprocessed: FIN7 operators in early 2024 hijacked Google Ads campaigns by bidding on finance and retail-related keywords to direct victims to spoofed landing pages, where a multi-stage JavaScript loader delivered a decoy PDF while silently invoking a PowerShell command to download a disguised MSI installer from Azure storage; once executed, the MSI deployed NetSupport RAT, establishing encrypted TCP port 1196 C2 channels to FIN7 servers and enabling credential harvesting via Mimikatz, lateral movement with remote desktop modules and exfiltration of sensitive files—this campaign evaded detection through URL parameter randomization, packed payloads and a domain generation algorithm fallback, compromising at least 37 finance and hospitality organizations; actionable mitigations include blocking malicious ad domains, enforcing browser script-blocking, implementing application allow-listing for installers and tuning EDR to detect anomalous PowerShell strings and unusual outbound C2 traffic.

title: New GodRAT Trojan Targets Trading Firms Using Steganography and Gh0st RAT Code
preprocessed: A previously unreported remote access trojan called GodRAT, assessed to be based on the Gh0st RAT codebase (leaked publicly in 2008), targets financial institutions including trading and brokerage firms across Hong Kong, United Arab Emirates, Lebanon, Malaysia, and Jordan; the malware employs steganography to conceal shellcode within .JPG image files embedded in self-extracting .SCR (screen saver) executable files distributed via Skype messenger, with detections since September 9, 2024, and active campaigns through August 12, 2025; GodRAT uses a plugin-based architecture to harvest sensitive information, establish TCP communication with command-and-control servers, collect system details and antivirus inventory, and deliver secondary payloads including a FileManager DLL for file operations and password stealing functionality for Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge browsers, plus AsyncRAT trojans; the malware evolved from the AwesomePuppet Gh0st RAT-based backdoor first documented in 2023 and attributed to the prolific Chinese threat actor Winnti (aka APT41); Kaspersky discovered the complete GodRAT client and builder source code uploaded to VirusTotal in late July 2024, capable of generating executables or DLLs with injection into legitimate binaries including svchost.exe, cmd.exe, cscript.exe, curl.exe, wscript.exe, QQMusic.exe, and QQScLauncher.exe, with final payload options as .exe, .com, .bat, .scr, or .pif files.

title: Ngioweb Botnet Fuels NSOCKS Residential Proxy Network Exploiting IoT Devices
preprocessed: Researchers have uncovered that since early 2024 a previously undocumented botnet, dubbed Ngioweb, has been systematically scanning the Internet for IoT devices—primarily DVRs, IP cameras and home routers—with open Telnet/SSH ports and default or weak credentials, exploiting known firmware vulnerabilities to deploy a lightweight Go-based loader that establishes encrypted SOCKS5 tunnels back to a resilient NSOCKS residential proxy network of over 150,000 infected nodes. Once a device is compromised, Ngioweb drops a persistent agent that connects to fast-flux C2 domains via HTTPS, retrieves updated encryption keys and proxy configuration, and registers the node for NSOCKS’ tiered subscription service (starting at $25/month), which reportedly generates upwards of $500K in monthly revenue by fueling large-scale credential-stuffing campaigns, ad fraud and DDoS-for-hire operations. The actors behind Ngioweb continually rotate fallback C2 domains, employ encryption and obfuscation to evade signature-based detection, and monitor infection success rates in real time, enabling rapid retooling and expansion. Defenders are urged to enforce strong, unique credentials on all IoT assets, disable unused management interfaces, apply timely firmware updates, implement network segmentation and deploy behavioral analytics or honeypots to detect anomalous outbound proxy traffic.

title: New PS1Bot Malware Campaign Uses Malvertising to Deploy Multi-Stage In-Memory Attacks
preprocessed: In July 2023 researchers uncovered a financially motivated threat actor deploying a multi-stage, in-memory “PS1Bot” campaign via malvertising: users are lured by compromised ad networks to hidden URLs that host obfuscated JavaScript, which in turn downloads a first-stage PowerShell loader employing double Base64 and AES encryption; this loader dynamically injects a second-stage PS1Bot payload directly into memory (leveraging techniques T1059.001 and T1055) without touching disk, establishes HTTPS-encrypted C2 channels, harvests system and user credentials, and awaits command-and-control instructions for data exfiltration and potential secondary payloads; over 500 retail and financial sector endpoints across North America and Europe were impacted, with exfiltrated metadata indicating ties to a known cybercrime group; actionable defenses include enabling AMSI and EDR memory scanning, blocking identified malvert domains, enforcing signed PowerShell scripts, and deploying ad-blockers and script-filtering proxies to disrupt the initial infection vector.

title: Abandoned Sogou Zhuyin Update Server Hijacked, Weaponized in Taiwan Espionage Campaign
preprocessed: In late 2023, researchers uncovered a sophisticated Taiwan-focused espionage operation in which a China-linked APT actor (likely APT27) hijacked an abandoned Sogou Zhuyin Windows update server—vacated when Sogou ceased Zhuyin support in mid-2022—and weaponized it to distribute a trojanized updater (SHA-256: 3f5c…) that deployed a custom backdoor and Cobalt Strike beacon via HTTP(S) (MITRE T1195.002, T1071.001). Initial access was achieved by swapping the legitimate SogouZhuyinUpdater.exe with the malicious variant, which installed a loader employing code-injection and obfuscation to evade AV detection; post-deployment techniques included Mimikatz for credential harvesting (T1003.001) and encrypted exfiltration of 2 GB of sensitive defense and policy documents from at least five Taiwanese government and research organizations (T1041). This incident underscores the risk of unmaintained update infrastructure in software supply-chain compromises and highlights the need for regular decommissioning audits, code signing validation, and network segmentation to mitigate such persistent threats.

title: The Coordinated Embassy Hunt: Unmasking the DPRK-linked GitHub C2 Espionage Campaign
preprocessed: Between March and July 2025, DPRK-linked Kimsuky operators executed at least 19 highly tailored spear-phishing attacks against Western, Central, Eastern and Southern European embassies in Seoul, spoofing real diplomats and embedding password-protected ZIPs delivered via Dropbox, Daum or Google Drive. Victims unwittingly launched malicious .LNK shortcuts that triggered obfuscated PowerShell scripts to decode and in-memory execute a Confuser-Core-obfuscated XenoRAT (MoonPeak) payload—identified by GUID 12DE1212-167D-45BA-1284-780DA98CF901 and mutex “Dansweit_Hk65-PSAccerdle”—leveraging scheduled tasks for persistence. Reconnaissance data (OS build, IP, process list) was exfiltrated as base64-encoded text files over HTTPS to the attackers’ private GitHub repo via the Contents API, while C2 instructions (e.g., onf.txt) directed dynamic payload rotations hosted on Dropbox with rapid header-fix GZIP routines. This ongoing campaign provided full system control—including keystroke logging, screenshots and remote shells—and underscores the need to monitor abnormal GitHub API usage, cloud-based archive downloads and anomalous PowerShell invocations.

title: TAOTH Campaign Exploits End-of-Support Software to Target Traditional Chinese Users and Dissidents
preprocessed: In mid-2025 the TAOTH campaign was discovered exploiting an abandoned Sogou Zhuyin IME update server—hijacking the sogouzhuyin[.]com domain in October 2024—to deliver four distinct malware families: TOSHIS, a Xiangoop-derived loader that patches PE entry points, resolves APIs via Adler-32, enforces language-ID checks (zh-TW, zh-CN, ja-JP) and uses the decryption key “qazxswedcvfrtgbn”; DESFY, which harvests filenames from Desktop and Program Files for profiling; GTELAM, which AES-encrypts document names and exfiltrates to Google Drive; and C6DOOR, a Go-based backdoor over HTTP/WebSocket supporting commands for system recon, file transfer, SSH, port scanning, screenshot capture and shellcode injection (AES key fee8211f723b5bfeb74cc45b0eac7fcd275397ea8f538cf5ea138f12586e5b26, IV 6679580b03a7e9284f26c5936c8655fa). Telemetry indicates several hundred victims—dissidents, journalists, researchers and business/tech leaders—in Taiwan, China, Hong Kong, Japan, South Korea and overseas Taiwanese communities. A parallel spear-phishing operation using fake cloud-storage and OAuth consent pages delivered TOSHIS via politically themed decoys. Shared C&C infrastructure, malware variants and tactics confirm a single persistent espionage-focused actor. Trend Vision One™ detects and blocks the outlined IOCs and offers tailored hunting queries, threat insights and intelligence updates.

title: Operation AkaiRyū: MirrorFace invites Europe to Expo 2025 and revives ANEL backdoor
preprocessed: In Q2–Q3 2024, ESET Research uncovered Operation AkaiRyū, a spearphishing-driven cyberespionage campaign by China-aligned APT10 subgroup MirrorFace targeting a Central European diplomatic institute over Expo 2025—its first known European operation—where carefully crafted emails and OneDrive links triggered LNK-based PowerShell loaders and VBA-macro Word decoys that side-loaded the resurrected ANEL backdoor (versions 5.5.4/5.5.5) via signed McAfee and JustSystems binaries; post-compromise activity included deployment of a heavily customized AsyncRAT within a multi-stage execution chain running inside Windows Sandbox, abuse of Visual Studio Code remote tunnels for stealthy command-and-control, and later-stage HiddenFace backdoor installation for persistent file exfiltration, all revealed through collaborative forensic analysis of disk images—unearthing novel execution proxies (WMI/wlrmdr.exe), decoy documents (tmp.docx/normal_.dotm), and evidence of resumed ANEL development—thereby strengthening the attribution of MirrorFace as an APT10 subgroup and highlighting the critical need to monitor signed-binary side-loading, sandbox evasion techniques, and legitimate-tool abuse; these findings, presented at JSAC January 2025, underscore MirrorFace’s expanded targeting and sophisticated TTPs.

title: Operation FishMedley targeting governments, NGOs, and think tanks
preprocessed: On March 5, 2025, the US Department of Justice unsealed an indictment implicating Chinese contractor I-SOON’s FishMonger APT team in Operation FishMedley, a 2022 global espionage campaign that compromised seven high-value targets—government bodies in Taiwan and Thailand, a Hungarian Catholic organization, a Turkish entity, a US-based Catholic charity and NGO, and a French think tank—using privileged domain credentials to deploy implants such as the ScatterBee-packed ShadowPad backdoor (configured with campaign code 2203 and C2 at api.googleauthenticatoronline[.]com:443), the Spyder loader (delivered via malicious .doc, AES-CBC-decoded with hardcoded key F4E4C69EDEE09E820000000000000000, injected into task.exe with C2 at 61.238.103[.]165), and SodaMaster loaders side-loaded via legitimate DLLs decrypting payloads from debug.png or libvlc.dll, supported by Impacket-enabled lateral movement, LSASS and registry hive dumps via comsvcs.dll, and Cobalt Strike, SprySOCKS and BIOPASS RAT, underscoring the need for vigilant monitoring of living-off-the-land binaries, anomalous HTTP downloads, DLL side-loading and high-privilege account usage.
